topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: The Berlin Wall falls: end of a bipolar world
topics.h: For 28 years a concrete wall cut one city in two. On a November night in 1989, ordinary Berliners climbed it with hammers, and an entire world order began to crack.
p: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961 to separate communist East Berlin from capitalist West Berlin. It became the most visible symbol of the Cold War divide between the two blocs.
In November 1989 crowds broke down the Wall. Its fall is remembered as the moment the Cold War began to end.
The two parts of Germany were unified in 1990, and in 1991 the Soviet Union itself broke up.
Bipolar world: two superpowers (USA and USSR) and their blocs dominate world politics. Unipolar world: a single superpower dominates.
The disintegration of the USSR ended the bipolar system and left the USA as the only superpower.

ex.q: Arrange and explain: Why do textbooks treat the fall of the Berlin Wall as the start of the end of bipolarity?
st: The Wall (1961) physically divided a city between the two rival blocs.
Its fall (November 1989) showed that people in the Soviet bloc were rejecting communist rule.
Germany reunified in 1990, removing the front line of the Cold War in Europe.
The USSR broke up in 1991, so only one superpower remained.
ex.a: Because the Wall was the symbol of the two-bloc divide, its fall marked the collapse of that divide, completed by the Soviet break-up in 1991.

topics.rl: Pieces of the Berlin Wall are displayed in many countries as reminders that walls built by politics can fall. India itself had to rethink its foreign policy after 1991, when its old partner, the USSR, disappeared.

rv.summary: The Berlin Wall (built 1961) symbolised the Cold War divide; its fall in November 1989 began the end of the bipolar world, completed when the USSR broke up in 1991, leaving the USA as the only superpower.
focus: Dates: Wall built 1961, fell November 1989, Germany unified 1990, USSR broke up 1991
Meaning of bipolar and unipolar world
Why the Soviet break-up ended bipolarity
remember: Berlin Wall separated communist East Berlin from capitalist West Berlin
Bipolar: two superpowers (USA and USSR) and their blocs dominate
Unipolar: a single superpower dominates
traps: Don't confuse the year the Wall was built (1961) with the year it fell (1989).
The Wall was within Berlin, not a national border.
The Wall's fall alone did not end bipolarity; the USSR's break-up in 1991 did.

topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: What was the Soviet system?
topics.h: Imagine a country where the state owns every factory and farm, there is no unemployment, and one party runs everything. That was the Soviet Union for over 70 years.
p: The USSR (Union of Soviet Socialist Republics) came into being after the socialist revolution in Russia in 1917, led by the Bolsheviks. It was inspired by socialist ideals and aimed at an egalitarian society.

After the Second World War, the East European countries freed by the Soviet army came under its control. This group was called the Second World or the socialist bloc, and the Warsaw Pact was its military alliance.
Key features: state ownership and control of productive assets, a centrally planned economy, and the dominance of the Communist Party, with no other parties allowed.
Achievements: the USSR became a great power with a strong industrial base, large energy resources, a vast communications network and a powerful military.
The state ensured a minimum standard of living: subsidised health, education and childcare, and no unemployment.

ex.q: Classify: Which of these are features of the Soviet system? (a) Many competing parties (b) State ownership of productive assets (c) Central planning (d) Free market prices
st: Many competing parties: no, only the Communist Party was allowed.
State ownership of productive assets: yes.
Central planning: yes, the state planned production.
Free market prices: no, the state controlled the economy.
ex.a: (b) and (c)

topics.rl: India's Planning Commission (1950) drew some inspiration from Soviet-style planning, though India kept democracy and a mixed economy. Steel plants like Bhilai were built with Soviet help.

rv.summary: The USSR arose from the 1917 Bolshevik revolution. Its system had state ownership, central planning and one-party rule; it became a great power and guaranteed a minimum standard of living.
focus: Features of the Soviet political and economic system
Second World and the Warsaw Pact
remember: USSR formed after the socialist revolution of 1917, led by the Bolsheviks
Second World = socialist bloc; Warsaw Pact = its military alliance
Features: state ownership, centrally planned economy, Communist Party dominance
traps: The Soviet system did not allow multi-party competition.
Welfare provision does not mean democracy.
The Warsaw Pact was the Soviet alliance; NATO was the Western one.

topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: Cracks in the system and Gorbachev's reforms
topics.h: The USSR could launch rockets into space, yet shoppers queued for hours for bread and shoes. By the 1980s, something had to give.
p: The system became bureaucratic and authoritarian. There was no freedom of speech, and the one-party rule of the Communist Party was not accountable to the people.
The USSR fell behind the West in technology and infrastructure (for example, computers), and consumer goods were scarce.
Russia dominated the other republics, and people in other regions felt neglected and suppressed.
The arms race with the US and the cost of supporting satellite states drained resources. The 1979 intervention in Afghanistan weakened the system further.
Mikhail Gorbachev became General Secretary of the Communist Party in 1985. His reforms were perestroika (restructuring of the economy) and glasnost (openness, more freedom of expression).

ex.q: A newspaper in 1987 Moscow prints open criticism of the government for the first time. Which reform does this reflect, and why?
st: Perestroika means restructuring the economy.
Glasnost means openness: more freedom to speak and publish.
Open criticism in a newspaper is about freedom of expression.
ex.a: Glasnost

topics.rl: Like a company that keeps old machines too long, the Soviet economy lost out in the computer age. Indian IT firms grew in the 1990s precisely when that technology gap had become huge.

rv.summary: The Soviet system became bureaucratic and authoritarian, lagged in technology and consumer goods, and was drained by the arms race and Afghanistan (1979). Gorbachev (1985) launched perestroika and glasnost.
remember: Gorbachev became General Secretary in 1985
Perestroika = restructuring of the economy
Glasnost = openness, more freedom of expression
traps: Don't swap perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness).
The USSR had no unemployment and a strong military; its weakness was lack of democracy.
Gorbachev wanted to reform the system, not end it.

topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: 1989 to 1991: the Soviet Union comes apart
topics.h: In August 1991 tanks rolled into Moscow to stop reform. Within four months the country those tanks belonged to no longer existed.
p: In 1989 people in East European countries (part of the Soviet bloc) rose up and overthrew their communist governments. The USSR did not intervene.

In 1991 a coup was attempted by Communist Party hardliners who opposed the reforms. It failed, and Boris Yeltsin, who had won a popular election as President of Russia, emerged as a national hero by opposing it.
In December 1991, under Yeltsin's leadership, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus (three major republics) declared that the USSR was dissolved. The Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) was formed.
Russia was accepted as the successor state of the USSR. It inherited the Soviet seat as a permanent member of the UN Security Council and took over the USSR's international treaties and commitments.

ex.q: Order these events: (a) Hardliners' coup fails (b) Gorbachev comes to power (c) East European communist governments fall (d) USSR dissolved, CIS formed
st: (b) 1985: Gorbachev comes to power.
(c) 1989: East European communist regimes fall.
(a) 1991 (August): coup attempt fails.
(d) December 1991: USSR dissolved and CIS formed.
ex.a: b, c, a, d

topics.rl: When a company is broken up, one unit usually keeps the brand and the seat on industry bodies. Russia did the same with the USSR's UN Security Council seat.

rv.summary: In 1989 East Europeans overthrew communist governments; in 1991 a hardliners' coup failed and Yeltsin emerged a hero. In December 1991 Russia, Ukraine and Belarus dissolved the USSR and formed the CIS; Russia became the successor state.
focus: Sequence of events from 1985 to December 1991
Role of Yeltsin and the failed coup
remember: Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declared the USSR dissolved in December 1991
CIS = Commonwealth of Independent States
Russia inherited the USSR's UN Security Council seat and treaties
traps: The coup came from hardliners, not reformers.
The Baltic states did not make the December 1991 declaration.
Yeltsin, not Gorbachev, became the hero of the coup's failure.

topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: Why did the Soviet Union disintegrate?
topics.h: A superpower with nuclear weapons and a huge army collapsed without losing a war. Explaining why is one of the favourite long answers in the board exam.
p: Internal weaknesses of political and economic institutions failed to meet people's aspirations. This is the most common explanation.
Economic stagnation over many years caused severe consumer shortages. The arms race and the cost of the satellite states in Eastern Europe and the Central Asian republics drained resources.
As information spread, ordinary citizens realised how far the USSR lagged behind the West. Gorbachev's reforms raised expectations but could not satisfy them quickly.
Gorbachev was opposed from both sides: reformers felt he was too slow, while Communist Party members and hardliners felt he was destroying the system.

Nationalism and the desire for sovereignty grew in the republics. It was strongest in the European and relatively prosperous parts, such as the Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania), Ukraine and Georgia.

ex.q: A board question asks for two economic and one political reason for the Soviet collapse. Build the answer.
st: Economic 1: long stagnation leading to consumer shortages.
Economic 2: huge spending on the arms race and on satellite states.
Political: a rigid, unaccountable one-party system, and rising nationalism in the republics.
ex.a: Stagnation and shortages; cost of the arms race and satellite states; an authoritarian system facing nationalist demands

topics.rl: Just as a cricket team can lose when the dressing room splits into camps, Gorbachev lost support from both the reformers and the old guard at the same time.

rv.summary: The USSR collapsed mainly from internal weaknesses: stagnation and shortages, the cost of the arms race and satellite states, reforms that raised unmet expectations, and nationalism strongest in the Baltic states, Ukraine and Georgia.
focus: Economic and political causes of the collapse
remember: Most common explanation: internal weaknesses of political and economic institutions
Baltic states: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania
Gorbachev was opposed by both reformers and hardliners
traps: The USSR was not defeated militarily.
Don't mix economic causes (stagnation, shortages) with political ones (nationalism, no free speech).
The late Soviet economy was stagnating, not the world's most productive.

topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: Consequences of the Soviet disintegration
topics.h: In 1991 the world map gained fifteen countries, lost a superpower and changed its economic rulebook almost overnight.
p: The Cold War confrontation ended. The ideological dispute between capitalism and socialism, and with it the arms race, came to an end.
Power relations changed: the USA became the sole superpower, giving a unipolar world. Some saw this as the triumph of capitalism.
Capitalism and liberal democracy became the dominant models. The World Bank and IMF became powerful advisers to many countries.
New countries emerged: the Baltic states, East European countries and Central Asian republics. Many East European and Baltic states sought to join the European Union and NATO.

ex.q: Identify the consequence: 'After 1991, advisers from the IMF and World Bank shaped the economic policies of many post-communist states.'
st: This is about which economic model spread.
It shows capitalism becoming dominant and the growing influence of global financial institutions.
ex.a: Dominance of capitalism and greater influence of the IMF and World Bank

topics.rl: The 1991 shift reached India too: with the USSR gone and a balance of payments crisis at home, India launched its own economic reforms the same year.

rv.summary: The Soviet collapse ended the Cold War and the arms race, left the USA as sole superpower, made capitalism and liberal democracy dominant with the World Bank and IMF as advisers, and created new states.
focus: New states and their wish to join the EU and NATO
remember: End of the ideological dispute and the arms race
USA became the sole superpower: unipolar world
World Bank and IMF became powerful advisers
traps: Don't list earlier Cold War events as consequences.
Russia did not become an equal superpower after 1991.

topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: Shock therapy: the overnight switch
topics.h: Picture switching a whole country's economy from 'the state owns everything' to 'the market decides' in a few months. Russia tried exactly that in the 1990s.
p: Shock therapy was the model of sudden transition from an authoritarian socialist system to a democratic capitalist system, adopted in Russia, Central Asia and Eastern Europe.
It was influenced by the World Bank and the IMF. Private ownership was to be the main pattern of ownership of property.

Its elements were privatisation of state assets, corporate ownership patterns, collective farms replaced by private farming, free trade, foreign direct investment, financial openness and currency convertibility.
It also broke up the old trade alliances of the Soviet bloc and redirected trade towards the West.

The privatisation was called 'the largest garage sale in history', because valuable state industries were sold to private individuals and companies at very low prices, often far below their real value.

ex.q: Which of these is NOT part of shock therapy? (a) privatisation (b) currency convertibility (c) stronger collective farms (d) free trade
st: Shock therapy replaced collective farms with private farming.
So strengthening collective farms goes against it.
Privatisation, convertibility and free trade are all elements.
ex.a: (c) stronger collective farms

topics.rl: India chose gradual reform after 1991, opening sectors step by step. Comparing India's path with Russia's shock therapy is a classic debate in economics and political science classes.

rv.summary: Shock therapy was the sudden switch from authoritarian socialism to democratic capitalism, influenced by the World Bank and IMF, with privatisation, free trade, currency convertibility and private farming.
remember: Private ownership became the main pattern of property
Elements: privatisation, collective farms replaced by private farming, free trade, FDI, currency convertibility
Trade was redirected towards the West
traps: Shock therapy was sudden, not gradual.
It did not strengthen collective farms.
'Garage sale' means state industries were sold at very low prices.

topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: Consequences of shock therapy
topics.h: Imagine your family's lifetime savings losing almost all their value within months. For millions in 1990s Russia, that was not a nightmare but the morning news.
p: The value of the rouble, the Russian currency, declined dramatically. High inflation wiped out people's savings.
The collective farm system disintegrated, leaving people without food security, and Russia began to import food. The old trading structure broke down without an alternative.
The old system of social welfare was destroyed. Withdrawal of government subsidies pushed many into poverty, the middle class was pushed to the margins, and many intellectuals migrated.
A mafia emerged and controlled many economic activities. Privatisation created new disparities, and inequality between rich and poor grew sharply.
Democratic institutions were built in a hurry: most countries got a strong executive president and a weak parliament, and the judicial culture and independence were not established.

ex.q: A pensioner in Moscow in 1993 finds that the savings that once bought a car now buy only a few loaves of bread. Which consequence of shock therapy explains this?
st: Shock therapy freed prices and the currency.
The rouble fell steeply and inflation soared.
Savings held in roubles lost their value.
ex.a: Fall in the value of the rouble and high inflation

topics.rl: India's own welfare safety nets, such as the public distribution system for food, show why the sudden loss of the Soviet welfare system hurt so many people.

rv.summary: Shock therapy caused a dramatic fall of the rouble and inflation, loss of food security, collapse of welfare, a mafia and growing inequality, and hastily built institutions with strong presidents and weak parliaments.
focus: Economic and social consequences of shock therapy
remember: Rouble declined dramatically; inflation wiped out savings
Collective farms disintegrated; Russia began importing food
Strong executive president, weak parliament, no judicial independence
traps: Market reform did not reduce inequality at once; it widened it.
Judicial independence was not established.

topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: Tensions and conflicts after the break-up
topics.h: The Cold War ended, but peace did not arrive everywhere. Across the former communist world, new borders sparked new wars.
p: In Russia, Chechnya and Dagestan saw violent secessionist movements. Moscow's response, including military bombings, led to serious human rights violations.
Yugoslavia broke apart into several provinces after 1991. Ethnic conflict followed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Kosovo NATO intervened with bombing of Yugoslavia in 1999.
Tajikistan suffered a civil war that went on for about ten years, until 2001.
In Azerbaijan, local Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh wanted to separate and join Armenia. In Georgia, two provinces demanded independence.
Central Asia's rich hydrocarbon (oil and gas) reserves attracted competition among outside powers, including Russia, China and the USA, and the region became a zone of rivalry.

ex.q: Match each conflict to its country: Chechnya, Nagorno-Karabakh, Kosovo.
st: Chechnya: secessionist movement inside Russia.
Nagorno-Karabakh: region in Azerbaijan claimed by local Armenians.
Kosovo: province of the former Yugoslavia, where NATO intervened.
ex.a: Chechnya - Russia; Nagorno-Karabakh - Azerbaijan; Kosovo - former Yugoslavia

topics.rl: India buys oil and gas from many regions to keep fuel flowing for its railways, vehicles and power plants. That is why Central Asia's energy wealth matters to New Delhi too.

rv.summary: After the break-up, conflicts broke out: secessionism in Chechnya and Dagestan, the break-up of Yugoslavia with conflict in Bosnia and NATO bombing over Kosovo (1999), Tajikistan's civil war, Nagorno-Karabakh, and rivalry over Central Asian oil and gas.
focus: Why Central Asia became a zone of rivalry
remember: Chechnya and Dagestan: inside Russia
Nagorno-Karabakh: region in Azerbaijan claimed by local Armenians
Kosovo: NATO bombed Yugoslavia in 1999; Tajikistan civil war till 2001
traps: Kosovo and Bosnia are in former Yugoslavia, not the former USSR.
The end of the Cold War did not bring peace everywhere.

topics.ch: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity
topics.t: India and the post-communist countries
topics.h: Generations of Indians grew up with Russian picture books and Soviet-built steel plants, while Russians hummed Raj Kapoor's songs. That friendship had to be rebuilt after 1991.
p: During the Cold War India and the USSR were close: the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation was signed in August 1971. The USSR backed India on Kashmir at the UN and helped with steel plants, defence equipment and culture.

India has kept good relations with all post-communist countries, and its strongest ties are with Russia. The two share a vision of a multipolar world: several powers coexisting, collective security, negotiated settlement of disputes and decision-making through bodies like the UN.

More than 80 agreements were signed under the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement of 2001. India is one of the biggest buyers of Russian arms, and Russia has helped India's nuclear energy and space programmes.
For India, Russia matters for its stand on Kashmir, energy supplies, sharing information on terrorism, access to Central Asia, and balancing relations with China.
India also builds ties with energy-rich Central Asian states such as Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, to diversify its energy sources and improve connectivity.

ex.q: Exam-style: List two reasons why Russia is important for India and one reason why India is important for Russia.
st: Russia for India: support on Kashmir; energy supplies.
Also: access to Central Asia, intelligence on terrorism, balancing ties with China.
India for Russia: one of the largest markets for Russian arms.
ex.a: Kashmir support and energy for India; a big arms market for Russia

topics.rl: Fighter jets of the Indian Air Force, the Kudankulam nuclear power plant in Tamil Nadu and joint space work all show how deep India-Russia cooperation runs.

rv.summary: India and the USSR were close during the Cold War (1971 treaty). India keeps good ties with all post-communist states, strongest with Russia, sharing a multipolar vision; Russia supplies arms and energy and helps on Kashmir and Central Asia.
focus: Why Russia matters to India and India to Russia
remember: Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation: August 1971
Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement 2001: over 80 agreements
India is one of the biggest buyers of Russian arms
traps: Don't confuse the 1971 treaty with the 2001 Strategic Agreement.
India backs a multipolar, not unipolar, world.
Two true related facts are not always cause and effect.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power
topics.t: New centres of power and the roots of European unity
topics.h: After 1991 one superpower stood tall. Yet regional groupings and fast-growing economies began building their own power, and Europe led the way.
p: After the Cold War, regional organisations (such as the EU and ASEAN) and rising states (such as China) emerged as alternative centres of political and economic power, limiting US dominance.
These centres draw their influence mainly from economic strength and from regional cooperation that turns neighbours from rivals into partners.

After the Second World War, Europe's economies were ruined. Under the Marshall Plan, the USA gave massive financial help, and the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC) was set up in 1948 to channel this aid.
The Council of Europe was set up in 1949, another step in political cooperation among European states.
Cooperation began with economics: the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) linked six western European countries.

ex.q: Why did the OEEC matter for European integration?
st: It was created in 1948 to distribute Marshall Plan aid.
To get aid, western European states had to sit together and coordinate trade and economic issues.
This habit of working together laid the base for later bodies like the EEC.
ex.a: It made western European states cooperate on economic matters, paving the way for integration

topics.rl: India's own push for regional groupings, from SAARC to BIMSTEC, comes from the same idea: economic cooperation can build political trust among neighbours.

rv.summary: After the Cold War, regional groups like the EU and ASEAN and rising states like China became alternative centres of power, drawing influence from economic strength and cooperation. European unity began with the Marshall Plan, OEEC (1948), Council of Europe (1949) and ECSC (1951).
focus: What alternative centres of power are and where their power comes from
Early steps of European cooperation and their dates
remember: OEEC (1948) channelled Marshall Plan aid
Council of Europe: 1949
European Coal and Steel Community (1951): six countries
traps: The Marshall Plan was American, not Soviet.
The OEEC was an economic body, not a military alliance.
New centres of power rest on economics, not only military might.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power
topics.t: From the EEC to the European Union
topics.h: A German student can study in Spain, pay in euros and travel to France without showing a passport. That everyday freedom grew out of decades of treaties.
p: The Treaty of Rome (1957) set up the European Economic Community (EEC). Over time it deepened economic and political cooperation.
The European Union (EU) was established by the Maastricht Treaty, signed in 1992. It moved from an economic union towards a political one.
The EU set up a single market, a common foreign and security policy, cooperation on justice and home affairs, and a single currency.
The euro was introduced in 2002 as notes and coins in twelve member states, and is used by many EU members.
Like a state, the EU has its own flag, anthem, founding date and currency. Its flag is a circle of twelve gold stars on a blue background, standing for unity and harmony among the peoples of Europe.

ex.q: Order these milestones: euro notes and coins introduced; Treaty of Rome sets up the EEC; Maastricht Treaty creates the EU.
st: Treaty of Rome: 1957.
Maastricht Treaty: 1992.
Euro notes and coins: 2002.

topics.rl: Indian tourists and students in Europe often need just one Schengen visa and one currency to cross many borders, a direct result of EU integration.

rv.summary: The Treaty of Rome (1957) set up the EEC; the Maastricht Treaty (1992) created the EU, moving towards political union with a single market, common foreign policy and the euro (notes and coins 2002). The EU has state-like symbols.
focus: Order of EEC, EU and euro milestones
What the EU has set up
remember: Treaty of Rome 1957 → EEC; Maastricht 1992 → EU; euro cash 2002
EU flag: circle of twelve gold stars on blue
The EU has its own flag, anthem, founding date and currency
traps: The flag always has twelve stars; they do not count members.
The EU has no single army replacing national armies.
Don't confuse the OEEC (1948) with the EEC (1957).

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power
topics.t: The EU as a power and its limits
topics.h: The EU can block a merger between two American tech giants, yet its members still argue over whether to send soldiers abroad. That is power with limits.
p: Economic power: the EU is one of the largest economies in the world, and its currency, the euro, can rival the US dollar. Its share of world trade is very large.

Political and diplomatic power: France, an EU member, is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, and several EU members serve as non-permanent members. The EU influences the US and others on trade and climate.
Military power: the combined armed forces of EU members are among the largest in the world, and France is a nuclear power. The EU is also strong in space and communication technology.
Limits: members keep their own foreign and defence policies and often disagree. There is Euroscepticism, as some people resist giving more power to the EU.
In 2016 the UK voted in a referendum to leave the EU, and it formally left in 2020 (Brexit).

ex.q: Classify each as economic, political or military power of the EU: euro rivals the dollar; France has a UNSC permanent seat; France is a nuclear power.
st: Euro rivalling the dollar: economic.
UNSC permanent seat: political/diplomatic.
Nuclear weapons: military.
ex.a: Economic; political; military

topics.rl: When the EU negotiates a trade deal with India, it bargains as one bloc of many economies. That is why the India-EU free trade talks are so closely watched in Indian markets.

rv.summary: The EU is a great economic power (euro rivals the dollar), has political weight (France holds a permanent UNSC seat) and military strength (large combined forces, French nuclear power), but members keep separate foreign and defence policies; Euroscepticism and Brexit show its limits.
focus: Classify EU power as economic, political or military
Limits of the EU as a power
remember: France is the EU's permanent UNSC member
Euroscepticism = resistance to more EU power
UK referendum 2016; formally left 2020
traps: Don't confuse the referendum year (2016) with the exit year (2020).
The EU does not have a foreign policy that all members always obey.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power
topics.t: ASEAN and the ASEAN Way
topics.h: In 1967 five nervous neighbours in Southeast Asia signed a short declaration in Bangkok. Decades later their group is among the most important regional bodies in Asia.
p: ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) was set up in 1967 by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, by signing the Bangkok Declaration. Others such as Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia joined later.
Its aims: speed up economic growth, social progress and cultural development, and promote regional peace and stability based on the rule of law and the UN Charter.
The 'ASEAN Way' is a style of working that is informal, non-confrontational and cooperative, and that respects national sovereignty.
In 2003 ASEAN agreed to set up an ASEAN Community with three pillars: the ASEAN Security Community, the ASEAN Economic Community and the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community.
The ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF), set up in 1994, carries out coordination on security and foreign policy.

ex.q: Name the three pillars of the ASEAN Community agreed in 2003.
st: Pillar 1: Security Community (peace, settling disputes without armed conflict).
Pillar 2: Economic Community (common market and production base).
Pillar 3: Socio-Cultural Community.
ex.a: Security, Economic and Socio-Cultural Communities

topics.rl: Indian leaders attend ASEAN summits regularly, and Indian classical arts and Ramayana traditions are celebrated across Thailand, Indonesia and Cambodia, linking cultures as well as trade.

rv.summary: ASEAN was founded in 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration by five states to promote growth and regional peace. The ASEAN Way is informal and respects sovereignty; in 2003 it agreed a Community with security, economic and socio-cultural pillars, and the ARF (1994) handles security.
focus: Founders and founding document of ASEAN
Three pillars of the ASEAN Community
remember: Founders: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand
Three pillars: Security, Economic, Socio-Cultural Communities
ASEAN Regional Forum: 1994
traps: Vietnam was not a founder.
There is no ASEAN military alliance pillar.
ASEAN is not supranational like the EU.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power
topics.t: ASEAN's economy and India's Look East policy
topics.h: Many cars, phones and garments you buy carry parts made across Southeast Asia. ASEAN's economic engine is humming right in India's neighbourhood.
p: ASEAN is one of the fastest-growing regions in the world. Its economic community aims at a common market and production base and aids social and economic development.
The ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) and the ASEAN Investment Area aim to lower trade barriers and attract investment.
ASEAN Vision 2020 set out an outward-looking role for ASEAN in the international community, building on its policy of encouraging negotiation over conflict.

In the early 1990s (usually dated to 1991, under the P.V. Narasimha Rao government) India adopted a Look East policy to strengthen ties with Southeast Asia, signed free trade agreements with Singapore and Thailand, and later an ASEAN-India free trade agreement. Since 2014 this has been carried forward as the Act East policy.
ASEAN's economic and strategic importance makes it an attractive partner for China, Japan, the USA and India.

ex.q: Why did India turn its foreign policy towards ASEAN in the 1990s?
st: After 1991 India opened its economy and sought new trade partners.
ASEAN was a fast-growing economic region next door.
Closer ties could bring trade, investment and strategic balance.
ex.a: To gain from ASEAN's fast-growing economy through trade, investment and strategic ties (Look East policy)

topics.rl: India's North-Eastern states, such as Manipur and Mizoram, are seen as India's gateway to Southeast Asia, which is why road and port projects towards Myanmar matter under the Act East policy.

rv.summary: ASEAN is one of the fastest-growing regions, with AFTA and an Investment Area to cut barriers and Vision 2020 for an outward role. India's Look East policy (1991), carried forward as Act East (2014), built trade ties including FTAs with Singapore and Thailand.
focus: India's Look East and Act East policies
remember: AFTA = ASEAN Free Trade Area
Look East from 1991; Act East since 2014
Early FTAs with Singapore and Thailand
traps: Don't confuse the start of Look East (1991) with Act East (2014).
ASEAN has no single currency like the euro.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power
topics.t: China's road to reform
topics.h: In 1978 China was poorer than India on many measures. A generation later it was the world's factory. The turnaround began with one leader's decision to open the door.
p: After the communist revolution of 1949 under Mao Zedong, China followed the Soviet model: state-owned heavy industries were built using capital from agriculture, and China cut off links with the capitalist world.

This model gave limited growth: industrial production did not grow fast enough, agricultural output was too low to support industry, and foreign trade was minimal. In 1973 Zhou Enlai proposed four modernisations: agriculture, industry, science and technology, and the military.
In 1978 Deng Xiaoping announced the 'open door' policy, aiming to generate higher productivity by inviting foreign capital and technology.
China did not use shock therapy; it opened up step by step. Agriculture was privatised in 1982 and industry in 1998.
Special Economic Zones (SEZs) were set up where foreign investors could set up businesses, and trade barriers were eased there first.

ex.q: Compare: How did China's reform path differ from Russia's shock therapy?
st: Russia: sudden, all-at-once switch to capitalism in the 1990s.
China: gradual opening from 1978 — agriculture privatised in 1982, industry in 1998, SEZs first.
China kept its political system while changing the economy step by step.
ex.a: China reformed gradually and in stages, while Russia used sudden shock therapy

topics.rl: India copied the SEZ idea in its own SEZ Act of 2005, and export hubs in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu show the same logic of special zones for investors.

rv.summary: After 1949 China followed the Soviet model with limited growth. Zhou Enlai proposed four modernisations (1973) and Deng Xiaoping's open door policy (1978) opened China step by step: agriculture privatised 1982, industry 1998, with SEZs.
focus: China's early Soviet-style model and its limits
Open door policy and gradual reforms
How China differed from shock therapy
remember: Deng Xiaoping: open door, 1978
Agriculture privatised 1982; industry 1998
Four modernisations: agriculture, industry, science and technology, military
traps: Mao did not launch the open door policy.
China did not use shock therapy; it reformed gradually.
Don't swap the order of farm (1982) and industry (1998) privatisation.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power
topics.t: China as a global economic power: gains and problems
topics.h: From toys to solar panels to smartphones, 'Made in China' is everywhere. But growth at that speed came with a bill.
p: China joined the World Trade Organisation in 2001, further opening its economy to the world. Foreign trade and investment grew rapidly.
China became a huge economy and a major destination for foreign direct investment, with large foreign exchange reserves.
Problems: not everyone benefited. There was unemployment, environmental degradation, corruption and rising inequality between rural and urban areas and between coastal and inland regions.

China's economic weight increased its regional and global influence. It built economic ties with its neighbours, including ASEAN states, Japan and South Korea, and its trade with the USA and India grew.

ex.q: Sort into gains and problems of China's reforms: foreign investment; inequality between coast and inland; WTO entry; environmental damage.
st: Gains: foreign investment, WTO entry (integration into world trade).
Problems: regional inequality, environmental damage.
ex.a: Gains: investment, WTO entry; Problems: inequality, pollution

topics.rl: Indian cities like Delhi face air-quality crises too; China's experience shows how fast industrial growth can come at a heavy environmental cost if not managed.

rv.summary: China joined the WTO in 2001 and became a huge economy and investment destination, raising its regional and global influence, but reforms brought unemployment, pollution, corruption and inequality between coast and inland.
remember: China joined the WTO in 2001
Coastal areas gained more than inland and rural areas
China is a major destination for foreign investment
traps: Reforms did not reduce inequality; they widened it.
China did not suffer a shortage of foreign investment.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power
topics.t: India and China: rivalry and cooperation
topics.h: Buddhist monks carried ideas across the Himalayas two thousand years ago. In 1962 soldiers fought on those same mountains. India-China ties have swung between both extremes.
p: India and China had old cultural and economic links, such as the spread of Buddhism and trade along routes across Asia. After independence, relations began warmly with the slogan 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'.
The military conflict of 1962 over a border dispute damaged relations badly. Full diplomatic relations were restored only in 1976.
Rajiv Gandhi's visit to China in December 1988 began a process of normalisation. Both sides agreed to work on the border issue through talks and to expand other ties.
Trade between India and China has grown very fast, and they cooperate in many multilateral forums, such as on trade talks and climate change.
Differences remain over the border, China's close ties with Pakistan, and competition for influence in the region.

ex.q: Put these in order: Rajiv Gandhi visits China; India-China war; full diplomatic relations restored.
st: 1962: India-China war.
1976: full diplomatic relations restored.
1988: Rajiv Gandhi's visit.

topics.rl: Many electronics parts used by Indian startups and phone makers are imported from China, while India pushes 'Make in India' to reduce this dependence. Cooperation and rivalry run side by side.

rv.summary: India and China had old links and warm 1950s ties ('Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'), damaged by the 1962 war. Relations were restored in 1976, normalisation began with Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit, and today they mix fast-growing trade and cooperation with border disputes and rivalry.
focus: Order of key events in India–China relations
Areas of cooperation and of friction
remember: 1962 war; 1976 full relations restored; 1988 Rajiv Gandhi visit
Friction: border, China–Pakistan ties, regional rivalry
Cooperation: trade and multilateral forums
traps: Don't confuse 1976 (relations restored) with 1988 (Rajiv Gandhi's visit).
Cooperation does not mean the border dispute is settled.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power
topics.t: Japan and South Korea as emerging powers
topics.h: Your family car might be a Suzuki or Hyundai, your TV a Sony or Samsung. Two East Asian nations built global brands from post-war ruins.
p: Japan has few natural resources and imports most raw materials, yet it became a leading economic and technological power, with brands like Sony, Panasonic, Canon, Toyota, Honda and Suzuki. It is a member of the G-7 (formerly G-8).

Japan is the only country to have suffered nuclear bombing (Hiroshima and Nagasaki, 1945). Article 9 of its Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right, so its military role is limited. Japan is one of the largest contributors to the UN budget.

South Korea grew rapidly from the 1960s to the 1980s. This rise is called the 'Miracle on the Han River'. Factors included land reform, rural development, investment in human resources and rapid industrialisation.
South Korea joined the OECD in 1996 and is a member of the G-20. Its global brands include Samsung, LG and Hyundai.
Comparing centres of power: the EU and ASEAN are regional groups that pool members' strength, while China, Japan and South Korea are individual states that rose through economic growth.

ex.q: Board-style: Give two reasons why Japan is considered an important centre of power.
st: Economic and technological strength with global brands, despite few natural resources.
Major contributor to the UN budget and member of the G-7.
(Its military role is limited by Article 9.)
ex.a: Strong technology-based economy; major UN funder and G-7 member

topics.rl: Japan has funded the Delhi Metro and the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project, while Korean firms like Hyundai and Samsung run big factories in Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh.

rv.summary: Japan, with few natural resources, became a leading technological economy and big UN funder, with a military limited by Article 9. South Korea's rapid rise, the 'Miracle on the Han River', came from land reform, human resources and industrialisation; it joined the OECD in 1996.
focus: Why Japan is a centre of power
How states differ from regional unions as centres of power
remember: Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right
Japan: only country to suffer nuclear bombing (1945)
South Korea joined the OECD in 1996
traps: The 'Miracle on the Han River' is South Korea, not Japan.
Economic power does not need natural resources.
Japan is a single state, the EU a regional union.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary South Asia
topics.t: What is South Asia?
topics.h: One mountain range, one ocean, and around a quarter of humanity in between. South Asia is a region of shared geography but very different political systems.
p: South Asia usually includes Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Afghanistan and Myanmar are often included in discussions of the region.
Geography gives the region a natural unity: the Himalayas in the north, the Indian Ocean, the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal to the south, west and east.

Politically the region is very diverse: India and Sri Lanka have kept democratic systems since independence, Pakistan and Bangladesh have alternated between civilian and military rule, Nepal moved from monarchy to a republic, and Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy.

Map work: Islamabad (Pakistan), Dhaka (Bangladesh), Kathmandu (Nepal), Thimphu (Bhutan), Malé (the Maldives), New Delhi (India), Kabul (Afghanistan). Sri Lanka's official capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, with Colombo as its commercial capital.

ex.q: A map question asks you to mark the capitals of three Himalayan neighbours of India. Name them.
st: Nepal: Kathmandu.
Bhutan: Thimphu.
Pakistan: Islamabad (its north lies in the Himalaya-Karakoram region).
ex.a: Kathmandu, Thimphu, Islamabad

topics.rl: The monsoon that waters Indian farms also feeds rivers flowing through Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh. Shared rivers and weather tie the region together.

rv.summary: South Asia's core is Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, often with Afghanistan and Myanmar. The Himalayas and the seas give it geographic unity, but its political systems are diverse.
focus: Countries and capitals of South Asia
remember: Thimphu (Bhutan), Kathmandu (Nepal), Malé (Maldives), Dhaka, Islamabad, Kabul
Sri Lanka: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte official, Colombo commercial
Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy; Nepal is now a republic
traps: Indonesia is Southeast Asia, not South Asia.
Don't mix up Thimphu and Kathmandu.
Bhutan is not a republic.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary South Asia
topics.t: The military and democracy in Pakistan
topics.h: Pakistan's history reads like a relay race between generals and elected leaders, with the baton changing hands again and again.
p: After Pakistan framed its first constitution, General Ayub Khan took over in 1958 and soon got himself elected. Popular dissatisfaction forced him out, and General Yahya Khan took over in 1969.

After the 1971 war, an elected government under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto ruled from 1971 to 1977. General Zia-ul-Haq removed it in 1977. A pro-democracy movement led to an elected government under Benazir Bhutto in 1988.

Elected governments of Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif followed. In 1999 the army under General Pervez Musharraf took over again. Since 2008 elected civilian governments have ruled, but the army keeps great influence.

Reasons for weak democracy: the social dominance of the military, the clergy and the landowning aristocracy; conflict with India strengthening pro-military groups; and support for military rule from the USA and others during the Cold War.

ex.q: Order these leaders in Pakistan's history: Zia-ul-Haq, Ayub Khan, Pervez Musharraf, Benazir Bhutto.
st: Ayub Khan: took over in 1958.
Zia-ul-Haq: took over in 1977.
Benazir Bhutto: elected in 1988.
Pervez Musharraf: took over in 1999.
ex.a: Ayub Khan → Zia-ul-Haq → Benazir Bhutto → Pervez Musharraf

topics.rl: When Indian and Pakistani teams meet at cricket, commentators often note how differently the two countries' institutions evolved after 1947, even though both started from the same colonial system.

rv.summary: Pakistan swung between military and civilian rule: Ayub Khan (1958), Yahya Khan (1969), Bhutto (1971–77), Zia (1977), Benazir Bhutto (1988), Musharraf (1999), civilians since 2008. Democracy stayed weak due to dominant elites, conflict with India and Cold War outside support.
focus: Reasons democracy did not take root
remember: Ayub 1958 → Zia 1977 → Benazir 1988 → Musharraf 1999
Military, clergy and landowning aristocracy dominate society
The army keeps great influence even under elected governments
traps: Zia, not Yahya Khan, removed Bhutto in 1977.
Benazir Bhutto (1988) came before Nawaz Sharif.
Elections alone have not removed military influence.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary South Asia
topics.t: Democracy in Bangladesh
topics.h: In 1971 a people won a war to protect their language and their vote. Building a stable democracy afterwards proved just as hard as winning freedom.
p: From 1947 to 1971, Bangladesh was East Pakistan. Its people resented domination by West Pakistan and the imposition of Urdu. Sheikh Mujibur Rahman of the Awami League led the struggle for autonomy.

In the 1970 elections, the Awami League won almost all the seats in East Pakistan (160 of 162), giving it a majority in the proposed Constituent Assembly. The West Pakistan leadership refused to accept this, and the army under General Yahya Khan cracked down and arrested Sheikh Mujib.
Millions fled to India as refugees. India supported the freedom struggle, and after war in December 1971, Bangladesh became independent.

Bangladesh's constitution declared it secular, democratic and socialist. In 1975 Sheikh Mujib changed it to a presidential system and abolished all parties except the Awami League; he was assassinated that year in a military uprising.

Military-led rule followed (Ziaur Rahman, then H.M. Ershad). A mass protest movement forced Ershad to step down in 1990, and since 1991 Bangladesh has had a representative democracy with multi-party elections.

ex.q: Order: Ershad steps down; Bangladesh becomes independent; Awami League wins 1970 elections; Sheikh Mujib assassinated.
st: 1970: Awami League sweeps elections in East Pakistan.
1971: independence after war.
1975: Sheikh Mujib assassinated.
1990: Ershad steps down after mass protests.

topics.rl: Bangladesh's garment factories now dress the world, and India and Bangladesh share rail, road and power links. The two countries share a history from 1971.

rv.summary: East Pakistan resented West Pakistan's domination and Urdu imposition. The Awami League under Sheikh Mujib swept the 1970 polls and, with India's support, Bangladesh became free in 1971. Military-led rule followed 1975; multi-party democracy since 1991.
focus: Causes of the Bangladesh freedom struggle
remember: Awami League won 160 of 162 East Pakistan seats in 1970
1975: presidential system, one party; Mujib assassinated
Ershad stepped down 1990; democracy since 1991
traps: Bangladesh did have military-led rule (Ziaur Rahman, Ershad).
Don't confuse independence (1971) with democracy restored (1991).
India supported the struggle; it did not annex the region.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary South Asia
topics.t: Monarchy and democracy in Nepal
topics.h: In 2008 a country with one of the world's oldest ruling dynasties voted to abolish its monarchy. Nepal's path from king to republic took decades of protest.
p: Nepal was a Hindu kingdom in the past, and then a constitutional monarchy for many years in the modern period.
A strong pro-democracy movement in 1990 forced the king to accept a new democratic constitution. Democratic governments that followed were short-lived and troubled.
In the 1990s the Maoists, who opposed the monarchy and the ruling elite, built an armed insurgency in many parts of Nepal. In 2002 the king abolished the parliament and dismissed the government.
In April 2006 massive, country-wide pro-democracy protests by the Seven-Party Alliance (SPA), the Maoists and social activists forced the king to restore the House of Representatives.
In 2008 Nepal abolished the monarchy and became a democratic republic. A new Constitution was adopted in 2015.

ex.q: Order these milestones in Nepal: monarchy abolished; king accepts democratic constitution after protests; new Constitution adopted; king restores parliament after mass protests.
st: 1990: king accepts a democratic constitution.
2006: king restores the House of Representatives.
2008: monarchy abolished.
2015: new Constitution.

topics.rl: India and Nepal share an open border; millions of Nepali citizens work in India and many have served in the Indian Army's Gorkha regiments, so Nepal's political changes are followed closely in India.

rv.summary: Nepal moved from monarchy towards democracy: a 1990 democratic constitution, a Maoist insurgency, the king dissolving parliament in 2002, the 2006 movement restoring it, the monarchy abolished in 2008 and a new Constitution in 2015.
focus: Role of the Maoists and the 2006 movement
remember: 1990 democratic constitution; 2006 House restored
2008 monarchy abolished, republic formed
2015 new Constitution
traps: Don't confuse 2008 (republic) with 2015 (Constitution).
The 2006 movement restored parliament; it did not itself end the monarchy.
Democracy after 1990 was not stable.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary South Asia
topics.t: Ethnic conflict and democracy in Sri Lanka
topics.h: Sri Lanka has kept holding elections since 1948, yet for over two decades it also fought one of Asia's longest civil wars.
p: Sri Lanka has remained a democracy since independence in 1948, but faced a serious ethnic conflict. Sinhala nationalists believed Sri Lanka should belong to the Sinhala majority and resisted concessions to the Tamil minority.

Neglect of Tamil concerns led to militant Tamil nationalism. From 1983 the LTTE (Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam) fought an armed struggle against the army, demanding 'Tamil Eelam', a separate country for Sri Lankan Tamils.

In 1987 India signed an accord with Sri Lanka and sent the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) to help stabilise the situation. The IPKF got into fighting with the LTTE, and the move was unpopular among many Sri Lankans and Tamils in India. The IPKF was withdrawn without achieving its aim.
The conflict ended in 2009 when the LTTE was defeated by the Sri Lankan army.

Despite the conflict, Sri Lanka recorded considerable economic growth and high levels of human development. It was one of the first developing countries to control population growth and the first in the region to liberalise its economy.

ex.q: Explain why the LTTE demanded Tamil Eelam.
st: Sinhala majority nationalism dominated politics after 1948.
Tamil concerns were neglected, causing alienation.
Militant Tamil groups, led by the LTTE from 1983, demanded a separate country, Tamil Eelam.
ex.a: Because of Sinhala majoritarianism and neglect of Tamil concerns

topics.rl: Tamil Nadu and northern Sri Lanka are separated only by the narrow Palk Strait, which is why events in Sri Lanka have always drawn strong interest in Indian politics.

rv.summary: Sri Lanka stayed democratic since 1948 but Sinhala majoritarianism and neglect of Tamils led to the LTTE's armed struggle for Tamil Eelam from 1983. India's IPKF (1987) was unpopular and withdrawn; the LTTE was defeated in 2009. Sri Lanka still achieved high human development.
remember: LTTE = Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam
IPKF sent in 1987; LTTE defeated in 2009
First in the region to liberalise its economy
traps: The IPKF fought the LTTE; it did not support it.
The war did not create Tamil Eelam.
The conflict does not explain why democracy survived.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary South Asia
topics.t: India-Pakistan conflicts
topics.h: Two countries born on the same night in 1947 have fought several wars, share rivers, and in 1998 both declared themselves nuclear powers.
p: Kashmir has been the core issue between India and Pakistan since Partition. They fought wars in 1947-48 and 1965. In 1971 war broke out over East Pakistan, leading to Bangladesh. In 1999 they fought the Kargil conflict.
Other disputes include control of the Siachen glacier and the boundary line in Sir Creek, a strip of water in the Rann of Kutch.
River waters: the Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960, with the World Bank's mediation, to share the waters of the Indus river system.
Both countries tested nuclear devices in 1998 (India in May, Pakistan soon after). This intensified an arms race between them.
India has accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism and militant groups, while the two sides have also tried confidence-building measures and dialogue at times.

ex.q: List three non-Kashmir disputes between India and Pakistan.
st: Siachen glacier.
Sir Creek in the Rann of Kutch.
Sharing of river waters (Indus system).
ex.a: Siachen, Sir Creek, river waters

topics.rl: Farmers in Punjab depend on the Indus river system, which is why the 1960 water treaty matters as much to agriculture as to diplomacy.

rv.summary: Kashmir is the core India–Pakistan issue, with wars in 1947–48, 1965, 1971 and Kargil in 1999. Other disputes are Siachen, Sir Creek and river waters (Indus Waters Treaty 1960, World Bank). Both tested nuclear devices in 1998.
focus: Wars and disputes between India and Pakistan
remember: Indus Waters Treaty: 1960, mediated by the World Bank
Sir Creek: boundary in the Rann of Kutch; Siachen: glacier
Nuclear tests 1998; Kargil 1999
traps: Don't confuse Kargil (1999) with the nuclear tests (1998).
Sir Creek is not the Siachen glacier.
The Indus treaty was World Bank-mediated, not Soviet.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary South Asia
topics.t: India and its other neighbours
topics.h: When a coup attempt shook the Maldives in 1988, Indian paratroopers arrived within hours. India's ties with its smaller neighbours mix help, friction and deep connections.
p: India-Bangladesh: differences over sharing the waters of the Ganga and Brahmaputra, illegal migration into India and border management. They also cooperate on trade, energy, disaster management and connectivity, and Bangladesh is part of India's Look East policy.

India-Nepal: a treaty allows citizens of both countries to travel and work in each other's country without visas and passports. Friction has arisen over Nepal's ties with China, trade and the Maoist movement, yet economic, scientific and cultural ties remain strong.
India-Sri Lanka: the Tamil issue and the IPKF strained ties, but relations have improved. A free trade agreement was signed, and India helped Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami.
India-Bhutan: a very close relationship. India supports hydroelectric projects in Bhutan, and Bhutan's king helped flush out guerrillas from north-eastern India operating from Bhutanese territory.
India-Maldives: in 1988, when mercenaries attacked the Maldives, India's air force and navy responded quickly at the Maldives' request (Operation Cactus).

ex.q: Which neighbour fits each clue: (a) open border, no visa needed (b) hydroelectric partner (c) Operation Cactus (1988)?
st: (a) Nepal: open border by treaty.
(b) Bhutan: India supports hydro projects.
(c) Maldives: India foiled the 1988 coup attempt.
ex.a: Nepal, Bhutan, Maldives

topics.rl: Electricity from Bhutan's hydro plants lights homes in eastern India, and Nepali workers are a familiar part of many Indian cities.

rv.summary: India has mixed ties with neighbours: water, migration and border issues with Bangladesh; an open border with Nepal despite friction over China and Maoists; improved ties and an FTA with Sri Lanka; very close ties and hydro projects with Bhutan; Operation Cactus for the Maldives (1988).
focus: Key issues and cooperation with each neighbour
remember: Nepal: travel and work without visas
Bhutan: hydroelectric cooperation
Maldives: Operation Cactus, 1988
traps: Operation Cactus was the Maldives, not the IPKF in Sri Lanka.
Disputes do not rule out cooperation.

topics.ch: World Politics: Contemporary South Asia
topics.t: SAARC, SAFTA and outside powers
topics.h: South Asia is home to a huge share of the world's people, yet trade among its countries remains small. SAARC was meant to change that.
p: The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) was set up in 1985 by the South Asian states to cooperate by peaceful means. Afghanistan later joined, and its secretariat is in Kathmandu.
Members signed the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) agreement in 2004, aiming to lower trade barriers across the region. It came into effect in 2006.
Some neighbours feared SAFTA would let India dominate their markets, while India's small neighbours also saw benefits from its large market.
SAARC's progress has been limited mainly by India-Pakistan tensions and political differences among members.

Outside powers matter in South Asia: China has close strategic ties with Pakistan and growing links with other neighbours, and the USA has become an important player, keeping good relations with both India and Pakistan. Comparing democracy across states and evaluating SAARC are common exercise themes.

ex.q: Evaluate SAARC in two points: one achievement and one limitation.
st: Achievement: SAFTA (2004) as a step towards regional free trade.
Limitation: progress held back by India-Pakistan tensions.
ex.a: SAFTA was achieved, but India-Pakistan tensions limit SAARC

topics.rl: Students from all eight SAARC countries study at the South Asian University in New Delhi, set up by SAARC states, showing cooperation beyond trade.

rv.summary: SAARC (1985) promotes peaceful regional cooperation; members signed SAFTA in 2004 (in effect 2006) to lower trade barriers, though some feared India's dominance. India–Pakistan tensions limit SAARC; China and the USA are important outside powers.
focus: SAARC and SAFTA dates and aims
remember: SAARC 1985; secretariat in Kathmandu
SAFTA signed 2004, in effect 2006
China has close strategic ties with Pakistan
traps: Don't confuse SAFTA signing (2004) with its start (2006).
SAARC was formed by South Asian states, not ASEAN.

topics.ch: World Politics: International Organisations
topics.t: Why international organisations? The birth of the UN
topics.h: Climate change, pandemics and wars do not stop at borders. Countries need a common table where they can talk before they fight. That table is the United Nations.
p: International organisations help countries cooperate on issues of war and peace and on shared problems such as disease, poverty and the environment. They are not a world government; they work through the cooperation of member states.
They provide rules, a forum for discussion and information, which make collective action easier and cheaper. They can also help resolve disputes before they become wars.
The League of Nations, set up after the First World War, failed to prevent the Second World War. The United Nations was founded in 1945 as its successor, and 51 states signed the UN Charter.
The UN's main aims are to prevent international conflict and to foster cooperation among states for social and economic development.
The UN has 193 member states today, making it the most important international organisation.

ex.q: Why did the world create the UN in 1945 when the League of Nations already existed?
st: The League had failed to prevent the Second World War.
The war's destruction convinced states they needed a stronger body.
So the UN was set up in 1945 as the League's successor, to prevent conflict and promote cooperation.
ex.a: Because the League of Nations had failed to prevent the Second World War

topics.rl: Indian Army peacekeepers serve under the blue UN flag in Africa and the Middle East, a direct example of countries working together through an international organisation.

rv.summary: International organisations help states cooperate on war, peace and shared problems through rules, forums and information; they are not a world government. The UN was founded in 1945 by 51 states as successor to the failed League of Nations and now has 193 members.
focus: Why and when the UN was founded
remember: UN founded 1945; 51 states signed the Charter
193 members today
Aims: prevent international conflict and foster cooperation
traps: Don't confuse 51 founding members with 193 today.
The UN is not a world government and cannot guarantee peace.

topics.ch: World Politics: International Organisations
topics.t: Principal organs of the UN and the Security Council
topics.h: Five countries can stop any big UN decision with a single word: 'No'. That word is the veto, and it sits at the heart of the Security Council.
p: The UN has six principal organs: the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), the International Court of Justice, the Secretariat and the Trusteeship Council.

The General Assembly includes all members, each with one vote. ECOSOC deals with economic and social issues. The International Court of Justice at The Hague settles legal disputes between states. The Trusteeship Council has suspended its operations.

The Security Council is responsible for international peace and security. It has 15 members: 5 permanent members (USA, Russia, UK, France, China) and 10 non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms.
The permanent members (P5) have the veto: a negative vote by any one of them blocks a substantive decision, even if all others agree. Non-permanent members do not have the veto.

ex.q: A resolution in the Security Council gets 14 'yes' votes and 1 'no' vote from France. Does it pass?
st: France is a permanent member.
A 'no' from a permanent member is a veto.
A veto blocks a substantive resolution regardless of other votes.
ex.a: No. France's negative vote is a veto

topics.rl: India has served many terms as a non-permanent member of the Security Council, most recently in 2021-22, but has no veto, which is why it campaigns for a permanent seat.

rv.summary: The UN has six principal organs. The Security Council keeps peace with 15 members: 5 permanent members (USA, Russia, UK, France, China) with the veto and 10 non-permanent members elected for two years.
focus: The six principal organs and their roles
remember: P5: USA, Russia, UK, France, China
10 non-permanent members, two-year terms; total 15
ICJ at The Hague; Trusteeship Council suspended
traps: Germany is not a permanent member.
One P5 'no' vetoes a resolution even with 14 'yes' votes.
Non-permanent members have no veto.

topics.ch: World Politics: International Organisations
topics.t: The Secretary-General and UN agencies
topics.h: Childhood vaccines, refugee camps, heritage sites like the Taj Mahal: the UN family touches daily life in ways most people never notice.
p: The Secretary-General heads the Secretariat and is the chief administrative officer and representative of the UN. The Secretary-General is appointed by the General Assembly on the Security Council's recommendation.

Secretaries-General in order: Trygve Lie (Norway), Dag Hammarskjöld (Sweden), U Thant (Burma, now Myanmar), Kurt Waldheim (Austria), Javier Pérez de Cuéllar (Peru), Boutros Boutros-Ghali (Egypt), Kofi Annan (Ghana), Ban Ki-moon (South Korea), António Guterres (Portugal, from 2017).
WHO (World Health Organisation) works for good health for all. UNDP (UN Development Programme) supports development. UNICEF (UN Children's Fund) protects children's rights and welfare.

UNESCO (UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) works on education, science and culture, including World Heritage Sites. UNHCR (UN High Commissioner for Refugees) protects refugees. UNHRC (UN Human Rights Council) monitors human rights.

ex.q: A town in India hosts a polio vaccination drive, and a nearby fort is named a World Heritage Site. Which UN agencies are involved?
st: Health and vaccination: WHO (with UNICEF supporting child immunisation).
World Heritage Sites: UNESCO.
ex.a: WHO (and UNICEF) for vaccines; UNESCO for heritage

topics.rl: India's victory over polio, declared in 2014, was achieved with support from WHO and UNICEF. Many Indian monuments, from Hampi to the Sundarbans, are on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

rv.summary: The Secretary-General heads the Secretariat and is appointed by the General Assembly on the Security Council's recommendation. Agencies include WHO, UNDP, UNICEF, UNESCO, UNHCR and UNHRC.
focus: Match UN agencies to their work
remember: Trygve Lie (Norway) first; U Thant (Burma); Kofi Annan (Ghana); Guterres (Portugal, from 2017)
UNESCO: education, science, culture, World Heritage Sites
UNHCR: refugees; UNHRC: human rights
traps: Don't confuse UNHCR (refugees) with UNHRC (human rights).
Don't mix up Annan (Ghana) and Boutros-Ghali (Egypt).

topics.ch: World Politics: International Organisations
topics.t: Why reform the UN? Expanding the Security Council
topics.h: The Security Council's permanent members were fixed in 1945, when many of today's members were still colonies. Should a council designed for 1945 still run the world?
p: After the Cold War, calls for reform grew: membership had risen from 51 to 193, the world had become unipolar, and new challenges such as terrorism, civil wars and climate change had emerged.

Reform has two parts: reform of the organisation's structures and processes, and a review of the issues within its jurisdiction. Most agree the Security Council's structure should change, especially by adding members.

In 1992 the General Assembly adopted a resolution reflecting complaints that the Security Council no longer represented contemporary political realities, that its decisions reflected only Western values and interests, and that it lacked equitable representation.

Criteria proposed for new permanent members include being a major economic power, a major military power, a substantial contributor to the UN budget, a big nation in terms of population, a nation that respects democracy and human rights, and a country that would make the Council more representative in geography, economic systems and culture.
Each criterion is debated: for example, how big an economy or how large a population is 'enough'. The future of the veto is also debated.

ex.q: A country has a large population and respects democracy but is not a major military power. Can it fully meet the proposed criteria?
st: Criteria include economy, military, budget contribution, population, democracy and representativeness.
It meets population and democracy.
It does not meet the military criterion, so it meets only some criteria; each one is debated.
ex.a: Only partly; it meets some criteria but not all

topics.rl: Debates on Security Council reform often feature India, Brazil, Germany and Japan, the 'G4' who support each other's claims to permanent seats.

rv.summary: After the Cold War, larger membership, unipolarity and new challenges led to calls for UN reform of structures and jurisdiction. The 1992 resolution said the Security Council did not reflect current realities; criteria for new permanent members are proposed but debated.
focus: Proposed criteria for new permanent members
remember: Membership grew from 51 to 193
Criteria: economic and military power, budget contribution, population, democracy, representativeness
1992 resolution: Council lacks equitable representation
traps: The criteria are debated, not agreed by all.
Reform is about structures and issues, not symbols.

topics.ch: World Politics: International Organisations
topics.t: Reforming the UN's jurisdiction: the 2005 decisions
topics.h: In 2005, at its 60th birthday, the UN made a list of promises. Some created new bodies that still work today.
p: Jurisdiction reform asks which issues the UN should deal with: peace and security (including peacekeeping), terrorism, human rights, climate change, poverty and development.
In September 2005, world leaders met to mark the UN's 60th anniversary and agreed on steps to make the UN more relevant.

Decisions included creating a Peacebuilding Commission, accepting the international community's responsibility to protect people if national governments fail to protect their own citizens from atrocities, and creating a Human Rights Council (operational since 2006).
They also agreed to achieve the Millennium Development Goals, condemned terrorism in all its forms, created a Democracy Fund, and agreed to wind up the Trusteeship Council.
Disagreements remain over issues such as the definition of terrorism and how to act when states fail to protect citizens.

ex.q: Which 2005 decision deals with helping countries recover after conflict?
st: The Peacebuilding Commission was created to plan and support recovery in post-conflict societies.
The Human Rights Council deals with human rights; the Democracy Fund supports democracy.
ex.a: The Peacebuilding Commission

topics.rl: Indian peacekeepers have served in many UN missions, and India was one of the early contributors to the UN Democracy Fund.

rv.summary: In September 2005, for the UN's 60th anniversary, leaders created a Peacebuilding Commission, accepted a responsibility to protect, set up a Human Rights Council (from 2006) and a Democracy Fund, backed the MDGs, condemned terrorism and agreed to wind up the Trusteeship Council.
remember: Peacebuilding Commission: post-conflict recovery
Human Rights Council operational since 2006
Trusteeship Council to be wound up
traps: The veto was not abolished in 2005.
No UN army or world currency was created.

topics.ch: World Politics: International Organisations
topics.t: India and UN reforms
topics.h: India sent peacekeepers to Korea, Congo, Lebanon and beyond, yet has no permanent seat at the UN's top table. Here is the case India makes, and the objections it faces.
p: India supports restructuring the UN to make it more democratic and effective, including enlarging the Security Council to make it more representative.

India's case for permanent membership: it is one of the world's most populous countries and the largest democracy; it has taken part in almost all UN initiatives; it has a long, substantial record in UN peacekeeping; its economy is among the largest; and it pays its UN dues regularly.

Objections and debates: some question India's nuclear weapons capability; some think rivalry with Pakistan would make India less effective; some argue other regions (such as Africa and South America) should be represented; and some oppose expanding the veto.
India's view: it should get a permanent seat with the same powers as current members.

ex.q: Build India's case in three points for a board answer.
st: Population and democracy: among the most populous countries and the largest democracy.
Contribution: long peacekeeping record and regular payment of dues.
Economic weight: one of the largest economies.
ex.a: Large democratic nation, major peacekeeper and regular contributor, large economy

topics.rl: Indian women peacekeepers formed the first all-female UN police unit in Liberia (2007), one of many examples India cites for its strong UN record.

rv.summary: India wants a more democratic, enlarged Security Council and a permanent seat with equal powers, citing its population, democracy, UN participation, peacekeeping record, economy and regular dues. Objections include its nuclear status, rivalry with Pakistan and other regions' claims.
focus: India's view on powers of new members
remember: Largest democracy and among the most populous countries
Long record in UN peacekeeping; pays dues regularly
India seeks the same powers as current permanent members
traps: India's claim is not supported by every member.
India does not want a lesser seat without equal powers.

topics.ch: World Politics: International Organisations
topics.t: The UN in a unipolar world
topics.h: The UN's headquarters is in New York, and one country pays the largest share of its budget. Can the UN still check that country's power?
p: After the Cold War, the USA's power grew and it faced few checks. Many hoped the UN could balance US dominance, but this is difficult.
The USA is the single largest contributor to the UN budget, the UN is physically located in the USA, and Americans hold many important positions in its bureaucracy.
The USA has a veto in the Security Council, so it can block moves against its interests. It also has great influence over the choice of the Secretary-General.

Despite these limits, the UN remains an important forum: it lets states discuss and criticise policies (including US policies), share concerns and seek compromise. Without it, the world would be worse off.

ex.q: Give two reasons why the UN finds it hard to check US power.
st: The USA is the largest contributor to the UN budget.
It holds a veto in the Security Council and can block decisions.
ex.a: Largest budget contributor; holds the veto

topics.rl: Indian diplomats use UN debates to raise issues such as terrorism and climate justice even when big powers disagree, showing how the UN works as a forum for all.

rv.summary: In a unipolar world the UN finds it hard to check the USA, which is the largest budget contributor, hosts the UN in New York, holds key posts and has a veto. Still, the UN remains a valuable forum for dialogue and criticism.
focus: Sources of US influence in the UN
remember: USA: largest contributor to the UN budget
UN headquarters in New York
US veto can block Council action
traps: Limits on the UN do not make it useless.
The UN cannot tax citizens or order a government to change.

topics.ch: World Politics: International Organisations
topics.t: IMF, World Bank and WTO
topics.h: In 1991 India faced a severe balance of payments crisis and turned to the IMF for help. These institutions shape the economic choices of nations.
p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) oversees financial institutions and regulations that act at the international level. Voting is not equal: each country's vote is weighted by how much it has contributed, and the richest countries, led by the USA, hold the largest shares.

The World Bank was created in 1944 and works for development: human development (education, health), agriculture and rural development, environmental protection, infrastructure (roads, electricity) and governance. It gives loans and grants to member countries.
The World Bank is criticised for setting the economic agenda of poorer countries, attaching strict conditions to its loans and pushing free market reforms.
The World Trade Organisation (WTO), set up in 1995 as the successor to GATT (the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, created after the Second World War), sets the rules for global trade.
WTO decisions are taken by consensus, but the major economic powers such as the USA, the EU and Japan have dominated its rule-making. Developing countries often complain that the rules are not fair.

ex.q: Match each need to an institution: (a) a loan to build rural roads (b) a dispute over import duties (c) help to manage a currency crisis.
st: (a) Development project: World Bank.
(b) Trade rules and disputes: WTO.
(c) International financial stability: IMF.
ex.a: World Bank, WTO, IMF

topics.rl: Indian farmers' groups and the government regularly debate WTO rules on farm subsidies, because these rules affect minimum support prices and food security programmes.

rv.summary: The IMF oversees international finance with votes weighted by contribution, so rich countries dominate. The World Bank (1944) funds development but is criticised for loan conditions. The WTO (1995), successor to GATT, sets trade rules dominated by major powers.
focus: Roles of the IMF, World Bank and WTO
remember: World Bank 1944; WTO 1995 (succeeded GATT)
IMF votes weighted by financial contribution
World Bank criticised for strict conditions and free-market push
traps: Don't confuse the World Bank (1944) with the WTO (1995).
The IMF does not use one country, one vote.

topics.ch: World Politics: International Organisations
topics.t: IAEA, ILO, NGOs and the future of international organisations
topics.h: Inspectors with radiation meters, labour experts in Geneva, volunteers documenting abuses: international cooperation goes far beyond politicians giving speeches.
p: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), set up in 1957, grew out of US President Eisenhower's 'Atoms for Peace' proposal. It promotes the peaceful use of nuclear energy and works to prevent its military use; its inspectors regularly visit nuclear facilities.

The International Labour Organisation (ILO), founded in 1919 and later a UN specialised agency, sets international labour standards and promotes workers' rights. Governments, employers and workers are all represented in it.

Amnesty International is an NGO that campaigns for the protection of human rights all over the world and publishes reports on violations. Human Rights Watch is an international NGO that does research and advocacy on human rights and draws media attention to abuses.
NGOs are not set up by governments, but they influence states and international organisations by gathering information and mobilising public opinion.

The future: international organisations are imperfect but essential. They need reform to stay relevant, and countries like India seek a bigger voice in them. Common exercises ask you to match organisations with their functions and argue for or against Security Council reform.
