topics.rl: Many trade unions and farmers' groups in Kerala and West Bengal trace their history to the communist movement, while socialist ideas shaped later parties across north India.

rv.summary: The Congress Socialist Party (1934) left in 1948 when dual membership was barred; leaders included Narendra Dev, Lohia and JP. Communists, inspired by the Bolshevik revolution, formed the CPI, the largest opposition in 1952 with 16 seats; it split in 1964 to form the CPI(M).
focus: Origins and leaders of the CPI
remember: Congress Socialist Party 1934; left Congress 1948
Socialists: Narendra Dev, Lohia, Jayaprakash Narayan
CPI: Gopalan, Dange, Namboodiripad; split 1964
traps: Jayaprakash Narayan was a socialist, not a communist.
Don't confuse 1934 (formation) with 1948 (exit).

topics.ch: Politics in India: Era of One-Party Dominance
topics.t: Bharatiya Jana Sangh, Swatantra Party and the role of the opposition
topics.h: Nehru's first cabinet included leaders who would later found or lead rival parties. Early Indian democracy valued a strong opposition voice.
p: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was formed in 1951, with Syama Prasad Mookerjee as its founder-president. It emphasised the idea of one country, one culture and one nation, believing the country could become modern and strong on the basis of Indian culture and traditions. It favoured Hindi as the official language. Leaders included Deen Dayal Upadhyaya and Balraj Madhok. It is the precursor of the Bharatiya Janata Party.

The Swatantra Party was formed in August 1959 after the Congress's Nagpur resolution called for land ceilings, state trading in food grains and cooperative farming. Its leaders included C. Rajagopalachari, K.M. Munshi, N.G. Ranga and Minoo Masani.
The Swatantra Party favoured a free-market economy and less government control. It opposed central planning, nationalisation and the licence system, and favoured closer ties with the USA.

Although they won few seats, opposition parties played a crucial role: they offered principled criticism of Congress policies, kept the ruling party accountable and prevented resentment from becoming anti-democratic.

Early leaders respected the opposition: Nehru's first cabinet after independence (before the first general election) included non-Congress figures like B.R. Ambedkar and Syama Prasad Mookerjee. Exercise tip: match parties with their leaders and explain Congress dominance.

ex.q: Match each party with its founding leader: Bharatiya Jana Sangh, Swatantra Party, Socialist Party.
st: Bharatiya Jana Sangh: Syama Prasad Mookerjee (1951).
Swatantra Party: C. Rajagopalachari (1959).
Socialist Party: Acharya Narendra Dev, among others.
ex.a: BJS - Mookerjee; Swatantra - Rajagopalachari; Socialist - Narendra Dev

topics.rl: Parliament's Question Hour, when opposition members question ministers, continues the tradition of accountability that early opposition parties built.

rv.summary: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh (1951, Syama Prasad Mookerjee) stressed one country, one culture, one nation. The Swatantra Party (1959, Rajagopalachari) opposed the Nagpur resolution and favoured free markets. Opposition parties, though small, kept the Congress accountable.
focus: Jana Sangh and Swatantra Party: founders and ideas
remember: Jana Sangh 1951: Mookerjee; precursor of the BJP
Swatantra 1959: Rajagopalachari, Munshi, Ranga, Masani
Nehru's first cabinet included Ambedkar and Mookerjee
traps: Don't confuse the Jana Sangh (1951) with Swatantra (1959).
Swatantra favoured free markets, not planning.

topics.ch: Politics in India: Politics of Planned Development
topics.t: Political contestations over development
topics.h: A hill rich in iron ore can mean a steel plant and thousands of jobs, or forests lost and villages displaced. Which path should a state choose, and who decides?
p: Development decisions are political: they involve choices between different groups with competing interests, and so they are contested in a democracy.
No single decision suits everyone. What benefits one group, such as industry or urban consumers, may harm another, such as tribal communities or farmers.
Example: Odisha has some of the largest untapped reserves of iron ore in India. The state government signed agreements with steel companies to set up plants, hoping for investment and jobs.

Tribal communities feared displacement from their land and loss of livelihood; environmentalists warned of pollution and damage to forests; others argued that industry was essential for the state's growth.
Such debates show that the question of development is not just technical but also about values and whose interests count.

ex.q: List the groups with competing views on iron-ore mining and steel plants in Odisha.
st: State government and industry: want investment, jobs and growth.
Tribal communities: fear displacement and loss of livelihood.
Environmentalists: fear pollution and destruction of forests.
ex.a: Government and industry; tribal communities; environmentalists

topics.rl: Debates over new airports, expressways, dams or mines in your own state follow the same pattern: jobs and growth on one side, displacement and environment on the other.

rv.summary: Development decisions are political because they involve choices between groups with competing interests. In Odisha, steel plants on iron-ore reserves promised investment and jobs but tribal communities feared displacement and environmentalists feared pollution.
focus: Groups and views in the Odisha example
remember: Odisha: large untapped iron-ore reserves
Tribals: fear of displacement and loss of livelihood
Environmentalists: pollution and forest damage
traps: Development is not purely technical.
Not everyone supported the mining projects.

topics.ch: Politics in India: Politics of Planned Development
topics.t: Ideas of development: which model?
topics.h: In 1947 India had two famous models to copy: the American and the Soviet. It chose neither completely.
p: In the 1940s and 1950s, development was often understood as becoming 'modern', which meant becoming like the industrialised countries of the West. Modernisation was linked with growth, industrialisation and material progress.
There were two models of modern development: the liberal-capitalist model, as in the USA and much of Europe, and the socialist model, as in the USSR.
Many Indian leaders, including Nehru, were impressed by the Soviet model of rapid industrialisation, but India did not copy either model fully.

Left and right: the 'left' favoured pro-poor policies and a strong role for the state to reduce inequality; the 'right' favoured free competition and a market economy, with less government interference.
India's leaders agreed that development could not be left to private actors alone; the state had to play a key role. They disagreed about how much.

ex.q: Classify these views as left or right: (a) the state should own key industries to reduce inequality (b) markets should decide prices with minimal government role.
st: (a) Strong state role for the poor: left.
(b) Free market and less interference: right.
ex.a: (a) left; (b) right

topics.rl: Debates today about privatising public sector banks or Air India are modern versions of the old left-right debate on the state's role.

rv.summary: In the 1950s development meant becoming modern like the industrialised West, through the liberal-capitalist (USA) or socialist (USSR) model. The left favoured a strong pro-poor state, the right free markets; India combined both, agreeing the state must play a key role.
remember: Liberal-capitalist: USA, Europe; socialist: USSR
Left: strong state, pro-poor; right: market, less interference
India copied neither model fully
traps: Don't swap left and right positions.
Leaders did not reject a state role.

topics.ch: Politics in India: Politics of Planned Development
topics.t: Planning: the Bombay Plan, the Planning Commission and NITI Aayog
topics.h: Surprisingly, one of the strongest calls for state planning in India came from big industrialists, in 1944.
p: There was a broad consensus that India should plan its development. In 1944, a group of big industrialists drafted a joint proposal for a planned economy, called the Bombay Plan. It wanted the state to take major initiatives in industrial and other economic investments.

The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by a simple resolution of the Government of India. It had an advisory role, and the Prime Minister was its chairperson. It was not set up by the Constitution or by a separate law.

A Five Year Plan is a document in which the government sets out its plan for income and expenditure over five years. Planning lets the government focus on the larger picture and make long-term interventions in the economy.
The Planning Commission was replaced by the NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) in 2015.

ex.q: Was the Planning Commission a constitutional body?
st: It was set up in March 1950.
It was created by a simple resolution of the Government of India.
So it was neither constitutional nor statutory; it was advisory.
ex.a: No; it was set up by a government resolution and was advisory

topics.rl: NITI Aayog now publishes indices like the SDG India Index and works with states, instead of drawing up Five Year Plans.

rv.summary: There was broad consensus for planning — even industrialists' Bombay Plan (1944) wanted state initiative. The Planning Commission (March 1950), set up by a government resolution and chaired by the PM, made Five Year Plans; NITI Aayog replaced it in 2015.
focus: Five Year Plans and NITI Aayog
remember: Bombay Plan 1944: big industrialists
Planning Commission March 1950: advisory, PM as chair
NITI Aayog replaced it in 2015
traps: The Planning Commission was not constitutional or statutory.
The Bombay Plan was not a government plan.

topics.ch: Politics in India: Politics of Planned Development
topics.t: The First and Second Five Year Plans
topics.h: The First Plan said: feed the nation first. The Second Plan said: build steel, power and machines fast. Two plans, two philosophies.
p: The First Five Year Plan (1951-56) focused on the agrarian sector, including investment in dams and irrigation. Agriculture had been badly hit by Partition, and land reforms were seen as key to development.
K.N. Raj, a young economist who helped draft the First Plan, argued that India should 'hasten slowly' for the first two decades.
The Second Five Year Plan (1956-61) stressed heavy industrialisation, and was drafted under the leadership of P.C. Mahalanobis.
To protect domestic industries, the government imposed substantial tariffs on imports. Public sector industries were set up in steel, power and machinery.
Exam tip: First Plan = agriculture, dams, irrigation, K.N. Raj; Second Plan = heavy industry, P.C. Mahalanobis.

ex.q: Compare the First and Second Five Year Plans in a table.
st: First Plan (1951-56): agriculture, dams, irrigation; K.N. Raj ('hasten slowly').
Second Plan (1956-61): rapid heavy industrialisation; P.C. Mahalanobis; tariffs to protect domestic industry.
ex.a: First: agriculture-led (K.N. Raj); Second: heavy industry-led (Mahalanobis)

topics.rl: The Bhakra Nangal dam, which irrigates fields in Punjab and Haryana, and the Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur steel plants are symbols of the first two Plans.

rv.summary: The First Plan (1951–56) focused on agriculture, dams and irrigation, with K.N. Raj urging India to 'hasten slowly'. The Second Plan (1956–61), led by P.C. Mahalanobis, stressed heavy industry, protected by import tariffs and public sector units.
focus: Compare the First and Second Plans
Key people linked to each plan
remember: First Plan 1951–56: agriculture; K.N. Raj
Second Plan 1956–61: heavy industry; P.C. Mahalanobis
Tariffs protected domestic industry
traps: Don't swap the focus of the two plans.
'Hasten slowly' was K.N. Raj, not Mahalanobis.

topics.ch: Politics in India: Politics of Planned Development
topics.t: Public sector, import substitution and the mixed economy
topics.h: India's early steel plants were built by the state, while textile mills and shops stayed private. That mix had a name: the mixed economy.
p: The public sector (industries owned by the government) was given a leading role in key areas such as steel, mining, power and heavy machinery.
Import substitution meant producing at home the goods that were earlier imported, protected by tariffs and controls on imports.
India adopted a mixed economy: both the public sector and the private sector existed, but the state played a major role in planning and in key industries.

Critics from the right said the state controlled too much, creating a licence-permit system and inefficiency. Critics from the left said the private sector and the rich gained too much, and the poor too little.
Exercise tip: compare the First and Second Plans, and explain the two models of development and why India chose a mixed path.

ex.q: Explain the term 'mixed economy' with an Indian example.
st: A mixed economy has both public and private sectors.
Example: the state built steel plants (public sector), while private firms ran textile mills and consumer goods industries.
The state also planned and regulated the economy.
ex.a: An economy with both public and private sectors, with a key planning role for the state

topics.rl: Companies like SAIL (steel), BHEL (heavy electricals) and ONGC (oil) are public sector firms whose origins lie in the planning era.

rv.summary: India built a mixed economy: the public sector led in steel, mining and power, import substitution was protected by tariffs, and private firms also operated. The right criticised the licence-permit raj; the left said the rich gained more than the poor.
remember: Mixed economy: public and private sectors
Import substitution: make at home what was imported
Right: too much control; left: too little for the poor
traps: India did not copy the Soviet model completely.
Don't swap the left and right criticisms.

topics.ch: Politics in India: India's External Relations
topics.t: India's foreign policy: context, Article 51 and Nehru's goals
topics.h: India became free just as the Cold War split the world into two armed camps. A poor, newly independent country had to find its own way between them.
p: India became independent in a world shaped by the Cold War rivalry between the USA-led and USSR-led blocs. Newly independent India wanted to protect its freedom while building its economy.

Article 51 of the Constitution, a Directive Principle of State Policy, asks the state to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
Jawaharlal Nehru was both Prime Minister and Foreign Minister from 1946 to 1964, and he played a central role in shaping India's foreign policy.
Nehru's three major objectives: to preserve the hard-earned sovereignty of the country, to protect its territorial integrity, and to promote rapid economic development.

ex.q: Which part of the Constitution guides India's foreign policy towards peace, and what does it say?
st: It is Article 51, in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
It asks the state to promote international peace and security and just relations between nations.
It also asks for respect for international law and settlement of disputes by arbitration.
ex.a: Article 51: promote peace and security, just relations, respect for international law, settlement by arbitration

topics.rl: When Indian diplomats call for dialogue and peaceful settlement at the UN, they are echoing the spirit of Article 51.

rv.summary: Independent India entered a Cold War world. Article 51, a Directive Principle, asks for peace, just relations, respect for international law and arbitration. Nehru, PM and Foreign Minister from 1946 to 1964, aimed for sovereignty, territorial integrity and rapid economic development.
remember: Article 51 is a Directive Principle, not a Fundamental Right
Nehru: PM and Foreign Minister, 1946-1964
Goals: sovereignty, territorial integrity, economic development
traps: Article 51 is not enforceable in courts
Article 51 says nothing about military alliances

topics.ch: Politics in India: India's External Relations
topics.t: Non-alignment and Afro-Asian unity
topics.h: Choosing not to join either superpower's camp did not mean sitting on the fence. Non-alignment let India decide each issue on its merits.
p: Non-alignment meant keeping away from the military alliances of both the US-led and the Soviet-led blocs, while staying free to take an independent position on each issue.
Non-alignment was not isolation or neutrality: India took active stands, for example on decolonisation and disarmament, and developed relations with both blocs.
India championed Afro-Asian unity. Nehru convened the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi in March 1947, before independence.
The Afro-Asian conference at Bandung, Indonesia, in 1955 marked a high point of solidarity among newly independent countries and paved the way for the Non-Aligned Movement.
The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was held in Belgrade in September 1961. Nehru was a co-founder, along with Josip Broz Tito of Yugoslavia and Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt.

ex.q: Order: First NAM summit; Asian Relations Conference; Bandung Conference.
st: March 1947: Asian Relations Conference, New Delhi.
1955: Bandung Conference, Indonesia.
1961: First NAM summit, Belgrade.

topics.rl: India still describes its foreign policy as one of 'strategic autonomy', a modern descendant of non-alignment.

rv.summary: Non-alignment meant staying out of both blocs' military alliances while taking independent stands; it was not isolation or neutrality. The Asian Relations Conference (New Delhi, 1947) and Bandung (Indonesia, 1955) led to the first NAM summit in Belgrade in 1961.
focus: The first NAM summit and its founders
remember: Order: New Delhi 1947 → Bandung 1955 → Belgrade 1961
NAM co-founders: Nehru, Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt)
India took active stands on decolonisation and disarmament
traps: Non-alignment is not neutrality or isolation
Bandung was not the first NAM summit; Belgrade 1961 was

topics.ch: Politics in India: India's External Relations
topics.t: Panchsheel and the Tibet issue
topics.h: In 1954 India and China agreed on five principles for living as good neighbours. Five years later, a young monk crossed the Himalayas into India, and the friendship began to strain.
p: Panchsheel, the five principles of peaceful coexistence, was signed by Nehru and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai on 29 April 1954.

The five principles: mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty; mutual non-aggression; mutual non-interference in each other's internal affairs; equality and mutual benefit; and peaceful coexistence.
Tibet had historically been an area of friction. China took control of Tibet in 1950, and India did not openly oppose it.
In 1959 a rebellion broke out in Tibet. The Dalai Lama crossed into India and sought political asylum, which India granted. China strongly objected, and relations worsened.

ex.q: List the five principles of Panchsheel.
st: 1. Mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty.
2. Mutual non-aggression.
3. Mutual non-interference in internal affairs.
4. Equality and mutual benefit.
5. Peaceful coexistence.
ex.a: Territorial integrity and sovereignty; non-aggression; non-interference; equality and mutual benefit; peaceful coexistence

topics.rl: Dharamshala in Himachal Pradesh has hosted the Dalai Lama and a large Tibetan community since he sought asylum in India.

rv.summary: Nehru and Zhou Enlai signed Panchsheel, five principles of peaceful coexistence, on 29 April 1954. China took control of Tibet in 1950. In 1959 the Dalai Lama sought asylum in India; China strongly objected and relations worsened.
focus: The Tibet issue and the 1959 asylum
remember: Panchsheel: 29 April 1954, Nehru and Zhou Enlai
Sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, peaceful coexistence
1950 China takes Tibet; 1959 Dalai Lama's asylum
traps: Panchsheel was signed with China, not Pakistan
Zhou Enlai (Premier), not Mao, signed it

topics.ch: Politics in India: India's External Relations
topics.t: The Chinese aggression of 1962 and after
topics.h: In October 1962 Chinese troops attacked across the Himalayas. The short war shook India's confidence and changed its politics.
p: Border disputes, mainly over Aksai Chin in the Ladakh region and much of what was then NEFA (now Arunachal Pradesh), had grown after the 1950s.
In October 1962 China launched a swift and massive invasion on both disputed regions. India's forces were unprepared, and China declared a unilateral ceasefire after advancing.
The defeat hurt India's image and Nehru's standing. Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon had to leave the cabinet. The first no-confidence motion against Nehru's government was moved in the Lok Sabha.
The war also affected domestic politics: differences over China contributed to the split in the Communist Party of India in 1964.

Normalisation took time: full diplomatic relations were restored in 1976. Atal Bihari Vajpayee visited China as External Affairs Minister in 1979, and Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit started a new phase of ties.

ex.q: List two domestic consequences of the 1962 war in India.
st: Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon had to leave the cabinet.
The first no-confidence motion against the Nehru government was moved; the CPI later split partly over China.
ex.a: Krishna Menon's exit; first no-confidence motion against Nehru (and the CPI split)

topics.rl: India later created strong mountain divisions and built roads and tunnels in Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh, partly as a lesson from 1962.

rv.summary: In October 1962 China invaded Aksai Chin and NEFA (now Arunachal Pradesh). The defeat hurt Nehru: Krishna Menon left, the first no-confidence motion was moved, and the CPI split in 1964. Ties were restored in 1976; Vajpayee visited in 1979 and Rajiv Gandhi in 1988.
focus: Causes and areas of the 1962 war
remember: Disputed areas: Aksai Chin (Ladakh) and NEFA
Krishna Menon's exit; first no-confidence motion; CPI split 1964
1976 relations restored → 1979 Vajpayee → 1988 Rajiv Gandhi
traps: The war did affect domestic politics
1988 was Rajiv Gandhi's visit, not the restoration of ties

topics.ch: Politics in India: India's External Relations
topics.t: Wars and peace with Pakistan: 1947-48 to 1965
topics.h: Within weeks of independence, India and Pakistan were at war over Kashmir. Yet in 1960 they signed a water treaty that survived the wars of 1965 and 1971.
p: Soon after independence, a conflict broke out over Kashmir in 1947-48, often described as a proxy war, when Pakistan backed armed raiders. It ended with a ceasefire, and the issue was taken to the UN.
Despite conflict, the two countries cooperated on some issues. The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960 by Nehru and General Ayub Khan, with the World Bank's mediation.

In 1965 Pakistan launched armed attacks in the Rann of Kutch area of Gujarat in April, followed by a bigger offensive in Jammu and Kashmir in August-September. Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri ordered Indian forces to respond, and they advanced close to Lahore.
The war ended with UN intervention. The Tashkent Agreement was signed in January 1966 by Shastri and General Ayub Khan, brokered by the Soviet Union.

ex.q: Match each agreement to its mediator: Indus Waters Treaty; Tashkent Agreement.
st: Indus Waters Treaty (1960): World Bank.
Tashkent Agreement (1966): Soviet Union.
ex.a: Indus - World Bank; Tashkent - Soviet Union

topics.rl: Canals fed by the Indus system water fields across Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan, which is why the 1960 treaty mattered so much to farmers.

rv.summary: The 1947-48 Kashmir conflict ended in a ceasefire after the issue went to the UN. Nehru and Ayub Khan signed the Indus Waters Treaty in 1960 with World Bank mediation. The 1965 war, under Shastri, ended with the Soviet-brokered Tashkent Agreement of January 1966.
remember: Indus Waters Treaty 1960: Nehru, Ayub Khan, World Bank
1965: Rann of Kutch in April, then J&K; PM Shastri
Tashkent, January 1966: Shastri and Ayub Khan, USSR as broker
traps: Tashkent ended 1965; Shimla came after 1971
The World Bank mediated Indus, not Tashkent

topics.ch: Politics in India: India's External Relations
topics.t: The Bangladesh War of 1971 and the Kargil conflict
topics.h: In December 1971, within about two weeks, India's forces helped create a new nation. Nearly three decades later, Indian soldiers fought on icy peaks in Kargil.
p: In 1970 East Pakistan voted overwhelmingly for the Awami League, but the West Pakistan leadership refused to accept the result. The Pakistani army began a crackdown in 1971, and about 80 lakh refugees fled to India.
India faced a hostile combination of the USA, Pakistan and China. To counter this, India signed a 20-year Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the Soviet Union in August 1971.

Full-scale war broke out in December 1971. Indian forces, with the support of local people, advanced quickly; within about ten days they had surrounded Dhaka, and the Pakistani army surrendered. Bangladesh became independent.
The Shimla Agreement between Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, signed in 1972, formalised the return of peace.
In 1999 Pakistani forces and militants occupied heights in the Kargil sector (including Mashkoh, Dras, Kaksar and Batalik). India responded strongly and recaptured the positions.

ex.q: Why did India sign the Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the USSR in 1971?
st: The USA and China were moving closer, with Pakistan's help.
India faced a possible hostile combination over the Bangladesh crisis.
A treaty with the USSR gave India diplomatic and possible military support.
ex.a: To counter the US-China-Pakistan combination during the Bangladesh crisis

topics.rl: Kargil Vijay Diwas is observed every year on 26 July in memory of the soldiers who fought in 1999.

rv.summary: After the 1971 crackdown in East Pakistan, about 80 lakh refugees came to India. India signed a 20-year treaty with the USSR in August 1971. The December 1971 war led to Bangladesh's independence; the Shimla Agreement (1972) followed. In 1999 India recaptured Kargil heights.
remember: About 80 lakh refugees from East Pakistan
Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace and Friendship, August 1971
Shimla 1972: Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto
Kargil 1999: Mashkoh, Dras, Kaksar, Batalik
traps: Shimla, not Tashkent, followed the 1971 war
80 lakh, not 8 lakh or 8 crore

topics.ch: Politics in India: India's External Relations
topics.t: India's nuclear policy
topics.h: Nehru called for the world to give up nuclear weapons. Decades later India tested its own. The story of India's nuclear policy is about principle meeting security.
p: Nehru had great faith in science and technology for building modern India, and he opposed nuclear weapons, pleading for comprehensive nuclear disarmament. The atomic energy programme was led by Homi J. Bhabha.

India conducted its first nuclear explosion at Pokhran in May 1974, calling it a peaceful nuclear explosion. In May 1998 India carried out a series of nuclear tests, and Pakistan tested soon afterwards.

India refused to sign the NPT (1968) and the CTBT (Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, 1996), calling them discriminatory because they allow existing nuclear powers to keep their weapons while denying others.

India's nuclear doctrine: no first use (India will not be the first to use nuclear weapons) and credible minimum nuclear deterrence. India remains committed to global, verifiable and non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament.
Exercise tip: order foreign policy events by date and explain NAM and its relevance.

ex.q: Explain India's nuclear doctrine in two phrases.
st: No first use: India will use nuclear weapons only in retaliation.
Credible minimum deterrence: enough capability to deter an attack, not an arms race.
ex.a: No first use; credible minimum deterrence

topics.rl: India's civilian nuclear power plants, run by the Nuclear Power Corporation, and research at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre in Mumbai grew from the programme Homi Bhabha began.

rv.summary: Nehru opposed nuclear weapons and urged disarmament; Homi J. Bhabha led the atomic energy programme. India tested at Pokhran in 1974 and in May 1998. It rejects the NPT and CTBT as discriminatory. Its doctrine is no first use with credible minimum deterrence.
focus: Why India rejects the NPT and CTBT
remember: Pokhran 1974 (peaceful explosion); tests in May 1998
NPT and CTBT seen as discriminatory
No first use + credible minimum deterrence
traps: Faith in science did not mean Nehru wanted bombs
No first use means retaliation only, never first strike

topics.ch: Politics in India: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
topics.t: The challenge of political succession: Nehru to Shastri to Indira
topics.h: Many new democracies collapsed when their founding leader died. When Nehru died in May 1964, the world watched to see whether India would too.
p: Nehru died in May 1964. Many feared a crisis of succession, but the transition was smooth: Lal Bahadur Shastri was chosen unanimously as the leader of the Congress parliamentary party and became Prime Minister.
Shastri was Prime Minister from 1964 to 1966. He faced food shortages and the 1965 war with Pakistan, and gave the famous slogan 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'.

Shastri died suddenly at Tashkent in January 1966, soon after signing the Tashkent Agreement. The contest for leadership was between Morarji Desai and Indira Gandhi, and Indira Gandhi won in a secret ballot among Congress MPs, with more than two-thirds of their support.

The 'Syndicate' was an informal group of senior Congress leaders who controlled the party organisation. It was led by K. Kamaraj, Congress President, and included S.K. Patil, S. Nijalingappa, N. Sanjeeva Reddy and Atulya Ghosh.
The Syndicate played a key role in choosing both Shastri and Indira Gandhi, and expected Indira to depend on its advice.

ex.q: Why was the succession after Nehru's death considered a test for Indian democracy?
st: Nehru had dominated politics since independence.
Many newly independent countries had seen turmoil or military takeover after a founding leader's death.
India's smooth transfer of power to Shastri, and then to Indira Gandhi, showed that its democratic institutions worked.
ex.a: Because a smooth transfer of power without crisis proved democracy's strength

topics.rl: 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan' is still quoted on Republic Day and in farmer and soldier tributes across India.

rv.summary: After Nehru died in 1964, Shastri was chosen unanimously and led until his death at Tashkent in 1966. Indira Gandhi then beat Morarji Desai in a secret ballot. The Syndicate, led by K. Kamaraj, helped pick both leaders.
focus: Indira Gandhi's 1966 contest and the Syndicate
remember: Shastri: PM 1964-66, 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan', died at Tashkent
1966: Indira Gandhi beat Morarji Desai in a secret ballot
Syndicate: Kamaraj, S.K. Patil, Nijalingappa, Sanjeeva Reddy, Atulya Ghosh
traps: Indira Gandhi did face a contest in 1966
Shastri died at Tashkent, not Shimla

topics.ch: Politics in India: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
topics.t: The fourth general election, 1967: a 'political earthquake'
topics.h: In 1967 the Congress still won the Lok Sabha, but lost power in several states and saw many big leaders defeated. Observers called it a 'political earthquake'.
p: The period before 1967 was one of economic crisis: monsoon failure, widespread drought, a fall in agricultural production, serious food shortages, depletion of foreign exchange reserves, a drop in industrial production and exports, and higher military spending.
In June 1966 the government devalued the rupee, a step widely seen as taken under US pressure. Prices rose sharply, and protests spread.

Non-Congressism: Ram Manohar Lohia gave this strategy, arguing that the opposition parties should come together to defeat the Congress, which he saw as undemocratic and opposed to the interests of the poor.

Results of the 1967 election: the Congress got a majority in the Lok Sabha but with its lowest tally since 1952. Half the ministers in Indira Gandhi's cabinet and leaders like K. Kamaraj lost their seats. The Congress lost its majority in seven states, and in two more, defections prevented it from forming a government.
In Madras, the regional DMK came to power with a clear majority, helped by its leadership of the anti-Hindi agitation.

ex.q: Give two economic reasons for the Congress's setback in 1967.
st: Food shortages after drought and poor monsoons.
Devaluation of the rupee and rising prices; depletion of foreign exchange reserves.
ex.a: Food shortages and drought; devaluation and price rise

topics.rl: Even today, inflation and farm distress can swing election results in Indian states, just as they did in 1967.

rv.summary: Drought, food shortages and the June 1966 devaluation fed discontent. Lohia's non-Congressism united the opposition. In 1967 the Congress kept a reduced Lok Sabha majority but lost seven states; the DMK won Madras.
remember: Rupee devalued in June 1966
Congress lost majority in 7 states; defections blocked it in 2 more
Half the cabinet and Kamaraj lost their seats
traps: The Congress did not lose its Lok Sabha majority
Non-Congressism was Lohia's idea, not JP's

topics.ch: Politics in India: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
topics.t: Coalitions and defections after 1967
topics.h: After 1967, parties that had little in common ideologically shared power in the states. And one MLA changed sides so often that he gave Indian politics a new phrase.
p: The 1967 elections brought coalition governments in many states. They were called Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments, meaning 'joint legislature party'.

These coalitions were ideologically varied. In Bihar the SVD government included the two socialist parties (SSP and PSP), the CPI on the left and the Jana Sangh on the right. In Punjab the 'Popular United Front' included the two rival Akali groups, the CPI, the CPI(M), the SSP, the Republican Party and the Jana Sangh.
Defection means an elected representative leaving the party on whose symbol he or she was elected and joining another party. Defections caused frequent rise and fall of state governments after 1967.
The phrase 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' comes from Gaya Lal, an MLA in Haryana, who changed his party three times within a fortnight in 1967.
Defections were later checked by the anti-defection law, added to the Constitution in 1985.

ex.q: Why were SVD governments in states unstable?
st: They were coalitions of parties with very different ideologies.
Members often defected to other parties.
So disagreements and defections frequently brought them down.
ex.a: Ideological differences and frequent defections

topics.rl: Debates about MLAs switching sides before a trust vote in today's state assemblies are linked to the 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' politics that began in 1967.

rv.summary: After 1967 many states had SVD (joint legislature party) coalitions of mixed ideologies, such as Bihar's and Punjab's Popular United Front. Frequent defections, shown by Gaya Lal's 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram', made them unstable.
focus: SVD coalitions and their mixed ideologies
remember: SVD = Samyukta Vidhayak Dal
Bihar SVD: SSP, PSP, CPI and Jana Sangh; Punjab: Popular United Front
Gaya Lal, Haryana MLA, changed party three times in a fortnight
traps: SVD coalitions were not ideologically uniform
Gaya Lal was from Haryana, not Bihar

topics.ch: Politics in India: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
topics.t: Indira Gandhi versus the Syndicate: the road to the split
topics.h: In 1969 a sitting Prime Minister campaigned against her own party's official candidate for President, and won.
p: Indira Gandhi faced challenges from the Syndicate, which expected her to follow its advice. She gradually built her own independent position and tried to give the party a more radical, pro-poor image.

In 1967 the Congress Working Committee adopted a Ten-Point Programme, including social control of banks, nationalisation of general insurance, ceilings on urban property and income, public distribution of food grains, land reforms and house sites for the rural poor.
In 1969 President Zakir Hussain died. The Syndicate got N. Sanjeeva Reddy nominated as the official Congress candidate, despite Indira Gandhi's reservations.

Indira Gandhi encouraged the then Vice-President, V.V. Giri, to file his nomination as an independent. Just before the election she nationalised fourteen leading private banks (July 1969) and removed Morarji Desai as Finance Minister.
She called for a 'conscience vote', asking Congress MPs and MLAs to vote as they wished. V.V. Giri won, and the official Congress candidate lost.

ex.q: Order these events of 1969: V.V. Giri elected President; Zakir Hussain dies; banks nationalised; Sanjeeva Reddy nominated.
st: Zakir Hussain dies (May 1969).
Sanjeeva Reddy nominated as official candidate.
Fourteen banks nationalised (July 1969).
V.V. Giri elected President (August 1969).
ex.a: Zakir Hussain's death → Reddy nominated → banks nationalised → Giri elected

topics.rl: Many public sector banks you see today, such as Bank of Baroda or Canara Bank, were among those nationalised in 1969.

rv.summary: Indira Gandhi built her own position against the Syndicate. In 1969 the Syndicate made N. Sanjeeva Reddy the official presidential candidate; she backed V.V. Giri, nationalised 14 banks, removed Morarji Desai and called for a conscience vote. Giri won.
focus: Bank nationalisation and the conscience vote
remember: Official candidate: N. Sanjeeva Reddy; winner: V.V. Giri
14 private banks nationalised, July 1969
Conscience vote: members vote as they wish
traps: The official Congress candidate lost in 1969
Indira Gandhi and the Syndicate disagreed on the candidate

topics.ch: Politics in India: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
topics.t: The Congress splits; privy purses abolished
topics.h: By late 1969 the party that had led the freedom struggle had broken into two. One side was called the 'Organisation', the other the 'Requisitionists'.
p: The defeat of the official candidate formalised the split. The Congress President, S. Nijalingappa, expelled Indira Gandhi from the party in November 1969.
The Congress split into two: the Congress (O), for 'Organisation', led by the Syndicate, and the Congress (R), for 'Requisitionists', led by Indira Gandhi.
Indira Gandhi presented the split as an ideological fight between socialists and conservatives, the pro-poor and the pro-rich.
Privy purses were grants paid by the government to the former rulers of princely states and their heirs, promised at the time of integration. Indira Gandhi supported their abolition.

Her government's attempt to amend the Constitution in 1970 failed in the Rajya Sabha, and its order 'de-recognising' the princes was struck down by the Supreme Court. Privy purses were finally abolished by a constitutional amendment after the 1971 election.

ex.q: Explain the meaning of Congress (O) and Congress (R).
st: Congress (O): 'Organisation', the faction led by the Syndicate that controlled the party organisation.
Congress (R): 'Requisitionists', the faction led by Indira Gandhi.
The split came in 1969.
ex.a: Congress (O) = Organisation (Syndicate); Congress (R) = Requisitionists (Indira Gandhi)

topics.rl: Some former royal families still live in their palaces, but since 1971 they no longer receive privy purses from the government.

rv.summary: After the 1969 presidential poll, Nijalingappa expelled Indira Gandhi. The party split into Congress (O) and Congress (R). She called it socialists versus conservatives. Privy purses for ex-rulers were abolished only after the 1971 election.
remember: Congress (O) = Organisation (Syndicate); Congress (R) = Requisitionists
Nijalingappa expelled her, November 1969
1970 amendment failed in Rajya Sabha; Supreme Court struck down de-recognition
traps: Privy purses ended after, not before, the 1971 election
'R' means Requisitionists, not Radicals

topics.ch: Politics in India: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
topics.t: The 1971 election and the restoration of Congress dominance
topics.h: The opposition's slogan was 'Indira hatao'. Her reply was 'Garibi hatao'. In 1971 voters chose the second by a landslide.
p: Indira Gandhi recommended dissolving the Lok Sabha in December 1970, and fresh elections were held in February 1971, ahead of schedule.

The non-communist, non-Congress opposition parties, including the Congress (O), formed a 'Grand Alliance' with the slogan 'Indira hatao' (remove Indira). Indira Gandhi offered a positive programme with the slogan 'Garibi hatao' (remove poverty).
The Congress (R) and CPI alliance won more seats and votes than the Congress had won in any of the first four elections. The Congress (R) alone won 352 seats, while the Congress (O) won only 16.

Restoration: the Congress system was restored, but it was different. The new Congress depended heavily on the popularity of a single leader, Indira Gandhi, and had fewer factions and a weaker organisation.

The victory in the Bangladesh war in December 1971 further raised Indira Gandhi's popularity, and the Congress swept the state assembly elections of 1972. Exam tip: order the events of 1964-71 by date.

ex.q: Compare the restored Congress of 1971 with the old Congress system.
st: Old system: coalition of many groups and factions, strong organisation, internal opposition.
Restored Congress: dominance built around one popular leader, Indira Gandhi.
Fewer factions and less tolerance of internal opposition.
ex.a: The restored Congress depended on one leader rather than a broad coalition of factions

topics.rl: Election slogans still matter in India: like 'Garibi hatao', a short catchy line can shape a whole campaign.

rv.summary: In the early 1971 election, the Grand Alliance's 'Indira hatao' met Indira Gandhi's 'Garibi hatao'. The Congress (R) won 352 seats and the Congress (O) only 16. The restored Congress rested on one leader, helped further by the Bangladesh victory.
remember: 'Garibi hatao' = Indira; 'Indira hatao' = Grand Alliance
Congress (R) 352 seats; Congress (O) 16 seats
Restored Congress: one leader, fewer factions, weaker organisation
traps: Do not swap the two slogans
352 − 16 = 336 more seats, not 368

topics.ch: Politics in India: The Crisis of Democratic Order
topics.t: Background to the Emergency: economic crisis and popular movements
topics.h: Only three years after a historic election victory, students were protesting in Gujarat, Bihar was in turmoil, and the railways had ground to a halt.
p: Economic context: after 1971, the 'Garibi hatao' promise was not fulfilled. The costs of the Bangladesh crisis and refugees, the stopping of US aid, and a sharp rise in international oil prices in 1973 caused high inflation. Industrial growth was low and unemployment was high, especially among educated rural youth.

Gujarat movement (January 1974): students protested against rising prices of food grains, cooking oil and other essentials, and against corruption at high levels. Major opposition parties joined, President's rule was imposed, and Morarji Desai went on an indefinite fast demanding fresh elections. In June 1975 the Congress lost the assembly election.

Bihar movement (March 1974): students protesting against price rise, food scarcity, unemployment and corruption invited Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) to lead them. JP accepted on the condition that the movement remain non-violent and not be confined to Bihar.

JP gave the call for 'Total Revolution' (Sampoorna Kranti) to establish what he saw as true democracy. He demanded the dismissal of the Congress government in Bihar, and in 1975 led a people's march to Parliament, one of the largest political rallies ever held in the capital.

In May 1974 the National Coordination Committee for Railwaymen's Struggle, led by George Fernandes, called a nationwide railway strike for bonus and better service conditions. The government declared it illegal, and it was called off after twenty days.

ex.q: List three developments of 1973-74 that added to tension before the Emergency.
st: Rising prices after the 1973 oil price hike and economic slowdown.
Student-led movements in Gujarat and Bihar against price rise and corruption, with JP's call for Total Revolution.
The nationwide railway strike led by George Fernandes.
ex.a: Price rise, the Gujarat and Bihar movements, and the railway strike

topics.rl: Patna's Gandhi Maidan and Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, sites of huge rallies in 1974-75, remain the stages for mass political gatherings today.

rv.summary: After 1971, war costs, the end of US aid and the 1973 oil price rise caused inflation and unemployment. Students led movements in Gujarat and Bihar; JP called for Total Revolution. George Fernandes led a 1974 railway strike, declared illegal.
focus: JP's Total Revolution and the railway strike
remember: Gujarat (Jan 1974): students; Morarji Desai's fast
Bihar (Mar 1974): JP, non-violent and national
Railway strike, May 1974: George Fernandes, called off after 20 days
traps: Total Revolution was JP's call, not Lohia's
The railway strike did not win its demands

topics.ch: Politics in India: The Crisis of Democratic Order
topics.t: Conflict with the judiciary and the Allahabad High Court verdict
topics.h: On 12 June 1975, a High Court judge in Allahabad declared the Prime Minister's own election invalid. Within two weeks India was under Emergency.
p: The government and the ruling party had serious differences with the judiciary over whether Parliament could abridge Fundamental Rights, curtail the right to property, and amend the Constitution to give primacy to Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights.
In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament could amend the Constitution but could not change its basic structure.

In 1973, when the post of Chief Justice of India fell vacant, the government set aside the convention of appointing the senior-most judge. It appointed Justice A.N. Ray, superseding three senior judges who had ruled against the government. This was criticised as an attack on judicial independence.

On 12 June 1975, Justice Jagmohan Lal Sinha of the Allahabad High Court declared Indira Gandhi's election to the Lok Sabha invalid, on a petition filed by Raj Narain, a socialist leader who had contested against her in 1971.
On 24 June 1975 the Supreme Court granted a partial stay: she could remain an MP but could not take part in Lok Sabha proceedings until her appeal was decided.

ex.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in the Kesavananda Bharati case?
st: The question was how far Parliament could amend the Constitution.
The Court held that Parliament can amend the Constitution.
But it cannot alter the Constitution's basic structure.
ex.a: Parliament can amend the Constitution but not its basic structure

topics.rl: The 'basic structure' doctrine from Kesavananda Bharati is still cited by courts whenever a constitutional amendment is challenged.

rv.summary: The government clashed with the judiciary. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) protected the basic structure. In 1973 A.N. Ray was made CJI over three senior judges. On 12 June 1975 Justice Sinha voided Indira Gandhi's election on Raj Narain's petition.
focus: Kesavananda Bharati and the basic structure
The Allahabad verdict and partial stay
remember: Basic structure cannot be changed by amendment
12 June 1975: election invalid (Justice Jagmohan Lal Sinha)
24 June 1975: partial stay — MP, but no part in proceedings
traps: Parliament can amend the Constitution, just not its basic structure
The verdict did not uphold her election

topics.ch: Politics in India: The Crisis of Democratic Order
topics.t: Declaration of Emergency and the government's response
topics.h: On the night of 25 June 1975, newspaper offices lost their electricity, and before dawn hundreds of opposition leaders were arrested. India had entered the Emergency.
p: On 25 June 1975 the opposition held a massive rally in Delhi's Ramlila grounds, where JP called for nationwide protests and urged the army, police and government employees not to obey 'illegal and immoral orders'.

That night the government declared a national Emergency under Article 352, citing a threat of 'internal disturbance'. President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed issued the proclamation, and the cabinet was informed early the next morning.
Electricity to major newspaper offices was cut, and opposition leaders were arrested in large numbers. Press censorship was imposed: newspapers needed prior approval for what they published.
Organisations such as the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and the Jamaat-e-Islami were banned. Protests, strikes and public agitations were not allowed.

Preventive detention was widely used, mainly under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA). In the ADM Jabalpur case (1976), the Supreme Court accepted the government's view that citizens could not move the courts for habeas corpus during the Emergency, a decision later widely criticised.

ex.q: Under which article was the 1975 Emergency declared, and on what ground?
st: The Constitution allows a national emergency under Article 352.
In 1975 the ground cited was 'internal disturbance'.
The President proclaimed it on 25 June 1975.
ex.a: Article 352, on the ground of internal disturbance

topics.rl: Some newspapers, like The Indian Express and The Statesman, protested censorship by leaving blank spaces where censored news would have appeared.

rv.summary: After JP's 25 June 1975 rally, a national Emergency was declared under Article 352 citing 'internal disturbance'; President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed it. Leaders were arrested, the press censored, RSS and Jamaat-e-Islami banned, and MISA used.
focus: MISA and the ADM Jabalpur case
remember: 25 June 1975, Article 352, 'internal disturbance'
Press censorship needed prior approval
ADM Jabalpur (1976): no habeas corpus during the Emergency
traps: Article 352, not 356 or 360
'Armed rebellion' came later, with the 44th Amendment

topics.ch: Politics in India: The Crisis of Democratic Order
topics.t: Consequences of the Emergency
topics.h: Blank columns in newspapers, writers returning their awards, and more than a lakh people detained without trial: the Emergency touched almost every democratic institution.
p: Civil liberties were badly affected: fundamental rights were in effect suspended, people could not easily approach courts, and the press was censored. Some writers returned their awards in protest; for example, Kannada writer Shivarama Karanth returned his Padma Bhushan and Hindi writer Phanishwar Nath Renu returned his Padma Shri.
The independence of the judiciary was weakened, as rulings like ADM Jabalpur showed.

Constitutional changes: an amendment of 1975 (the 39th) declared that the elections of the Prime Minister, President and Vice-President could not be challenged in court. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made a whole series of changes: for example, it extended the term of the Lok Sabha and state assemblies from five to six years, and it limited the powers of the courts.
There were serious excesses: compulsory sterilisation drives and demolition of slums and jhuggis in places like Delhi, carried out forcibly.

After the Emergency, the Janata government appointed the Shah Commission (May 1977), headed by Justice J.C. Shah, a retired Chief Justice of India, to inquire into the excesses. It found that a very large number of people, over one lakh, had been arrested under preventive detention laws.

ex.q: Name the commission that inquired into the Emergency and one of its findings.
st: It was the Shah Commission, set up in May 1977 by the Janata government.
It was headed by Justice J.C. Shah.
It found that over one lakh people had been arrested under preventive detention laws, among other excesses.
ex.a: The Shah Commission; it found large-scale detentions and excesses

topics.rl: The Emergency is still remembered in Indian public life, and debates about press freedom often refer back to those blank newspaper columns of 1975.

rv.summary: The Emergency curbed civil liberties and judicial independence. The 39th Amendment shielded the top offices' elections; the 42nd (1976) made terms six years and limited courts. Forced sterilisation and slum demolitions occurred. The Shah Commission (1977) probed excesses.
focus: Effects on civil liberties and the judiciary
remember: 42nd Amendment, 1976: Lok Sabha term 5 → 6 years
39th: elections of President, VP, PM beyond courts
Shah Commission, May 1977: over one lakh detained
traps: The 42nd Amendment curbed courts, it did not strengthen them
The Shah Commission was set up after the Emergency

topics.ch: Politics in India: The Crisis of Democratic Order
topics.t: Lessons of the Emergency
topics.h: In 1977, voters who had been silenced for nearly two years used the ballot to speak. The Emergency taught India that democracy is not easily switched off.
p: The Emergency showed both the weaknesses and the strengths of Indian democracy. It proved that it is extremely difficult to do away with democracy in India: within about two years, democratic politics returned through elections.
It brought out ambiguities in the emergency provisions. The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced the ground of 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' for a national emergency on internal grounds.
The 44th Amendment also made it necessary for the President to act on the written advice of the Council of Ministers when proclaiming an emergency.
The Emergency made people more aware of civil liberties. Many civil liberties organisations emerged afterwards.
It also highlighted the need for an independent judiciary and a police and bureaucracy that follow the law rather than the ruling party.

ex.q: How did the 44th Amendment respond to the experience of 1975?
st: In 1975, 'internal disturbance' had been a vague ground.
The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced it with 'armed rebellion'.
It also required the Council of Ministers' advice to the President to be in writing.
ex.a: It changed the ground to 'armed rebellion' and required written cabinet advice

topics.rl: Organisations working on civil liberties and human rights in India, many of which grew after 1977, continue to monitor police and detention practices.

rv.summary: The Emergency showed it is very hard to end democracy in India. The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' and required written cabinet advice. Civil liberties groups grew, and the need for neutral officials and courts was clear.
remember: 44th Amendment, 1978: 'armed rebellion'
Cabinet advice to the President must be in writing
Awareness of civil liberties grew
traps: Do not mix up the 42nd (1976) and 44th (1978) Amendments
The lesson is democracy's strength, not its fragility

topics.ch: Politics in India: The Crisis of Democratic Order
topics.t: Politics after the Emergency: the Janata experiment and its legacy
topics.h: In March 1977 the Prime Minister lost her own seat, and for the first time a non-Congress government took charge in New Delhi.
p: In January 1977, the government announced elections and released opposition leaders. The major opposition parties came together to form the Janata Party, under the guidance of JP. Some Congress leaders opposed to the Emergency, such as Jagjivan Ram, left the Congress and formed the Congress for Democracy, which later merged with the Janata Party.

In the March 1977 Lok Sabha election, the Congress won only 154 seats, while the Janata Party and its allies won 330 of 542 seats. Indira Gandhi lost from Rae Bareli. The election was seen as a referendum on the Emergency.

Morarji Desai became Prime Minister, with Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram as rival claimants to the post. The Janata government lacked a common programme and clear leadership, and Morarji Desai's government lost its majority in 1979. Charan Singh then formed a government on the assurance of Congress support, but it lasted only a few months.
Fresh elections in January 1980 brought the Congress back to power under Indira Gandhi, with 353 seats.

Legacy: the 1977 election made anti-Congress politics a stronger force and saw the rise of backward-class politics, especially in north India. The Janata government appointed the Mandal Commission. Exam tip: list causes and consequences of the Emergency and evaluate its lessons.

ex.q: Why did the Janata government collapse so quickly?
st: The Janata Party was a coalition of very different parties united mainly by opposition to the Emergency.
It lacked a common programme and a clear direction.
Rivalry among leaders like Morarji Desai, Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram added to the instability.
ex.a: Lack of a common programme and leadership rivalry

topics.rl: The 1977 election is often cited by Indian voters and commentators as proof that the ballot can change any government.

rv.summary: In 1977 the Janata Party, formed with JP's guidance, won 330 of 542 seats; the Congress got 154 and Indira Gandhi lost Rae Bareli. Desai became PM but the government fell in 1979. The Congress returned in 1980 with 353 seats.
focus: The Janata government and its collapse
remember: 1977: Janata and allies 330, Congress 154
PM Morarji Desai; then Charan Singh, briefly
1980: Congress back with 353 seats
traps: Congress won 154 in 1977, not 353 (1980)
330 − 154 = 176 seats, the Janata lead

topics.ch: Politics in India: Regional Aspirations
topics.t: Region and the nation: the Indian approach
topics.h: India has hundreds of languages and many regions with distinct histories. Holding them together without flattening them is one of democracy's hardest jobs.
p: The Indian approach to diversity: regional aspirations are to be accommodated through democratic means. Unity is not seen as uniformity; regions are allowed to express their identity within the nation.

After independence, many regions voiced demands: some for autonomy or new states, some for special status, and a few for secession. The areas of greatest tension included Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab and the North-East, along with linguistic and regional movements elsewhere.
The Constitution provides flexible arrangements, such as reorganisation of states, special provisions for some regions, and autonomous councils for tribal areas.
The aim is to balance national unity and integrity with respect for regional diversity, so that regional aspirations strengthen rather than weaken democracy.

ex.q: Explain the Indian approach to regional diversity in one line, and give an example.
st: India accommodates regional demands through democratic negotiation, not suppression.
Example: creating linguistic states or new states like Mizoram after peace talks.
ex.a: Accommodation of regional aspirations through democratic means, e.g. creating new states

topics.rl: Indian cricket teams draw players from every region, from Kashmir to Kerala, a small example of unity with diversity.

rv.summary: India accommodates regional aspirations through democratic means; unity is not uniformity. Demands ranged from autonomy and new states to, in a few cases, secession, with J&K, Punjab and the North-East as key areas. Flexible constitutional arrangements help balance unity and diversity.
remember: Unity with diversity, not uniformity
Key areas: J&K, Punjab, North-East
Tools: new states, special provisions, autonomous councils
traps: Regional demands are not anti-national by default
Accommodation, not suppression, is India's approach

topics.ch: Politics in India: Regional Aspirations
topics.t: Jammu and Kashmir: roots of the issue and early politics
topics.h: In October 1947, armed raiders from across the new border moved towards Srinagar. The Maharaja's decision in those days shaped the region's future.
p: Jammu and Kashmir has three regions: Jammu, the Kashmir valley and Ladakh. Before 1947 it was a princely state ruled by Maharaja Hari Singh, who did not want to join either India or Pakistan.

In October 1947, Pakistan sent tribal infiltrators to capture Kashmir. The Maharaja asked India for military help. India sent its army, after the Maharaja signed the Instrument of Accession with India, and the infiltrators were driven back from the Kashmir valley.

External dispute: a part of the state remained under Pakistan's occupation, known in India as Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (POJK). Pakistan has claimed Kashmir, and the issue has been central to India-Pakistan conflicts.

Internal dispute: there were debates about the state's status within India. Article 370 gave the state special status and greater autonomy than other states, and some groups demanded still greater autonomy.

Sheikh Abdullah of the National Conference, a leader of the popular movement against the Maharaja, became Prime Minister of the state in 1948. He was dismissed in 1953 and kept in detention for years. After an agreement with Indira Gandhi in 1974, he became Chief Minister.

ex.q: Why did Maharaja Hari Singh sign the Instrument of Accession in October 1947?
st: Tribal infiltrators sent from Pakistan were advancing to capture Kashmir.
He asked India for military help.
India sent its army after he signed the Instrument of Accession.
ex.a: To get India's military help against infiltrators sent from Pakistan

topics.rl: Ladakh's Hemis festival, Jammu's Vaishno Devi pilgrimage and Kashmir's Dal Lake show how the region's three parts have very different cultures.

rv.summary: J&K had three regions under Maharaja Hari Singh. In October 1947 Pakistan sent infiltrators; he signed the Instrument of Accession and India sent its army. The issue has an external side (POJK) and an internal side (Article 370, autonomy). Sheikh Abdullah led the National Conference.
remember: Regions: Jammu, Kashmir valley, Ladakh
Instrument of Accession signed after the October 1947 invasion
Sheikh Abdullah: PM 1948, dismissed 1953, CM after the 1974 accord
traps: Hari Singh first wanted to join neither country
POJK belongs to the external dispute

topics.ch: Politics in India: Regional Aspirations
topics.t: Jammu and Kashmir: insurgency, elections and the 2019 change
topics.h: On 5 August 2019, Parliament changed the constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir. The decision came after decades of militancy, elections and coalition politics.
p: Farooq Abdullah succeeded his father as Chief Minister after 1982. The 1987 assembly election was won by the National Conference-Congress alliance, but many believed the election did not reflect the people's choice.

From 1989 the state saw a militant movement, supported from across the border, that demanded a separate Kashmiri nation or merger with Pakistan. The state was under President's rule for several years, and violence caused great suffering, including the displacement of Kashmiri Pandits from the valley.

Elections were held again in 1996. In 2002 the National Conference lost, and a coalition of the People's Democratic Party (PDP) and the Congress formed the government under Mufti Mohammad Sayeed. Later elections produced other coalition governments, including a PDP-BJP coalition after 2014.

On 5 August 2019, the provisions of Article 370 that gave special status to Jammu and Kashmir were abrogated. Under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, the state was reorganised into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.

ex.q: What changes took place in Jammu and Kashmir in 2019?
st: The special status under Article 370 was ended on 5 August 2019.
The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 was passed.
The state became two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.
ex.a: Article 370 abrogated; state reorganised into the UTs of J&K and Ladakh

topics.rl: Ladakh, now a Union Territory, is home to high-altitude solar projects and is a gateway to India's northern borders.

rv.summary: The disputed 1987 election was followed by militancy from 1989, years of President's rule and the displacement of Kashmiri Pandits. Elections resumed in 1996; a PDP-Congress coalition ruled after 2002. On 5 August 2019 Article 370's special status ended and two UTs were formed.
remember: 1987 election seen as unfair; militancy from 1989
2002: PDP-Congress under Mufti Mohammad Sayeed
5 August 2019: J&K Reorganisation Act, UTs of J&K and Ladakh
traps: Two UTs were formed, not three states
2002 was PDP-Congress, not NC-Congress

topics.ch: Politics in India: Regional Aspirations
topics.t: Punjab: from Punjabi Suba to the Punjab Accord
topics.h: Punjab went from being a hub of the Green Revolution to a decade of violence, and then back to peace. Its story shows both the dangers and the healing power of democracy.
p: The Akali Dal, formed in 1920 as the political wing of the Sikhs, led the movement for a 'Punjabi Suba'. In 1966 Punjab was reorganised: Haryana was carved out of it as a new state, and its hill areas were merged with Himachal Pradesh. The Akali Dal came to power in 1967 and in 1977, in coalition governments.
In 1973 the Akali Dal passed the Anandpur Sahib Resolution. It asserted regional autonomy and wanted to redefine centre-state relations in India, and spoke of the aspirations of the Sikh community.

A cycle of violence followed: militant groups demanded a separate Sikh state and made the Golden Temple in Amritsar their headquarters. In June 1984 the Government of India carried out 'Operation Blue Star', an army operation to remove militants from the Golden Temple, which deeply hurt Sikh sentiments.

On 31 October 1984, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her bodyguards. Large-scale violence against the Sikh community followed in Delhi and many parts of north India, in which thousands were killed.

Road to peace: in July 1985 Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and Harchand Singh Longowal, the Akali Dal president, signed the Punjab Accord. Violence continued for some years, but by the mid-1990s normalcy returned and elections restored democratic politics.

ex.q: Order these: Anandpur Sahib Resolution; Punjab reorganised; Rajiv Gandhi-Longowal Accord; Operation Blue Star.
st: 1966: Punjab reorganised (Punjabi Suba).
1973: Anandpur Sahib Resolution.
June 1984: Operation Blue Star.
July 1985: Rajiv Gandhi-Longowal Accord.

topics.rl: Today Punjab's Golden Temple welcomes lakhs of visitors of all faiths, and its community kitchen, the langar, feeds everyone who comes.

rv.summary: The Akali Dal's Punjabi Suba movement led to the 1966 reorganisation. The 1973 Anandpur Sahib Resolution sought autonomy. Militancy led to Operation Blue Star (June 1984) and Indira Gandhi's assassination (31 October 1984). The 1985 Rajiv Gandhi-Longowal Accord began the road to peace.
focus: Violence of 1984 and the Punjab Accord
remember: Anandpur Sahib: regional autonomy, centre-state relations
Punjab Accord: Rajiv Gandhi and Harchand Singh Longowal
traps: Blue Star was June 1984; the assassination was October 1984
1966 was Punjab's reorganisation, not the 1956 Act

topics.ch: Politics in India: Regional Aspirations
topics.t: The North-East: autonomy, new states and secessionist movements
topics.h: A strip of land only about 22 km wide links the North-East to the rest of India. Beyond it lie seven states with remarkable diversity.
p: The North-East has seven states, called the 'seven sisters': Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. It is home to about 4 per cent of India's population and is linked to the rest of India by a narrow corridor about 22 km wide.
The region borders China, Myanmar, Bangladesh and Bhutan. It has great ethnic and linguistic diversity, and its relative isolation and lack of development caused grievances.

Demands for autonomy: at independence, most of the region was part of Assam. Non-Assamese groups felt the Assamese language was being imposed, and tribal leaders demanded separation. Over time Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura (1972), and Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh (1987) became states.

Mizo movement: after a famine in 1959 that people felt the Assam government had not handled well, the Mizo National Front (MNF) under Laldenga began an armed struggle for independence in 1966. After two decades, Rajiv Gandhi and Laldenga signed the Mizoram Accord in 1986. Mizoram became a full state, and Laldenga became Chief Minister.

Naga movement: under Angami Zapu Phizo, a section of Nagas declared independence from India on 14 August 1947 and launched an armed struggle. Nagaland became a state in 1963, but the Naga issue has continued to be negotiated.

ex.q: How did the Mizo insurgency end, and why is it cited as a success?
st: The MNF under Laldenga fought an armed struggle from 1966.
Negotiations led to the Mizoram Accord with Rajiv Gandhi in 1986.
Mizoram became a state and Laldenga became Chief Minister; Mizoram has been largely peaceful since.
ex.a: Through the 1986 Mizoram Accord; insurgents joined democratic politics

topics.rl: Hornbill Festival in Nagaland and Chapchar Kut in Mizoram celebrate the distinct cultures of the North-East.

rv.summary: The seven sisters, linked by a corridor about 22 km wide, have great diversity. Resentment at Assamese dominance led to new states: Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura (1972), Mizoram and Arunachal (1987). The Mizo struggle ended with the 1986 Mizoram Accord; the Naga issue continues.
remember: Seven sisters: Assam, Arunachal, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura
Mizoram Accord 1986: Rajiv Gandhi and Laldenga (MNF)
Naga movement: Phizo, independence declared 14 August 1947
traps: Sikkim is not one of the seven sisters
Laldenga = Mizo; Phizo = Naga

topics.ch: Politics in India: Regional Aspirations
topics.t: The Assam movement and national integration
topics.h: From 1979 to 1985, students in Assam led one of the longest mass movements in independent India, on the question of who is an outsider.
p: Movements against 'outsiders' arose in the North-East because large-scale migration was seen as a threat by local communities, who feared becoming a minority and losing jobs, land and political power.

The Assam Movement (1979-1985) was led by the All Assam Students' Union (AASU), a students' group. It demanded that illegal migrants, mainly from Bangladesh, be identified and sent back, and that their names be removed from voters' lists. The movement had wide support and was largely non-violent, though there were incidents of violence.

In 1985 the Rajiv Gandhi government and the AASU leaders signed the Assam Accord. Foreigners who had migrated to Assam during and after the Bangladesh war (that is, from 1971) were to be identified and deported.
After the accord, the AASU leaders formed a political party, the Asom Gana Parishad (AGP), which came to power in Assam in 1985 with Prafulla Kumar Mahanta as Chief Minister.
The Assam case shows that even very difficult issues can be addressed through democratic negotiation, though the problem of migration has not been fully resolved.

ex.q: What did the Assam Accord of 1985 decide about migrants?
st: It was signed by the Rajiv Gandhi government and AASU leaders.
Foreigners who came to Assam during and after the Bangladesh war (from 1971) were to be identified.
They were to be deported.
ex.a: Those who migrated from 1971 onwards were to be identified and deported

topics.rl: Debates in Assam about citizenship and voter lists continue to refer back to the 1971 cut-off set in the Assam Accord.

rv.summary: Fear of becoming a minority fuelled movements against 'outsiders'. AASU led the Assam Movement (1979-85) to identify and deport illegal migrants, mainly from Bangladesh. The 1985 Assam Accord targeted those who came from 1971; the AGP under Prafulla Kumar Mahanta then won power.
remember: AASU led the movement, 1979-1985
Accord: migrants from 1971 to be identified and deported
AGP, CM Prafulla Kumar Mahanta, 1985
traps: The Assam Movement was not secessionist
Assam Accord 1985; Mizoram Accord 1986

topics.ch: Politics in India: Regional Aspirations
topics.t: Accommodation and national integration: the lessons
topics.h: Rebels who became Chief Ministers, autonomy councils in tribal hills, and new states on the map: India's regional story has many lessons.
p: Lesson 1: regional aspirations are a part of democratic politics. Expressing regional issues is not abnormal or anti-national.
Lesson 2: the best way to respond is through democratic negotiation rather than suppression. Accords in Punjab, Mizoram and Assam show this.
Lesson 3: power sharing matters. Regions and groups need a real share in decision-making at the state and national levels.
Lesson 4: regional imbalance in economic development can feed feelings of discrimination, so balanced development is necessary.

Lesson 5: the Constitution's flexibility, such as special provisions and the Sixth Schedule's autonomous councils for tribal areas, helps accommodate diversity. Exam tip: practise matching movements with their leaders and accords, and map work on these regions.

ex.q: Match each accord with its leaders: Punjab Accord, Mizoram Accord, Assam Accord.
st: Punjab Accord (1985): Rajiv Gandhi and Harchand Singh Longowal.
Mizoram Accord (1986): Rajiv Gandhi and Laldenga.
Assam Accord (1985): Rajiv Gandhi government and AASU leaders.
ex.a: Punjab - Longowal; Mizoram - Laldenga; Assam - AASU

topics.rl: Special constitutional provisions for states like Nagaland and Mizoram, protecting local customs and land, are examples of accommodation at work.

rv.summary: Regional aspirations are part of democratic politics. Negotiated accords in Punjab, Mizoram and Assam work better than force. Real power sharing and balanced development reduce grievances, and the flexible Constitution, including the Sixth Schedule, helps accommodate diversity.
remember: Punjab Accord: Longowal; Mizoram: Laldenga; Assam: AASU
Sixth Schedule: autonomous councils for tribal areas
Former insurgents in elected government = power sharing
traps: Sixth Schedule, not the Tenth (anti-defection)
The Constitution is flexible, not rigid

topics.ch: Politics in India: Recent Developments in Indian Politics
topics.t: The context of the 1990s
topics.h: Between 1989 and 1992, India saw a hung Parliament, a former Prime Minister assassinated, an economic crisis and the biggest caste and religious mobilisations in decades. The decade reshaped Indian politics.
p: In 1984, after Indira Gandhi's assassination, Rajiv Gandhi led the Congress to a massive victory. But in 1989 the Congress lost its majority, ending the era of Congress dominance often called the 'Congress system'.
Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated on 21 May 1991, during the election campaign, by members of the LTTE. After the election, P.V. Narasimha Rao became Prime Minister.

Key developments of the period: the defeat of the Congress in 1989 and the end of the Congress system; the Mandal issue (1990), which brought backward-caste politics to the centre; the New Economic Policy of 1991, which began economic reforms; and the Ayodhya movement, which culminated in the events of December 1992.
These developments led to multi-party competition at the national level. No single party could easily win a majority, and coalition governments became common.

ex.q: List four developments of 1989-1992 that changed Indian politics.
st: End of the Congress system after the 1989 election.
Mandal issue: OBC reservations in 1990.
New Economic Policy of 1991.
The Ayodhya movement and the events of December 1992 (and Rajiv Gandhi's assassination in 1991).
ex.a: End of Congress dominance; Mandal; economic reforms; Ayodhya

topics.rl: Many of today's major regional parties, from Bihar to Tamil Nadu, became powerful national players in the coalition politics that began in this period.

rv.summary: After a huge win in 1984, the Congress lost its majority in 1989, ending the Congress system. Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated on 21 May 1991; Narasimha Rao became PM. Mandal (1990), the 1991 reforms and Ayodhya (1992) led to multi-party competition and coalitions.
focus: End of the Congress system in 1989
remember: 21 May 1991: Rajiv Gandhi assassinated by the LTTE
1990 Mandal; 1991 New Economic Policy; December 1992 Ayodhya
PM after 1991: P.V. Narasimha Rao
traps: 1989, not 1977, ended the Congress system
The Congress did not win a majority in 1989

topics.ch: Politics in India: Recent Developments in Indian Politics
topics.t: The era of coalitions: National Front and United Front
topics.h: From December 1989 to March 1998, six different leaders served as Prime Minister. Parties that had fought each other in elections propped up governments from outside.
p: In the 1989 election, the Congress emerged as the largest party but was far short of a majority. The National Front, an alliance of the Janata Dal and some regional parties, formed the government under V.P. Singh.
The National Front government received support from two very different sides: the BJP and the Left Front, both from outside the government. It lasted less than a year, after the BJP withdrew support.
In 1996, after a short-lived BJP government, the United Front, a coalition of regional and other non-Congress, non-BJP parties, formed the government with Congress support from outside.
The United Front Prime Ministers were H.D. Deve Gowda (1996-97) and I.K. Gujral (1997-98).
These governments showed that coalitions could bring regional parties to the centre of national power, but also that outside support made governments unstable.

ex.q: Why were the National Front and United Front governments unstable?
st: They depended on support from parties outside the government.
The supporting parties had very different ideologies (the BJP and the Left in 1989; the Congress in 1996-98).
When outside support was withdrawn, the governments fell.
ex.a: They relied on outside support from parties with different ideologies

topics.rl: Coalition politics made regional leaders like those from Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh important figures in national government.

rv.summary: In 1989 the National Front, led by the Janata Dal, formed the government under V.P. Singh with outside BJP and Left support; it fell when the BJP withdrew. In 1996 the United Front governed with outside Congress support under Deve Gowda and then Gujral.
focus: Why outside support made coalitions unstable
remember: National Front: V.P. Singh, Janata Dal, outside support of BJP and Left
United Front: Deve Gowda (1996-97), Gujral (1997-98), Congress support
Withdrawal of outside support brought governments down
traps: Do not swap 1989 (BJP and Left) and 1996 (Congress) supporters
Gujral led the United Front, not the National Front

topics.ch: Politics in India: Recent Developments in Indian Politics
topics.t: NDA and UPA: coalitions become the norm
topics.h: From 1989 to 2014, no single party won a Lok Sabha majority on its own. Governing meant building alliances.
p: In 1998 the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) formed the government under Atal Bihari Vajpayee. It lost a confidence vote in 1999, but returned to power after the 1999 election and ruled until 2004.

In 2004 the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) formed the government, with Manmohan Singh as Prime Minister. The UPA won again in 2009, and Manmohan Singh was Prime Minister from 2004 to 2014.
