From 1989 to 2014, coalition and alliance governments were the norm at the Centre. Both national parties had to share power with state-level and regional parties.
Coalition politics made bargaining and accommodation central to government. Alliances were often formed on practical, pragmatic grounds rather than shared ideology.
Exercise tip: order the coalition governments by date, from the National Front to the UPA.

ex.q: Order these governments: UPA under Manmohan Singh; National Front under V.P. Singh; NDA under Vajpayee; United Front under Deve Gowda.
st: 1989: National Front (V.P. Singh).
1996: United Front (Deve Gowda).
1998: NDA (Vajpayee).
2004: UPA (Manmohan Singh).
ex.a: National Front → United Front → NDA → UPA

topics.rl: Cabinet berths for allies from many states, from Bihar to Tamil Nadu, became a regular feature of the coalition era.

rv.summary: The BJP-led NDA ruled under Vajpayee from 1998, lost a confidence vote in 1999, and returned until 2004. The Congress-led UPA ruled from 2004 to 2014 under Manmohan Singh. From 1989 to 2014 coalitions were the norm, built on pragmatic bargaining.
remember: Order: National Front → United Front → NDA → UPA
NDA = BJP-led; UPA = Congress-led
Manmohan Singh: PM 2004-2014
traps: The UPA was not BJP-led
Manmohan Singh was Finance Minister, not PM, in 1991

topics.ch: Politics in India: Recent Developments in Indian Politics
topics.t: The political rise of the Other Backward Classes: Mandal and after
topics.h: In August 1990 a government decision on reservations sparked protests across north India and changed the shape of Indian politics for decades.
p: The Janata Party government set up the Second Backward Classes Commission in 1978 (announced in December 1978 and formally appointed on 1 January 1979), chaired by B.P. Mandal; it is known as the Mandal Commission. It submitted its report in 1980.

The Commission recommended reserving 27 per cent of seats in educational institutions and government jobs for the Other Backward Classes (OBCs). It also made other recommendations, such as land reform, to improve their conditions.

In August 1990, the National Front government under V.P. Singh decided to implement the recommendation of 27 per cent reservation for OBCs in central government jobs. This led to violent protests in many cities, especially by students opposed to the decision.

In the Indra Sawhney case (1992), the Supreme Court upheld OBC reservation, with conditions such as excluding the better-off sections (the 'creamy layer') and keeping overall reservations within limits.

Political fallout: OBC and Dalit-based parties grew. The Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), founded by Kanshi Ram in 1984, came to power in Uttar Pradesh in 1995. Other parties with strong OBC support also became powerful in north India.

ex.q: Summarise the Mandal story in four steps.
st: 1978: Mandal Commission set up by the Janata government.
1980: report recommends 27% reservation for OBCs.
1990: V.P. Singh government implements it in central jobs; protests follow.
1992: Supreme Court upholds it in the Indra Sawhney case.
ex.a: Commission (1978) → report (1980) → implementation (1990) → Indra Sawhney (1992)

topics.rl: OBC reservation in central government jobs and in central universities and institutions like IITs and AIIMS today traces back to the Mandal Commission's recommendation.

rv.summary: The Janata government set up the Mandal Commission in 1978; its 1980 report urged 27% OBC reservation. V.P. Singh's government implemented it in 1990 amid protests. The Supreme Court upheld it in Indra Sawhney (1992). OBC and Dalit parties like Kanshi Ram's BSP grew.
focus: The Mandal Commission and its report
Indra Sawhney and the political fallout
remember: Commission 1978 → report 1980 → implementation 1990 → Indra Sawhney 1992
27% reservation for OBCs
BSP: founded 1984 by Kanshi Ram; in power in UP 1995
traps: The Court upheld, not struck down, OBC reservation
Janata set up the Commission; V.P. Singh implemented it

topics.ch: Politics in India: Recent Developments in Indian Politics
topics.t: Ram Janmabhoomi movement, the 2019 verdict and the temple
topics.h: One site in Ayodhya was at the centre of a legal and political debate for decades, until a unanimous Supreme Court verdict in 2019 settled the dispute.
p: The Ram Janmabhoomi movement sought the construction of a Ram temple at the site in Ayodhya believed by many Hindus to be the birthplace of Lord Ram. In 1986 a Faizabad district court ordered the opening of the locks of the structure at the site. The movement grew into a major national issue, and the BJP made it a central part of its politics.
In 1990, BJP leader L.K. Advani led a Rath Yatra from Somnath in Gujarat towards Ayodhya to build public support for the movement.

On 6 December 1992, the three-domed structure at the disputed site was demolished by people who had gathered there. This was followed by communal violence in several parts of the country, and some state governments were dismissed.

The dispute went through a long legal process. On 9 November 2019, a five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court gave a unanimous verdict: the disputed land was to be given to a trust for building a Ram temple, and five acres of land elsewhere in Ayodhya were to be given for a mosque.

The verdict was accepted peacefully across the country, showing the strength of the legal process in resolving disputes. Construction of the Ram temple at the site began in 2020, and its consecration (pran pratishtha) ceremony was held in January 2024.

ex.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in November 2019?
st: A five-judge Constitution Bench heard the case.
It unanimously ruled that the disputed land would go to a trust for the construction of a Ram temple.
It directed that five acres of land elsewhere in Ayodhya be given for a mosque.
ex.a: Disputed land to a trust for a Ram temple; five acres elsewhere for a mosque

topics.rl: The peaceful acceptance of the 2019 verdict across India is often cited as an example of how courts can settle even the most sensitive disputes.

rv.summary: The Ram Janmabhoomi movement grew after 1986; Advani's 1990 Rath Yatra began at Somnath. The structure was demolished on 6 December 1992. On 9 November 2019 a five-judge bench unanimously gave the site for a temple and five acres for a mosque; the verdict was accepted peacefully.
remember: 6 December 1992: demolition
9 November 2019: unanimous five-judge verdict
Five acres for a mosque; consecration January 2024
traps: The Rath Yatra started at Somnath, not Ayodhya
Consecration was 2024, not 1992

topics.ch: Politics in India: Recent Developments in Indian Politics
topics.t: Emergence of a new consensus
topics.h: In 2014, for the first time since 1984, a single party won a majority in the Lok Sabha on its own. Yet many ideas that grew in the coalition era were shared across parties.
p: Lok Sabha elections from 2004 to 2019: the Congress-led UPA won in 2004 and 2009. In 2014 the BJP won a majority on its own (282 seats), the first time any party had done so since 1984, and it formed the government with its NDA allies under Narendra Modi. In 2019 the BJP won an even larger majority (303 seats). (In 2024 the BJP won 240 seats, short of a majority on its own, and the NDA formed the government with its allies, again under Narendra Modi.)
A growing consensus emerged among most parties on four points. First, agreement on the new economic policies: most parties support economic reforms, even if they differ on details.
Second, acceptance of the political and social claims of the backward castes: almost all parties support reservation for backward classes and seek their support.
Third, acceptance of the role of state-level parties in national governance: the line between regional and national parties has become less important.

Fourth, emphasis on pragmatic considerations rather than ideological positions: alliances are often made without full ideological agreement. Exercise tip: explain the political impact of Mandal and order the coalition governments by date.

ex.q: Name the four elements of the new consensus in Indian politics.
st: Agreement on new economic policies.
Acceptance of the claims of backward castes.
Acceptance of the role of state-level parties in national governance.
Pragmatism rather than ideology in forming alliances.
ex.a: Economic policy; backward-caste claims; role of state parties; pragmatism over ideology

topics.rl: GST was brought in with the support of almost all parties, and OBC reservation is backed by parties across the spectrum, showing how some areas of consensus have formed.

rv.summary: The UPA won in 2004 and 2009. In 2014 the BJP won 282 seats, the first single-party majority since 1984, and 303 in 2019. A new consensus formed on economic reforms, backward-caste claims, the role of state parties, and pragmatism over ideology.
focus: The four points of the new consensus
remember: BJP: 282 seats in 2014, 303 in 2019
First single-party majority since 1984
Consensus: reforms, backward castes, state parties, pragmatism
traps: Do not swap 282 (2014) and 303 (2019)
303 − 282 = 21 seats more, not 585

qa.q: In which year was the Berlin Wall built?
qa.e: The Wall went up in 1961 and stood until 1989.

qa.q: The fall of the Berlin Wall took place in:
qa.a: November 1989
qa.e: Crowds broke through the Wall in November 1989.

qa.q: What did the Berlin Wall symbolise?
qa.a: The division between the capitalist and communist worlds
qa.e: It divided East and West Berlin and stood for the Cold War split between the two blocs.

qa.q: A world in which two superpowers and their alliances dominate international politics is called:
qa.a: Bipolar
qa.e: 'Bi' means two; the Cold War world was bipolar.

qa.q: Which event completed the end of the bipolar world order?
qa.a: Disintegration of the Soviet Union in 1991
qa.e: Once the USSR broke up, only one superpower remained.

qa.q: The two parts of Germany were unified in:
qa.e: Unification came in 1990, a year after the Wall fell.

qa.q: Assertion (A): After 1991 the world was often described as unipolar. Reason (R): The disintegration of the USSR left the USA as the only superpower.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and the end of the USSR is exactly why the world came to be seen as unipolar.

qa.q: Case: A student writes, 'The Berlin Wall separated East Germany from Poland.' What is the correct correction?
qa.a: It separated East Berlin from West Berlin
qa.e: The Wall ran through Berlin, cutting the city into a communist East and a capitalist West.

qa.q: The Soviet Union came into being after the socialist revolution in Russia in:
qa.e: The Bolshevik-led revolution of 1917 created the Soviet state.

qa.q: Which military alliance bound the Soviet bloc countries together?
qa.a: Warsaw Pact
qa.e: The Warsaw Pact was the military alliance of the Soviet bloc; NATO was the Western alliance.

qa.q: The 'Second World' referred to:
qa.a: The socialist bloc of East European countries led by the USSR
qa.e: The First World was the Western bloc, the Second World the Soviet bloc, and the Third World the developing countries.

qa.q: Which was NOT a feature of the Soviet political system?
qa.a: Competition among several political parties
qa.e: Only the Communist Party was allowed, so there was no multi-party competition.

qa.q: Which achievement is correctly linked to the Soviet system?
qa.a: Ensuring a minimum standard of living with no unemployment
qa.e: The state guaranteed basic needs and jobs, though consumer goods were of lower quality than in the West.

qa.q: In the Soviet economy, who owned and controlled productive assets such as land and factories?
qa.a: The state
qa.e: Productive assets were owned and controlled by the state, and the economy was planned.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Soviet Union became a great power after the Second World War. Reason (R): It had a strong industrial base, large energy resources and a powerful military.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true and R explains A: its industrial and military strength made it a superpower.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Soviet system allowed many parties to compete in elections. Reason (R): The Soviet state subsidised health care and education.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false because only the Communist Party was allowed. R is true: welfare services were subsidised.

qa.q: Mikhail Gorbachev became the General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in:
qa.e: He took charge in 1985 and launched reforms.

qa.q: 'Perestroika' refers to:
qa.a: Restructuring
qa.e: Perestroika was the economic restructuring reform; glasnost was openness.

qa.q: 'Glasnost' refers to:
qa.a: Openness
qa.e: Glasnost allowed more freedom of speech and information.

qa.q: Which of these was a major weakness of the Soviet system?
qa.a: Lack of democracy and freedom of speech
qa.e: The system was authoritarian and stifled free expression; it actually had a strong military and no unemployment.

qa.q: Which event of 1979 drained Soviet resources and weakened the system?
qa.a: Intervention in Afghanistan
qa.e: The Afghanistan intervention was costly and weakened the USSR.

qa.q: Why did people in many Soviet republics feel neglected?
qa.a: Russia dominated the Union and their regions were suppressed
qa.e: Of the fifteen republics, Russia dominated; others felt their identities and interests were ignored.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Gorbachev introduced glasnost. Reason (R): He wanted to reform the system by allowing greater openness and debate.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, and R explains why glasnost was launched.

qa.q: Case: A Soviet citizen in 1984 could get free schooling and a job, but waited years for a car and could not criticise the government. Which pair best describes this?
qa.a: Basic welfare guaranteed, but consumer shortages and no freedom
qa.e: The system secured basic needs but suffered shortages and denied political freedom.

qa.q: Which three republics declared the dissolution of the USSR in December 1991?
qa.a: Russia, Ukraine and Belarus
qa.e: Under Yeltsin, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus announced that the USSR was dissolved.

qa.q: The 1991 coup in the USSR was attempted by:
qa.a: Communist Party hardliners opposed to reform
qa.e: Hardliners tried to reverse Gorbachev's reforms; the coup failed.

qa.q: Who emerged as a national hero by opposing the 1991 coup?
qa.a: Boris Yeltsin
qa.e: Yeltsin, the elected President of Russia, led the resistance to the coup.

qa.q: What was formed in place of the USSR in December 1991?
qa.a: Commonwealth of Independent States
qa.e: The CIS was set up as a loose association of former Soviet republics.

qa.q: After the break-up, which state inherited the Soviet seat in the UN Security Council?
qa.a: Russia
qa.e: Russia was accepted as the successor state and took the permanent seat.

qa.q: In 1989, what happened in East European countries of the Soviet bloc?
qa.a: People overthrew their communist governments
qa.e: Mass protests brought down communist regimes in 1989, and the USSR did not intervene.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Russia took over the international treaties of the USSR. Reason (R): Russia was accepted as the successor state of the Soviet Union.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; as successor state Russia inherited the USSR's seat and treaty commitments.

qa.q: How many years after Gorbachev took charge did the USSR dissolve?
qa.e: Gorbachev took charge in 1985 and the USSR was dissolved in December 1991: 1991 - 1985 = 6.

qa.q: According to the most common explanation, the Soviet Union disintegrated mainly because of:
qa.a: Internal weaknesses of its political and economic institutions
qa.e: The system failed to meet people's aspirations; it was not defeated militarily.

qa.q: In which regions of the USSR was the nationalist desire for sovereignty strongest?
qa.a: The Baltic states, Ukraine and Georgia
qa.e: The European and relatively prosperous regions led the push for independence.

qa.q: Which is an ECONOMIC reason for the Soviet collapse?
qa.a: Stagnation and severe consumer shortages
qa.e: Shortages and stagnation are economic; the others are political.

qa.q: Why did Gorbachev's reforms fail to save the USSR?
qa.a: They raised expectations they could not meet and were opposed by both reformers and hardliners
qa.e: Reformers found them too slow, hardliners found them too radical.

qa.q: Which three countries are the Baltic states?
qa.a: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania
qa.e: The three Baltic republics on the Baltic Sea were among the first to push for independence.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many Soviet citizens became openly dissatisfied in the 1980s. Reason (R): Greater openness let them learn how far the USSR lagged behind the West.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, and R explains A: once information flowed, the gap with the West became obvious.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The cost of the arms race was one reason for the Soviet collapse. Reason (R): The Soviet economy was the largest and most productive in the world in the 1980s.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: the Soviet economy was stagnating and lagging behind the West.

qa.q: Case: A Ukrainian student in 1990 says, 'We want our own government and our own language in schools.' This reflects which cause of the Soviet collapse?
qa.a: Rise of nationalism and demands for sovereignty
qa.e: Demands for self-rule in republics were a major cause of the break-up.

qa.q: Which of these was a consequence of the disintegration of the USSR?
qa.a: End of the Cold War arms race
qa.e: The collapse ended the rivalry and the arms race; the other events came much earlier.

qa.q: After 1991 the world was described as unipolar because:
qa.a: The USA was left as the only superpower
qa.e: With the USSR gone, the USA dominated alone.

qa.q: Which institutions became powerful advisers to many countries after 1991?
qa.a: World Bank and IMF
qa.e: These institutions promoted capitalist reforms in post-communist states.

qa.q: Which group of new states emerged from the former Soviet Union?
qa.a: Central Asian republics such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan
qa.e: Central Asian and Baltic republics became independent states.

qa.q: Many Baltic and East European states wanted to join which organisations after the Cold War?
qa.a: European Union and NATO
qa.e: They wanted closer ties with Western Europe for economic and security reasons.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Some observers saw the end of the USSR as a triumph of capitalism. Reason (R): Capitalism and liberal democracy became the dominant models after 1991.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the spread of capitalism after 1991 is why some called it a triumph.

qa.q: Which statement about power after 1991 is correct?
qa.a: The balance of power shifted in favour of the USA
qa.e: With its rival gone, the US was the dominant power.

qa.q: Case: In 1992, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have new flags and seats at the UN. Which consequence of the Soviet collapse does this show?
qa.a: Emergence of new independent countries
qa.e: The break-up created many new sovereign states.

qa.q: What was 'shock therapy'?
qa.a: A sudden transition from socialism to democratic capitalism
qa.e: It was a rapid, all-at-once switch to a market economy and democracy.

qa.q: Shock therapy was influenced mainly by:
qa.a: The World Bank and the IMF
qa.e: These institutions pushed the model in post-communist states.

qa.q: Which was an element of shock therapy?
qa.a: Currency convertibility
qa.e: Making the currency freely exchangeable was part of opening the economy.

qa.q: Why was the privatisation under shock therapy called 'the largest garage sale in history'?
qa.a: State industries were sold off at very low prices
qa.e: Valuable assets went to private buyers far below their real worth.

qa.q: Under shock therapy, the trade of post-communist countries was redirected towards:
qa.a: The West
qa.e: The old Soviet bloc trade links broke and trade shifted towards Western countries.

qa.q: In shock therapy, what was to be the dominant pattern of ownership of property?
qa.a: Private ownership
qa.e: The model made private ownership the main form of property.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Under shock therapy, collective farms were replaced by private farming. Reason (R): Shock therapy aimed at a complete shift to a capitalist economy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, and the aim of full capitalism explains the end of collective farms.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Shock therapy was a gradual transition to capitalism. Reason (R): It was promoted by the World Bank and IMF.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it was sudden, hence 'shock'. R is true.

qa.q: What happened to the rouble under shock therapy?
qa.a: Its value declined dramatically
qa.e: The currency fell sharply and inflation wiped out savings.

qa.q: Which consequence of shock therapy affected food security?
qa.a: Disintegration of the collective farm system
qa.e: As collective farms broke up, food security collapsed and Russia began importing food.

qa.q: The political institutions built after communism usually had:
qa.a: A strong executive president and a weak parliament
qa.e: Constitutions drafted in a hurry gave presidents wide powers.

qa.q: Which social consequence followed shock therapy?
qa.a: Rise of a mafia and widening inequality
qa.e: Privatisation created new disparities and organised crime grew.

qa.q: Why were many people pushed into poverty under shock therapy?
qa.a: Government subsidies were withdrawn and the welfare system collapsed
qa.e: Removing subsidies hit ordinary people hard.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Savings of many Russians were wiped out in the 1990s. Reason (R): High inflation followed the fall in the value of the rouble.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; inflation and a falling rouble destroyed the value of savings.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Judicial independence was firmly established in post-communist states. Reason (R): Democratic institutions there were built in a hurry.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: judicial culture and independence were not established. R is true.

qa.q: Case: An engineer and a professor from Russia take up jobs abroad in 1995 because their salaries became worthless. This reflects which consequence?
qa.a: Decline of the middle class and migration of intellectuals
qa.e: The middle class was pushed to the margins and many skilled people migrated.

qa.q: Which two regions of Russia saw violent secessionist movements after 1991?
qa.a: Chechnya and Dagestan
qa.e: Chechnya and Dagestan are inside Russia; the others are separate states or provinces elsewhere.

qa.q: Nagorno-Karabakh is a region where local Armenians wanted to separate from:
qa.a: Azerbaijan
qa.e: The region lies in Azerbaijan; its Armenian population sought to join Armenia.

qa.q: NATO intervened with bombing in 1999 over the conflict in:
qa.a: Kosovo
qa.e: The Kosovo crisis in Yugoslavia led to NATO's bombing of Yugoslavia.

qa.q: Which former Soviet republic saw a civil war that lasted about ten years, until 2001?
qa.a: Tajikistan
qa.e: Tajikistan's civil war ran for about a decade.

qa.q: Why has Central Asia become a zone of competition among outside powers?
qa.a: It has rich oil and gas reserves
qa.e: Its hydrocarbon wealth attracts Russia, China, the USA and others.

qa.q: The break-up of Yugoslavia led to ethnic conflict in:
qa.a: Bosnia-Herzegovina
qa.e: Bosnia-Herzegovina, a former Yugoslav province, saw ethnic conflict.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Moscow's handling of the Chechen rebellion drew criticism. Reason (R): Its military bombings led to many human rights violations.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the human rights violations explain the criticism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): All former communist states moved peacefully to democracy after 1991. Reason (R): Several regions witnessed civil wars and secessionist movements.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false, as the many conflicts show. R is true.

qa.q: In which year did India and the USSR sign the Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation?
qa.e: It was signed in August 1971, months before the Bangladesh war.

qa.q: India-Russia relations rest on a shared vision of:
qa.a: A multipolar world order
qa.e: Both favour several powers coexisting, collective security and decisions through the UN.

qa.q: Over 80 bilateral agreements were signed as part of the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement of:
qa.e: The Strategic Agreement dates from 2001.

qa.q: Why is India important for Russia?
qa.a: India is one of the largest buyers of Russian arms
qa.e: India is a major market for Russian defence equipment.

qa.q: Which of these is a reason why Russia is important for India?
qa.a: Access to Central Asia and energy supplies
qa.e: Russia matters for energy, Central Asian access, Kashmir and balancing China.

qa.q: India seeks partnership with Central Asian states such as Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan mainly for:
qa.a: Energy and connectivity
qa.e: These states are rich in oil and gas, so India seeks energy ties.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India keeps good relations with all post-communist countries. Reason (R): The strongest of these relations is with Russia.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A; the strength of ties with Russia is not the reason India is friendly with all.

qa.q: Case: An Indian diplomat says, 'We want many centres of power, decisions through the UN and disputes settled by talks.' Which country shares this vision most closely, according to your book?
qa.a: Russia
qa.e: India and Russia both favour a multipolar world with collective decision-making.

qa.q: The Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC) was established in 1948 to:
qa.a: Channel Marshall Plan aid to western Europe
qa.e: The OEEC was set up to distribute US aid under the Marshall Plan.

qa.q: The Council of Europe was established in:
qa.e: It came a year after the OEEC.

qa.q: Under which plan did the USA give massive financial help to rebuild Europe after 1945?
qa.a: Marshall Plan
qa.e: The Marshall Plan funded European recovery.

qa.q: After the Cold War, which of these emerged as an alternative centre of power to the USA?
qa.a: The European Union
qa.e: The EU, ASEAN and China are seen as alternative centres of power.

qa.q: What is the main source of influence of the new centres of power such as the EU and ASEAN?
qa.a: Economic strength and regional cooperation
qa.e: Their power rests largely on economic integration and cooperation.

qa.q: The European Coal and Steel Community (1951) brought together how many western European countries?
qa.e: Six countries formed it: France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Regional organisations can limit the dominance of a single superpower. Reason (R): They pool the economic strength of member states.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; combined economic weight is what lets them act as counterweights.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Marshall Plan was launched by the Soviet Union. Reason (R): European economies were badly damaged after the Second World War.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the USA launched the Marshall Plan. R is true.

qa.q: The European Union was established by the Maastricht Treaty in:
qa.e: The Maastricht Treaty, signed in 1992, founded the EU.

qa.q: The European Economic Community was set up in:
qa.e: The Treaty of Rome of 1957 created the EEC.

qa.q: Euro notes and coins were introduced in:
qa.e: The euro came into public use as cash in 2002.

qa.q: The EU flag shows:
qa.a: A circle of twelve gold stars on a blue background
qa.e: There are always twelve stars, standing for unity and harmony, not the number of members.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT something the EU has set up?
qa.a: A single army replacing all national armies
qa.e: Members still keep their own armed forces.

qa.q: The Maastricht Treaty moved Europe from mainly economic cooperation towards:
qa.a: Political union as well
qa.e: The EU added political cooperation, foreign policy and justice to the economic union.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The EU has started to act like a nation-state in some ways. Reason (R): It has its own flag, anthem, founding date and currency.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these state-like symbols and institutions explain the comparison.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The number of stars on the EU flag changes whenever a new member joins. Reason (R): The circle of stars stands for unity and harmony among European peoples.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the flag always has twelve stars. R is true.

qa.q: Which EU member holds a permanent seat in the UN Security Council?
qa.a: France
qa.e: France is one of the five permanent members; Germany and others are not.

qa.q: Which of these shows the EU's ECONOMIC influence?
qa.a: The euro can pose a challenge to the US dollar
qa.e: Currency strength is economic; the others are military or political.

qa.q: A major limitation of the EU as a power is that:
qa.a: Its members have their own foreign relations and defence policies
qa.e: Member states often disagree, which limits common action abroad.

qa.q: 'Euroscepticism' means:
qa.a: Resistance to the growing power and integration of the EU
qa.e: Eurosceptics oppose giving more authority to the EU.

qa.q: The United Kingdom formally left the European Union in:
qa.e: The referendum was held in 2016, but the exit took effect in 2020.

qa.q: Which is an example of the EU's MILITARY strength?
qa.a: The combined armed forces of its members are among the largest in the world
qa.e: Combined forces and France's nuclear capacity show military strength.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The EU is an important economic power. Reason (R): The EU has a common foreign policy that all members always obey.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: members keep their own foreign policies and often disagree.

qa.q: Case: In a crisis, two EU members support military action abroad while three others refuse. What limitation of the EU does this show?
qa.a: Member states keep separate foreign and defence policies
qa.e: Divisions over foreign and military action limit the EU's power.

qa.q: ASEAN was established in:
qa.e: It was founded by the Bangkok Declaration in 1967.

qa.q: Which country was NOT a founding member of ASEAN?
qa.a: Vietnam
qa.e: Vietnam joined later; the five founders were Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.

qa.q: ASEAN was set up by signing the:
qa.a: Bangkok Declaration
qa.e: The 1967 Bangkok Declaration founded ASEAN.

qa.q: The 'ASEAN Way' refers to:
qa.a: An informal, non-confrontational and cooperative style of interaction
qa.e: It stresses consensus and respect for sovereignty.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the three pillars of the ASEAN Community?
qa.a: ASEAN Military Alliance
qa.e: The three pillars are security, economic and socio-cultural; there is no military alliance pillar.

qa.q: The ASEAN Regional Forum, which coordinates security and foreign policy, was set up in:
qa.e: The ARF was created in 1994.

qa.q: Assertion (A): ASEAN has not tried to become a supranational body like the EU. Reason (R): The ASEAN Way stresses respect for national sovereignty and informal cooperation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the ASEAN Way explains why ASEAN avoids EU-style supranational structures.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The ASEAN Security Community is based on the idea that disputes should be settled without armed conflict. Reason (R): ASEAN was founded by the European Union.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: ASEAN was founded by five Southeast Asian states in 1967.

qa.q: AFTA stands for:
qa.a: ASEAN Free Trade Area
qa.e: AFTA aims to cut tariffs and boost trade among ASEAN members.

qa.q: India's policy of strengthening ties with Southeast Asia from 1991 was called the:
qa.a: Look East policy
qa.e: Look East (later Act East) built economic and strategic links with ASEAN.

qa.q: ASEAN Vision 2020 emphasised:
qa.a: An outward-looking role for ASEAN in the international community
qa.e: It aimed for ASEAN to play an active role globally.

qa.q: India's Look East policy was renamed and expanded as the Act East policy in:
qa.e: Act East began in 2014, building on Look East (1991).

qa.q: With which ASEAN countries did India sign bilateral free trade agreements?
qa.a: Singapore and Thailand
qa.e: These two were India's early FTA partners in ASEAN.

qa.q: Which statement about ASEAN's economy is correct?
qa.a: It is one of the fastest-growing regions in the world
qa.e: ASEAN's rapid growth makes it an attractive partner.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many big powers seek closer ties with ASEAN. Reason (R): ASEAN is economically dynamic and strategically placed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its economic and strategic importance attracts outside powers.

qa.q: Case: An Indian company sets up a factory in Thailand to sell across Southeast Asia with lower tariffs. Which ASEAN arrangement helps it most?
qa.a: The ASEAN Free Trade Area
qa.e: AFTA lowers tariffs among members, helping firms sell across the region.

qa.q: Who announced China's 'open door' policy in 1978?
qa.a: Deng Xiaoping
qa.e: Deng launched market reforms and opened China to foreign capital.

qa.q: After 1949, China's economy was modelled on:
qa.a: The Soviet model
qa.e: China built state-owned heavy industry like the USSR.

qa.q: Agriculture in China was privatised in:
qa.e: Farming was privatised in 1982, before industry.

qa.q: Which did China privatise in 1998?
qa.a: Industry
qa.e: Industry followed agriculture, in 1998.

qa.q: Who proposed the 'four modernisations' in 1973?
qa.a: Zhou Enlai
qa.e: Zhou Enlai proposed modernising agriculture, industry, science and technology, and the military.

qa.q: Which of these was one of the four modernisations?
qa.a: Science and technology
qa.e: The four were agriculture, industry, science and technology, and the military.

qa.q: Assertion (A): China did not follow shock therapy. Reason (R): It opened its economy step by step, starting with agriculture and Special Economic Zones.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the gradual, staged approach is the opposite of shock therapy.

qa.q: Assertion (A): China's early Soviet-style model produced very fast growth in agriculture. Reason (R): Under this model, China had cut its links with the capitalist world.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: agricultural output stayed low. R is true.

qa.q: China became a member of the World Trade Organisation in:
qa.e: China's WTO entry came in 2001.

qa.q: Which of these is a problem that came with China's economic reforms?
qa.a: Rising inequality between coastal and inland regions
qa.e: Benefits were uneven, and inequality grew.

qa.q: Which region of China gained more from reforms?
qa.a: Coastal areas
qa.e: Coastal areas with SEZs and ports drew most investment.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a problem of China's growth?
qa.a: A shortage of foreign investment
qa.e: China actually became a major destination for foreign investment.

qa.q: How did China's economic growth affect its position in Asia?
qa.a: It increased China's regional influence
qa.e: Economic power brought greater regional and global influence.

qa.q: Joining the WTO meant that China:
qa.a: Opened its economy further to world trade
qa.e: WTO membership required further opening of trade.

qa.q: Assertion (A): China's economic rise has made it an important centre of power. Reason (R): China has become a major destination for foreign investment and trade.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its economic weight explains its new status.

qa.q: Assertion (A): China's reforms reduced all forms of inequality. Reason (R): Coastal regions and cities gained more from the reforms than rural and inland areas.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows inequality grew.

qa.q: The military conflict between India and China took place in:
qa.e: The border war was fought in 1962.

qa.q: Whose visit to China in 1988 began normalisation of India-China relations?
qa.a: Rajiv Gandhi
qa.e: Rajiv Gandhi visited in December 1988.

qa.q: After the 1962 conflict, full diplomatic relations between India and China were restored in:
qa.e: Ambassador-level relations were restored in 1976; Rajiv Gandhi's visit came in 1988.

qa.q: Which of these is a continuing source of friction between India and China?
qa.a: The border dispute
qa.e: The unresolved border remains a major issue.

qa.q: Which statement best describes India-China relations today?
qa.a: A mix of competition and cooperation
qa.e: They trade heavily and cooperate in forums, yet compete and dispute the border.

qa.q: The slogan of warm India-China ties in the 1950s was:
qa.a: Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai
qa.e: This slogan captured early friendship.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Trade between India and China has grown fast since the 1990s. Reason (R): India and China fought a border war in 1962.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but the 1962 war does not explain the growth of trade.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India and China cooperate in multilateral forums. Reason (R): India and China have resolved all their border disputes.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: the border question remains unresolved.

qa.q: Which article of Japan's Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right?
qa.a: Article 9
qa.e: Article 9 limits Japan's military role.

qa.q: Japan is the only country to have suffered:
qa.a: Destruction by nuclear bombs
qa.e: Hiroshima and Nagasaki were bombed in 1945.

qa.q: The term 'Miracle on the Han River' refers to:
qa.a: South Korea's rapid economic growth
qa.e: It describes South Korea's fast industrial rise.

qa.q: South Korea became a member of the OECD in:
qa.e: It joined the OECD in 1996.

qa.q: Which is true of Japan's natural resources?
qa.a: It has few natural resources and imports most raw materials
qa.e: Japan's power rests on technology and industry, not natural resources.

qa.q: Which factor helped South Korea's rapid development?
qa.a: Land reform and investment in human resources
qa.e: Land reform, rural development, human resources and industrialisation fuelled growth.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Japan's military role is limited. Reason (R): Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; Article 9 explains the limited military role.

qa.q: Case: A class compares the EU with Japan as 'centres of power'. Which difference is correct?
qa.a: The EU is a regional union of states; Japan is a single state
qa.e: The EU pools many states' strength, whereas Japan is one country that rose through its economy.

qa.q: Which of these is the capital of Bhutan?
qa.a: Thimphu
qa.e: Thimphu is Bhutan's capital; Kathmandu is Nepal's.

qa.q: Which country is NOT usually counted in the core list of South Asian countries?
qa.a: Indonesia
qa.e: Indonesia is in Southeast Asia and belongs to ASEAN.

qa.q: Which two countries are often included in discussions of South Asia besides the seven core countries?
qa.a: Afghanistan and Myanmar
qa.e: Afghanistan and Myanmar are frequently discussed as part of the region.

qa.q: The capital of the Maldives is:
qa.a: Malé
qa.e: Malé is the capital of the island nation of the Maldives.

qa.q: Which natural feature forms South Asia's northern boundary?
qa.a: The Himalayas
qa.e: The Himalayas lie to the north; seas and the ocean lie to the south.

qa.q: Which statement about political systems in South Asia is correct?
qa.a: They are diverse: democracies, monarchies and periods of military rule
qa.e: The region has a wide variety of political systems.

qa.q: Assertion (A): South Asia has a distinctive geographic unity. Reason (R): It is bounded by the Himalayas in the north and by seas and the Indian Ocean in the south.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the natural boundaries give the region its unity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India and Sri Lanka have remained democracies since independence. Reason (R): Bhutan is a republic with no king.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy.

qa.q: Who took over Pakistan's administration in 1958?
qa.a: General Ayub Khan
qa.e: Ayub Khan's takeover in 1958 began military rule.

qa.q: Which general removed Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's government in 1977?
qa.a: Zia-ul-Haq
qa.e: General Zia-ul-Haq took over in 1977.

qa.q: In 1988, a democratically elected government came to power in Pakistan under:
qa.a: Benazir Bhutto
qa.e: Benazir Bhutto led the government elected in 1988.

qa.q: The army took over in Pakistan again in 1999 under:
qa.a: General Pervez Musharraf
qa.e: Musharraf removed the elected government in 1999.

qa.q: Which is a reason for the failure of democracy to take firm root in Pakistan?
qa.a: Social dominance of the military, clergy and landowning aristocracy
qa.e: These groups dominated society and weakened democratic institutions.

qa.q: How did the Cold War affect democracy in Pakistan?
qa.a: The USA and others backed military rulers for their own strategic interests
qa.e: Outside powers tolerated or supported military regimes that served their interests.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Pro-military groups in Pakistan became stronger over time. Reason (R): Pakistan's conflicts with India made the army's role seem more important.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; tension with India strengthened arguments for military influence.

qa.q: Case: A Pakistani elected government holds office, but major decisions on defence and foreign policy are shaped by army generals. Which feature of Pakistan's politics does this show?
qa.a: Continued army influence over elected governments
qa.e: Even under civilian rule, the army keeps strong influence.

qa.q: Before 1971, Bangladesh was known as:
qa.a: East Pakistan
qa.e: It was the eastern wing of Pakistan from 1947 to 1971.

qa.q: Who led the Awami League in the struggle for Bangladesh?
qa.a: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman
qa.e: Sheikh Mujib led the Awami League and the freedom movement.

qa.q: In the 1970 elections, the Awami League:
qa.a: Won almost all seats in East Pakistan
qa.e: Its sweep gave it a majority in the proposed Constituent Assembly.

qa.q: Which change did Sheikh Mujib make to the constitution in 1975?
qa.a: He introduced a presidential system and abolished all parties except the Awami League
qa.e: These changes concentrated power before his assassination later in 1975.

qa.q: Bangladesh has had representative democracy based on multi-party elections since:
qa.e: After Ershad stepped down in 1990, elections in 1991 restored democracy.

qa.q: India's role in 1971 was to:
qa.a: Support the freedom struggle of the people of East Pakistan
qa.e: India backed the struggle, and the December 1971 war led to Bangladesh's independence.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The people of East Pakistan resented West Pakistan's domination. Reason (R): Urdu was imposed on them, and their elected majority was not honoured.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains the resentment.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Bangladesh has never had military-led rule. Reason (R): The constitution of Bangladesh originally declared it secular, democratic and socialist.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Ziaur Rahman and Ershad led military-backed rule. R is true.

qa.q: Nepal abolished its monarchy and became a democratic republic in:
qa.e: The monarchy ended in 2008; the new Constitution came in 2015.

qa.q: Which group led an armed insurgency against the monarchy in Nepal from the 1990s?
qa.a: The Maoists
qa.e: The Maoists fought against the monarchy and the ruling elite.

qa.q: The April 2006 pro-democracy movement in Nepal forced the king to:
qa.a: Restore the House of Representatives
qa.e: The king restored the parliament he had dissolved.

qa.q: Nepal's new Constitution was adopted in:
qa.e: After the monarchy was abolished, a new Constitution came in 2015.

qa.q: What did the 1990 pro-democracy movement in Nepal achieve?
qa.a: The king accepted a new democratic constitution
qa.e: The 1990 movement brought a democratic constitution while the monarchy continued.

qa.q: Who were part of the 2006 movement for democracy in Nepal?
qa.a: The Seven-Party Alliance, the Maoists and social activists
qa.e: A broad coalition joined the protests.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Nepal is now a democratic republic. Reason (R): Its monarchy was abolished in 2008.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the abolition of the monarchy made Nepal a republic.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Democracy in Nepal was fully stable after 1990. Reason (R): The Maoist insurgency spread in many parts of Nepal in the 1990s.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the 1990s were turbulent. R is true.

qa.q: What does LTTE stand for?
qa.a: Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam
qa.e: The LTTE fought for Tamil Eelam.

qa.q: India sent the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) to Sri Lanka in:
qa.e: India signed an accord and sent the IPKF in 1987.

qa.q: The civil war in Sri Lanka ended in 2009 when:
qa.a: The LTTE was defeated by the Sri Lankan army
qa.e: The army defeated the LTTE in 2009.

qa.q: The root of the ethnic conflict in Sri Lanka was:
qa.a: Sinhala majoritarianism and neglect of the Tamil minority
qa.e: Majority domination alienated Tamils.

qa.q: Which statement about Sri Lanka's development is correct?
qa.a: It achieved high levels of human development despite the conflict
qa.e: It controlled population growth early and was the first in the region to liberalise.

qa.q: Why was the IPKF intervention unpopular?
qa.a: The IPKF ended up fighting the LTTE and many Sri Lankans saw it as interference
qa.e: It became entangled in fighting and was widely criticised.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sri Lanka has retained a democratic political system since independence. Reason (R): Sri Lanka faced a long ethnic conflict.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, but the conflict does not explain why democracy survived.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sri Lanka was the first country in South Asia to liberalise its economy. Reason (R): The LTTE won the civil war and created Tamil Eelam.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: the LTTE was defeated in 2009.

qa.q: The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan was signed in:
qa.e: It was signed in 1960 with World Bank mediation.

qa.q: Which institution mediated the Indus Waters Treaty?
qa.a: The World Bank
qa.e: The World Bank brokered the treaty.

qa.q: Sir Creek is a dispute over:
qa.a: A boundary line in the Rann of Kutch
qa.e: Sir Creek is a strip of water in the Rann of Kutch.

qa.q: The Kargil conflict between India and Pakistan took place in:
qa.e: It was fought in 1999, a year after the nuclear tests.

qa.q: In which year did both India and Pakistan conduct nuclear tests?
qa.e: India tested in May 1998 and Pakistan followed soon after.

qa.q: Which has been the core issue between India and Pakistan since 1947?
qa.a: Kashmir
qa.e: Kashmir has been central to most conflicts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The arms race between India and Pakistan intensified after 1998. Reason (R): Both countries conducted nuclear tests in 1998.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, and the tests explain the sharper arms race.

qa.q: How many years separate the first India-Pakistan war (1947-48 ended in 1948) and the Kargil conflict (1999)?
Which neighbour's citizens can travel and work in India without visas and passports under a treaty?
qa.a: Nepal
qa.e: The India-Nepal treaty allows this open movement.

qa.q: Operation Cactus (1988) refers to India's help to:
qa.a: The Maldives against a coup attempt by mercenaries
qa.e: India sent forces at the Maldives' request.

qa.q: Which neighbour has close cooperation with India on hydroelectric projects?
qa.a: Bhutan
qa.e: India supports many hydro projects in Bhutan.

qa.q: A major issue between India and Bangladesh has been:
qa.a: Sharing of Ganga and Brahmaputra waters
qa.e: Water sharing, migration and border issues are key topics.

qa.q: Which factor has caused friction in India-Nepal relations?
qa.a: Nepal's ties with China and the Maoist movement
qa.e: Nepal's warm ties with China and Maoist activity worried India.

qa.q: India helped Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami. Which other step improved ties?
qa.a: A free trade agreement
qa.e: The free trade agreement strengthened economic ties.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India-Bhutan relations are very close. Reason (R): Bhutan's king helped flush out guerrillas from north-eastern India, and India supports Bhutan's hydro projects.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; security cooperation and economic support explain the close ties.

qa.q: Case: Floodwaters in the Brahmaputra affect both Assam and Bangladesh, and both countries share early warning data. This shows:
qa.a: Cooperation on disaster management alongside disputes
qa.e: Neighbours cooperate on shared problems even when other disputes exist.

qa.q: SAARC was established in:
qa.e: SAARC came into being in 1985.

qa.q: The SAFTA agreement was signed in:
qa.e: SAFTA was signed in 2004 and came into effect in 2006.

qa.q: What is the main aim of SAFTA?
qa.a: Lowering trade barriers among South Asian countries
qa.e: SAFTA aims at freer trade in the region.

qa.q: The main obstacle to SAARC's progress has been:
qa.a: India-Pakistan tensions
qa.e: Rivalry between the two largest members has held SAARC back.

qa.q: Why did some smaller South Asian states fear SAFTA?
qa.a: They worried India would dominate their markets
qa.e: Smaller economies feared competition from India's large economy.

qa.q: Which outside power has close strategic ties with Pakistan?
qa.a: China
qa.e: China's partnership with Pakistan is a key factor in South Asia.

qa.q: Assertion (A): SAARC has made limited progress. Reason (R): Political differences, especially between India and Pakistan, have slowed it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R is the main reason for slow progress.

qa.q: Assertion (A): SAARC was formed by ASEAN countries. Reason (R): SAARC aims at regional cooperation by peaceful means.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: SAARC was formed by South Asian states. R is true.

qa.q: The United Nations was established in:
qa.e: It was founded right after the Second World War.

qa.q: How many states signed the UN Charter when the UN was founded?
qa.e: 51 states signed the Charter; membership has since grown to 193.

qa.q: How many member states does the UN have today?
qa.e: There are 193 member states.

qa.q: The UN was founded as a successor to:
qa.a: The League of Nations
qa.e: The League had failed; the UN replaced it.

qa.q: Which of these is an aim of the UN?
qa.a: Preventing international conflict and fostering cooperation
qa.e: The UN aims at peace and cooperation, not world government.

qa.q: Why are international organisations useful to states?
qa.a: They provide rules, forums and information that make cooperation easier
qa.e: They lower the costs of working together but cannot guarantee peace.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The UN was set up in 1945. Reason (R): The League of Nations had failed to prevent the Second World War.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the League's failure explains the creation of a new body.

qa.q: By how many has UN membership grown since the 51 founding members?
How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?
qa.e: There are 5 permanent members with veto power.

qa.q: How many non-permanent members does the Security Council have?
qa.e: Ten non-permanent members are elected for two-year terms.

qa.q: Non-permanent members of the Security Council are elected for a term of:
qa.a: 2 years
qa.e: They are elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms.

qa.q: Which of these countries is NOT a permanent member of the Security Council?
qa.a: Germany
qa.e: The P5 are the USA, Russia, the UK, France and China.

qa.q: The International Court of Justice is located at:
qa.a: The Hague
qa.e: The ICJ sits at The Hague in the Netherlands.

qa.q: Which UN principal organ has suspended its operations?
qa.a: Trusteeship Council
qa.e: With no trust territories left, the Trusteeship Council suspended operations.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A resolution can fail in the Security Council even if 14 members support it. Reason (R): Each permanent member can veto a substantive decision.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; a single veto from a P5 member blocks the resolution.

qa.q: What is the total membership of the Security Council?
qa.e: 5 permanent + 10 non-permanent = 15.

qa.q: Who was the first Secretary-General of the UN?
qa.a: Trygve Lie
qa.e: Trygve Lie of Norway was the first.

qa.q: Which Secretary-General came from Ghana?
qa.a: Kofi Annan
qa.e: Kofi Annan of Ghana served from 1997 to 2006.

qa.q: António Guterres, who became Secretary-General in 2017, is from:
qa.a: Portugal
qa.e: Guterres is Portuguese.

qa.q: Which UN agency deals with refugees?
qa.a: UNHCR
qa.e: UNHCR is the UN High Commissioner for Refugees.

qa.q: Which UN body lists World Heritage Sites?
qa.a: UNESCO
qa.e: UNESCO works on education, science and culture.

qa.q: Which Secretary-General came from Burma (now Myanmar)?
qa.a: U Thant
qa.e: U Thant was the first Asian Secretary-General.

qa.q: The Secretary-General is appointed by:
qa.a: The General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council
qa.e: The Security Council recommends and the General Assembly appoints.

qa.q: Assertion (A): UNHRC and UNHCR are the same body. Reason (R): UNHCR protects refugees, while UNHRC monitors human rights.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: they are different bodies. R is true and shows the difference.

qa.q: Which of these is a reason why the UN needs reform after the Cold War?
qa.a: Membership has grown and new challenges have emerged
qa.e: Growth in membership, unipolarity and new problems like terrorism call for reform.

qa.q: The two basic kinds of UN reform are:
qa.a: Reform of structures and processes, and review of issues within its jurisdiction
qa.e: Reform concerns how the UN works and what issues it handles.

qa.q: A complaint in the 1992 General Assembly resolution was that the Security Council:
qa.a: No longer represented contemporary political realities
qa.e: It was seen as reflecting the world of 1945 and mainly Western values.

qa.q: Which of these is a proposed criterion for new permanent members?
qa.a: A substantial contributor to the UN budget
qa.e: Budget contribution is among the proposed criteria.

qa.q: Which criterion aims at making the Security Council more representative?
qa.a: Adding countries that reflect the world's diversity of geography, economic systems and culture
qa.e: Representativeness is one proposed criterion.

qa.q: Which of these is a proposed criterion relating to political values?
qa.a: Respect for democracy and human rights
qa.e: Respect for democracy and human rights is a proposed criterion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many countries argue that the Security Council should be expanded. Reason (R): It was designed in 1945 and does not reflect today's membership and power balance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the outdated design explains demands for expansion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The proposed criteria for new permanent members are accepted by all countries without debate. Reason (R): One criterion is being a big nation in terms of population.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: each criterion is debated. R is true.

qa.q: Which body was created in 2005 to help post-conflict countries?
qa.a: Peacebuilding Commission
qa.e: The Peacebuilding Commission supports recovery after conflict.

qa.q: The 2005 world summit agreed to create:
qa.a: A Human Rights Council
qa.e: The Human Rights Council began work in 2006.

qa.q: Which UN organ did leaders agree to wind up in 2005?
qa.a: Trusteeship Council
qa.e: Its work was over, as no trust territories remained.

qa.q: The 2005 decisions included accepting the responsibility of the international community to:
qa.a: Protect people when national governments fail to protect them from atrocities
qa.e: This is the idea of the responsibility to protect.

qa.q: Which goals did leaders agree to achieve in 2005?
qa.a: Millennium Development Goals
qa.e: They committed to the Millennium Development Goals.

qa.q: The UN Democracy Fund was set up to:
qa.a: Support democracy around the world
qa.e: It supports democracy-building projects.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The UN reform debate includes the question of which issues the UN should handle. Reason (R): Problems like terrorism and climate change have grown in importance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; new problems are why the UN's jurisdiction is under review.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In 2005 the UN agreed to abolish the veto of the permanent members. Reason (R): In 2005 the UN created a Peacebuilding Commission.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the veto was not abolished. R is true.

qa.q: Which is a strong argument for India's permanent membership of the Security Council?
qa.a: Its long record in UN peacekeeping
qa.e: India's peacekeeping record is a key part of its case.

qa.q: Which is an objection raised against India's candidature?
qa.a: Concerns about its nuclear weapons capability
qa.e: Some states question India's nuclear status.

qa.q: What kind of Security Council does India want?
qa.a: An enlarged, more representative Council
qa.e: India supports enlargement to reflect today's world.

qa.q: India argues it should be a permanent member because it is:
qa.a: The largest democracy and among the most populous countries
qa.e: Population and democracy are central to India's claim.

qa.q: Which argument relates to regional representation in the debate on new members?
qa.a: Some say regions like Africa and South America also need permanent seats
qa.e: Representation of all regions is part of the debate.

qa.q: What does India say about the powers a new permanent member should have?
qa.a: The same powers as existing permanent members
qa.e: India seeks equal status, including the veto.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India has a strong claim to a permanent seat. Reason (R): India has taken part in almost all UN initiatives and in many peacekeeping missions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its UN record supports its claim.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Every UN member supports India's permanent membership. Reason (R): Some argue that India's rivalry with Pakistan would make it less effective.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: there are objections. R is true and is one such objection.

qa.q: Which is a source of US influence in the UN?
qa.a: It is the single largest contributor to the UN budget
qa.e: Funding gives the US great weight.

qa.q: The UN headquarters is located in:
qa.a: New York
qa.e: It is in New York; the ICJ is at The Hague.

qa.q: Why can the USA block Security Council action against its interests?
qa.a: It has a veto as a permanent member
qa.e: A single veto stops a substantive decision.

qa.q: Despite US dominance, the UN is useful because:
qa.a: It is a forum where states can discuss, criticise and seek compromise
qa.e: The UN provides an arena for dialogue.

qa.q: Who has great influence over the choice of the UN Secretary-General?
qa.a: The USA, among the permanent members
qa.e: The P5, especially the USA, strongly influence the choice.

qa.q: In a unipolar world, the UN's ability to balance the dominant power is:
qa.a: Limited
qa.e: The UN depends on the support of its strongest members.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The UN cannot easily balance US dominance. Reason (R): The USA has a veto and is the largest contributor to the UN budget.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the veto and funding explain the limit.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The UN has no value in a unipolar world. Reason (R): The UN offers states an arena to discuss and criticise even powerful countries' policies.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the UN remains valuable. R is true and shows why.

qa.q: The World Trade Organisation was set up in:
qa.e: The WTO began in 1995, succeeding GATT.

qa.q: The WTO succeeded which arrangement?
qa.a: GATT
qa.e: GATT was created after the Second World War and was replaced by the WTO.

qa.q: In the IMF, voting power depends on:
qa.a: The financial contribution of each member
qa.e: Votes are weighted, so rich countries hold more.

qa.q: Which is a criticism of the World Bank?
qa.a: It attaches strict conditions to its loans and pushes free market reforms
qa.e: Critics say it sets poor nations' economic agendas.

qa.q: Which area does the World Bank work in?
qa.a: Agriculture and rural development
qa.e: Its work includes human development, agriculture, environment, infrastructure and governance.

qa.q: Which is a common complaint about the WTO?
qa.a: Major economic powers dominate its rule-making
qa.e: Developing countries say the rules favour rich nations.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rich countries have the greatest say in the IMF. Reason (R): IMF votes are weighted according to each country's financial contribution.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; weighted voting explains the dominance of rich countries.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The World Bank was created in 1995. Reason (R): The World Bank gives loans and grants for development.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it was created in 1944; the WTO began in 1995. R is true.

qa.q: The International Atomic Energy Agency was established in:
qa.e: The IAEA was set up in 1957.

qa.q: The IAEA grew out of which proposal?
qa.a: 'Atoms for Peace' by US President Eisenhower
qa.e: Eisenhower's proposal led to the IAEA.

qa.q: What is the main role of the ILO?
qa.a: Setting labour standards and promoting workers' rights
qa.e: The ILO focuses on labour standards.

qa.q: Amnesty International is best described as:
qa.a: An NGO campaigning for human rights worldwide
qa.e: It is a non-governmental organisation.

qa.q: Which statement about Human Rights Watch is correct?
qa.a: It is an international NGO doing research and advocacy on human rights
qa.e: It draws attention to human rights abuses.

qa.q: Who is represented in the ILO's structure?
qa.a: Governments, employers and workers
qa.e: The ILO's structure brings together all three groups.

qa.q: Assertion (A): NGOs can influence governments and international organisations. Reason (R): NGOs gather information and mobilise public opinion.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; their research and campaigns are how they gain influence.

qa.q: Assertion (A): International organisations have become irrelevant and should be abolished. Reason (R): International organisations need reform to stay effective.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: they remain essential. R is true.

qa.q: In the simplest sense, security means:
qa.a: Freedom from threats
qa.e: Security at its core is freedom from threats.

qa.q: Which threats count as security threats?
qa.a: Those that endanger a society's core values and survival
qa.e: Only threats serious enough to endanger core values are security threats.

qa.q: In the traditional external notion of security, the greatest danger is:
qa.a: Military threat from another country
qa.e: Traditional security focuses on armed attack by other states.

qa.q: 'Deterrence' means:
qa.a: Preventing war by raising the costs of attack
qa.e: Deterrence works before war starts.

qa.q: 'Defence' as a security option is concerned with:
qa.a: Limiting or ending a war and denying the attacker its goals
qa.e: Defence operates once war has broken out.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the three basic options of a government facing war?
qa.a: Ignoring the threat completely
qa.e: The three options are surrender, deterrence and defence.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Security threats are seen as justifying extraordinary steps. Reason (R): Such threats endanger a society's core values and even its survival.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the seriousness of the threat explains the extraordinary response.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Traditional security mainly deals with threats such as epidemics. Reason (R): Traditional security focuses on military threats from other states.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: epidemics belong to non-traditional security. R is true.

qa.q: What is the aim of maintaining a balance of power?
qa.a: To prevent any one state from becoming strong enough to dominate others
qa.e: Balance of power stops any single state from dominating.

qa.q: Alliances are usually based on:
qa.a: National interests
qa.e: Because they rest on interests, alliances can shift when interests change.

qa.q: Why can alliances change over time?
qa.a: Because they are based on national interests, which can change
qa.e: Shifting interests lead to shifting alliances.

qa.q: Which of these is an INTERNAL security threat?
qa.a: A separatist movement
qa.e: Separatist movements arise within a state's borders.

qa.q: For many post-colonial states in Asia and Africa, the greater security threat came from:
qa.a: Internal conflicts and separatist movements
qa.e: Internal conflicts troubled many new states more than inter-state wars.

qa.q: In traditional security, how are states expected to protect their national interest if threatened?
qa.a: By building military strength and, if needed, using force
qa.e: Use of force is central to the traditional view.

qa.q: Assertion (A): States form alliances. Reason (R): Alliances help states deter or defend against attack by adding to their strength.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; added strength for deterrence and defence is why alliances form.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Alliances, once formed, never change. Reason (R): Alliances are based on national interests.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: alliances change as interests change. R is true.

qa.q: The Chemical Weapons Convention was signed in:
qa.e: The CWC came in 1992; the BWC was in 1972.

qa.q: Which is an example of DISARMAMENT?
qa.a: Biological Weapons Convention
qa.e: Disarmament bans whole classes of weapons, as the BWC does.

qa.q: The Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty of 1972 was signed between:
qa.a: The USA and the USSR
qa.e: It was a superpower arms control agreement.

qa.q: The NPT was signed in:
qa.e: The Non-Proliferation Treaty dates from 1968.

qa.q: Why does India regard the NPT as discriminatory?
qa.a: It allows states that tested before 1967 to keep nuclear weapons while denying others
qa.e: It freezes a world of nuclear 'haves' and 'have-nots'.

qa.q: Arms control differs from disarmament because arms control:
qa.a: Regulates the acquisition or development of weapons rather than banning a class of weapons
qa.e: Arms control limits and regulates; disarmament abolishes a class.

qa.q: Which is a confidence-building measure?
qa.a: Informing a rival about a planned military exercise
qa.e: Sharing information reduces suspicion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India has not signed the NPT. Reason (R): India considers the NPT discriminatory.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; India's view of the treaty as unfair explains its refusal.

qa.q: Human security gives priority to the protection of:
qa.a: People
qa.e: The focus shifts from the state to individuals.

qa.q: Which threat would the NARROW view of human security focus on?
qa.a: Violent threats to individuals
qa.e: The narrow view looks at violence against people.

qa.q: The broad view of human security adds which threats?
qa.a: Hunger, disease and natural disasters
qa.e: These kill more people than wars, so the broad view includes them.

qa.q: Which phrase sums up the broadest formulation of human security?
qa.a: Freedom from want and freedom from fear
qa.e: These two freedoms capture the wide scope of human security.

qa.q: Which is an example of a GLOBAL security threat?
qa.a: Global warming
qa.e: Global threats affect all countries and need joint action.

qa.q: Why do global security threats need international cooperation?
qa.a: No single country can deal with them alone
qa.e: Climate change and pandemics cross borders.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A state can be secure from external attack while its people are insecure. Reason (R): Human security focuses on threats to people, such as hunger and disease.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R shows why state security and human security can differ.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Non-traditional security deals only with threats from foreign armies. Reason (R): Non-traditional security includes threats like epidemics and global warming.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows the wider scope.

qa.q: Terrorism is best defined as:
qa.a: Political violence that targets civilians deliberately and indiscriminately
qa.e: Targeting civilians to spread fear is the core of terrorism.

qa.q: The 9/11 attacks took place in the USA in:
qa.e: Hijacked planes struck on 11 September 2001.

qa.q: Which is an ECONOMIC and SOCIAL right?
qa.a: Right to work
qa.e: The right to work is economic and social; the others are political rights.

qa.q: The debate on humanitarian intervention is about whether:
qa.a: The international community should intervene to stop abuses inside a country
qa.e: It concerns intervention to protect people from their own government.

qa.q: Which argument is raised by critics of humanitarian intervention?
qa.a: Powerful states decide when to intervene based on their own interests
qa.e: Critics see selective intervention driven by interests.

qa.q: Why is global poverty a security issue?
qa.a: It causes insecurity, conflict and migration
qa.e: Poverty and the North-South gap can fuel conflict and migration.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Terrorism is a non-traditional threat. Reason (R): Terrorists deliberately target civilians rather than only armies.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; targeting civilians to create fear makes terrorism different from traditional war.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The rights of indigenous peoples are a type of human right. Reason (R): Human rights include only freedom of speech and assembly.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: human rights also include economic, social and minority rights.

qa.q: What is the difference between refugees and internally displaced persons?
qa.a: Refugees cross international borders; IDPs stay within their own country
qa.e: Crossing a border is the key difference.

qa.q: Kashmiri Pandits who fled the Kashmir valley in the early 1990s are an example of:
qa.a: Internally displaced persons
qa.e: They moved within India, so they are IDPs.

qa.q: Which of these is a health epidemic mentioned as a global security threat?
qa.a: SARS
qa.e: SARS, HIV-AIDS, bird flu and COVID-19 are examples.

qa.q: How do epidemics spread across countries?
qa.a: Through migration, business, tourism and travel
qa.e: Global movement of people spreads disease.

qa.q: Why is migration an international security issue?
qa.a: Large movements of people affect many countries and are linked to poverty and conflict
qa.e: Migration from conflict and poverty involves many states.

qa.q: A family that flees a civil war and crosses into a neighbouring country to seek safety is:
qa.a: Refugees
qa.e: Crossing an international border makes them refugees.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The fight against epidemics needs international cooperation. Reason (R): Success in controlling a disease in one country depends on control in others.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because diseases cross borders, cooperation is essential.

qa.q: Assertion (A): HIV-AIDS is a traditional security threat. Reason (R): Epidemics spread through travel and migration.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: epidemics are non-traditional threats. R is true.

qa.q: Why do non-traditional threats need cooperation?
qa.a: They cross borders and cannot be dealt with by military force alone
qa.e: Threats like climate change and disease need joint action.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-governmental actor in cooperative security?
qa.a: The International Red Cross
qa.e: The Red Cross is an NGO; the others are intergovernmental.

qa.q: In cooperative security, force is used:
qa.a: Only as a last resort
qa.e: Force remains possible, but only when cooperation fails.

qa.q: Which personalities are cited as contributors to cooperative security?
qa.a: Nelson Mandela and Mother Teresa
qa.e: Moral leaders can mobilise cooperation.

qa.q: When may the international community sanction the use of force under cooperative security?
qa.a: When a government kills its own people or ignores their misery
qa.e: Force is a last resort against grave abuse.

qa.q: Cooperation between just two countries is called:
qa.a: Bilateral
qa.e: Bilateral means two-sided.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Businesses and corporations can contribute to cooperative security. Reason (R): Non-traditional threats need the cooperation of many actors besides governments.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the many actors involved explain why businesses matter.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Cooperative security means that no country ever uses force. Reason (R): Cooperation is preferred over confrontation in dealing with new threats.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: force can be a last resort. R is true.

qa.q: India conducted nuclear tests in which two years?
qa.e: India tested in 1974 and in 1998.

qa.q: Which of these is part of the component 'strengthening international norms and institutions'?
qa.a: Support for UN peacekeeping and disarmament
qa.e: International norms involve the UN, NAM and disarmament.

qa.q: India faced internal security challenges from militant groups in which regions, as listed in the book?
qa.a: Nagaland, Mizoram, Punjab and Kashmir
qa.e: These four regions are the book's examples.

qa.q: Why is economic development part of India's security strategy?
qa.a: Lifting citizens out of poverty and inequality makes people more secure
qa.e: Human security depends on reducing poverty.

qa.q: India joined the Kyoto Protocol in:
qa.e: India signed and ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2002.

qa.q: Which wars with Pakistan are mentioned as part of India's security experience?
qa.e: These are the India-Pakistan conflicts; 1962 was with China.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India has tried to deal with internal challenges through democratic means. Reason (R): India's political system gives communities a voice through elections and negotiation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the democratic system explains how India handles internal challenges.

qa.q: Case: India sends a medical battalion to a UN mission in South Sudan. Which component of its security strategy does this reflect?
qa.a: Strengthening international norms and institutions
qa.e: UN peacekeeping supports international institutions.

qa.q: 'Limits to Growth' (1972) was published by:
qa.a: The Club of Rome
qa.e: The Club of Rome, a global think tank, published it.

qa.q: The Brundtland Report was published in:
qa.e: 'Our Common Future' appeared in 1987.

qa.q: The title of the Brundtland Report was:
qa.a: Our Common Future
qa.e: It popularised sustainable development.

qa.q: Sustainable development means:
qa.a: Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
qa.e: It balances development with environmental protection.

qa.q: Which is listed as a global environmental concern?
qa.a: Depletion of the ozone layer
qa.e: Ozone depletion threatens all life on Earth.

qa.q: 'Limits to Growth' warned about:
qa.a: Depletion of Earth's resources with rapid population growth
qa.e: It linked population growth with resource depletion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Environmental issues became part of global politics. Reason (R): Problems like ozone depletion and loss of biodiversity cannot be solved by one state alone.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the global nature of the problems brought them into world politics.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Brundtland Report said traditional industrial growth was sustainable. Reason (R): The Brundtland Report popularised the idea of sustainable development.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it warned traditional growth was unsustainable. R is true.

qa.q: The Earth Summit was held in Rio de Janeiro in:
qa.e: The UN Conference on Environment and Development was held in June 1992.

qa.q: Agenda 21 is:
qa.a: A list of development practices for sustainable development adopted at Rio
qa.e: Agenda 21 was a key Rio outcome.

qa.q: Which was a major concern of the Global North at Rio?
qa.a: Ozone depletion and global warming
qa.e: Rich countries focused on these global issues.

qa.q: The Global South at Rio emphasised:
qa.a: The link between economic development and environmental management
qa.e: Developing countries stressed their right to develop.

qa.q: Which was a criticism of Agenda 21?
qa.a: It was biased in favour of economic growth over ecological conservation
qa.e: Critics felt growth was prioritised over ecology.

qa.q: Which conventions came out of the Rio Summit?
qa.a: Conventions on climate change and biodiversity
qa.e: Climate change and biodiversity conventions were Rio outcomes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Global South argued that the North should take more responsibility for environmental damage. Reason (R): Much of the damage was caused by industrialisation in developed countries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains the South's demand.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Only governments took part in the Rio Summit. Reason (R): Thousands of NGOs and many multinational corporations also took part.
