qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Which of these is a global commons?
qa.a: Outer space
qa.e: Outer space lies outside the jurisdiction of any one state.

qa.q: The Montreal Protocol (1987) deals with:
qa.a: Protection of the ozone layer
qa.e: It phases out ozone-depleting substances.

qa.q: The Antarctic Treaty was signed in:
qa.e: The Antarctic Treaty dates from 1959.

qa.q: The Antarctic Environmental Protocol was adopted in:
qa.e: It came in 1991.

qa.q: Why is cooperation over the global commons difficult?
qa.a: Scientific uncertainty and unequal technology between North and South
qa.e: Disagreement and inequality make joint management hard.

qa.q: 'Global commons' are best described as areas that:
qa.a: Lie outside the sovereign jurisdiction of any one state and need common governance
qa.e: No single state controls them.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The benefits of outer space are not shared equally. Reason (R): The North and South have very unequal technological and industrial capabilities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; unequal technology explains unequal benefits.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The ozone hole was discovered over the Arctic in the 1950s. Reason (R): The Montreal Protocol was adopted to protect the ozone layer.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the ozone hole over Antarctica was discovered in the mid-1980s. R is true.

qa.q: What does 'common but differentiated responsibilities' mean?
qa.a: All states share responsibility, but developed states bear more because of their past emissions and capabilities
qa.e: Common responsibility, differentiated by history and capacity.

qa.q: The Kyoto Protocol was agreed in:
qa.e: It was agreed at Kyoto, Japan, in 1997.

qa.q: Which countries were exempted from the targets under the Kyoto Protocol?
qa.a: India, China and other developing countries
qa.e: Developing countries were exempted under CBDR.

qa.q: The UNFCCC was adopted in:
qa.e: It came out of the Rio process in 1992.

qa.q: Why do developed countries bear more responsibility under CBDR?
qa.a: Their past industrialisation caused most greenhouse gas emissions
qa.e: Historical emissions are the key reason.

qa.q: The Paris Agreement of 2015 is different from Kyoto because:
qa.a: All countries make nationally determined contributions
qa.e: Paris brought all countries into climate action.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Developing countries argue they should not bear the same burden as developed countries. Reason (R): Their per capita emissions are low and their contribution to historical emissions is small.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R is the basis of the developing countries' argument.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Kyoto Protocol set targets for industrialised countries. Reason (R): The Kyoto Protocol was agreed in Rio de Janeiro.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: it was agreed in Kyoto, Japan.

qa.q: Common property resources are:
qa.a: Owned and managed by a community
qa.e: A group holds rights and duties over them.

qa.q: Which is an example of a common property resource in India?
qa.a: A sacred grove
qa.e: Sacred groves are protected by communities.

qa.q: Which of these is a reason for the decline of common property resources?
qa.a: Privatisation and population pressure
qa.e: Privatisation, intensive farming and population growth reduce them.

qa.q: Members of a group that holds common property have:
qa.a: Both rights and duties regarding its use and maintenance
qa.e: Rights come with duties of upkeep.

qa.q: How are rules for common property usually made?
qa.a: By mutual understanding and long-standing practice in the community
qa.e: Communities evolve their own norms.

qa.q: Why are sacred groves important environmentally?
qa.a: Community protection preserves biodiversity and water sources
qa.e: Cultural protection conserves nature.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sacred groves are often well protected. Reason (R): Local communities protect them through religious and cultural practices.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; community practices explain the protection.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Common property resources are increasing all over India. Reason (R): Intensive agriculture and population growth put pressure on them.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: they are declining. R is true and helps explain the decline.

qa.q: India signed and ratified the Kyoto Protocol in:
qa.e: India ratified it in August 2002.

qa.q: India's main argument at climate negotiations is that:
qa.a: Developing countries' per capita emissions are a tiny fraction of developed countries'
qa.e: Low per capita emissions support India's CBDR stand.

qa.q: The Energy Conservation Act was passed in:
qa.e: It came in 2001; the Electricity Act came in 2003.

qa.q: Which act encourages the use of renewable energy in India?
qa.a: Electricity Act 2003
qa.e: The Electricity Act 2003 promotes renewables.

qa.q: The Auto-fuel Policy aims to:
qa.a: Mandate cleaner fuels for vehicles
qa.e: It promotes cleaner fuels.

qa.q: What does India want developed countries to provide at climate summits?
qa.a: Finance and technology for developing countries
qa.e: India seeks climate finance and technology transfer.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India believes developed countries should lead in cutting emissions. Reason (R): Developed countries are responsible for most historical emissions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; historical responsibility underlies India's view.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India has taken no domestic steps on climate change. Reason (R): India argues for common but differentiated responsibilities.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: India has many domestic measures. R is true.

qa.q: The Narmada Bachao Andolan is an example of:
qa.a: An anti-dam movement
qa.e: It opposed large dams on the Narmada.

qa.q: The Franklin River campaign opposed a dam in:
qa.a: Australia
qa.e: This anti-dam campaign took place in Australia in the early 1980s.

qa.q: Groups in the Philippines campaigned against which company?
qa.a: Western Mining Corporation, an Australian company
qa.e: WMC was the target of anti-mining protests.

qa.q: Forest movements in the South are found in:
qa.a: Countries such as Mexico, Brazil, Indonesia and India
qa.e: Forest movements are widespread in the Global South.

qa.q: In Australia, opposition to mining came from:
qa.a: Anti-nuclear groups and defenders of indigenous rights
qa.e: These groups opposed mining in Australia.

qa.q: Which statement best describes environmental movements?
qa.a: They are diverse and among the most vibrant social movements
qa.e: They vary widely in issues, methods and regions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Anti-dam movements have spread to many countries. Reason (R): Large dams often displace people and change ecosystems.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the social and ecological costs of dams explain the spread of such movements.

qa.q: Assertion (A): All environmental movements focus only on dams. Reason (R): Some movements focus on forests and mining.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows the diversity.

qa.q: Resource geopolitics is about:
qa.a: Who gets what resources, when, where and how
qa.e: It concerns the politics of access to resources.

qa.q: Which region holds a large share of the world's oil reserves?
qa.a: West Asia, especially the Persian Gulf
qa.e: The Gulf region is central to oil geopolitics.

qa.q: Turkey, Syria and Iraq have had disputes over dams on which river?
qa.a: Euphrates
qa.e: Dams on the Euphrates have caused tension.

qa.q: During the Cold War, rich countries tried to secure:
qa.a: Steady supplies of strategic resources such as minerals and oil
qa.e: Strategic resources were vital for industry and defence.

qa.q: Why might freshwater lead to 'water wars'?
qa.a: It is scarce in many regions and rivers are shared by several countries
qa.e: Scarcity and shared rivers can cause conflict.

qa.q: Why does oil remain central to global politics?
qa.a: It is vital for the world economy and its wealth draws political struggle
qa.e: Oil's economic importance makes it strategic.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Shared rivers can cause disputes between countries. Reason (R): A dam built upstream can reduce the water flowing to downstream countries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains why shared rivers lead to disputes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Resource competition has played no role in history. Reason (R): Competition over resources contributed to European colonial expansion.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: The World Council of Indigenous Peoples was formed in:
qa.e: It was formed in 1975.

qa.q: Which is a key demand of indigenous peoples?
qa.a: Rights over their land and natural resources
qa.e: Land and resources are central to their survival.

qa.q: Indigenous peoples are best described as:
qa.a: Descendants of the original inhabitants of a territory before others arrived and became dominant
qa.e: They are the earlier inhabitants who were later dominated by newcomers.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of an indigenous people?
qa.a: The Mapuche of Chile
qa.e: The Mapuche are an indigenous people.

qa.q: Why do development projects often hurt indigenous peoples?
qa.a: They displace them from land central to their livelihood and culture
qa.e: Dams and mines often take their land.

qa.q: Which UN body did the UN set up to deal with indigenous issues?
qa.a: Working Group on Indigenous Populations
qa.e: This working group looked at indigenous peoples' rights.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indigenous peoples have brought their concerns to the UN. Reason (R): The World Council of Indigenous Peoples later received consultative status in the UN.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; consultative status is how their voice entered the UN.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indigenous peoples' issues are purely a matter of culture with no link to the environment. Reason (R): Indigenous peoples depend on land, forests and natural resources.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: their rights are closely tied to land and environment. R is true.

qa.q: Globalisation is fundamentally about:
qa.a: Flows of ideas, capital, goods and people across the world
qa.e: It is about worldwide flows that create interconnectedness.

qa.q: Which statement about globalisation is correct?
qa.a: It is multi-dimensional, with political, economic and cultural sides
qa.e: All three dimensions must be considered.

qa.q: What makes a set of flows count as globalisation?
qa.a: They are sustained and create worldwide interconnectedness
qa.e: Constant flows linking the world are the key.

qa.q: The effects of globalisation are best described as:
qa.a: Uneven across countries and groups
qa.e: Some gain more, some lose.

qa.q: Which is an example of a flow of PEOPLE?
qa.a: Nurses from Kerala working in the Gulf
qa.e: Migration for work is a flow of people.

qa.q: Which is an example of a flow of CAPITAL?
qa.a: A foreign company investing in an Indian factory
qa.e: Investment across borders is a capital flow.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Globalisation must not be seen only in economic terms. Reason (R): Globalisation also has political and cultural dimensions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Globalisation benefits every group in every country equally. Reason (R): Globalisation creates worldwide interconnectedness.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: effects are uneven. R is true.

qa.q: Which is the most important cause of globalisation according to your book?
qa.a: Technology
qa.e: Technological change made flows faster and easier.

qa.q: Which invention is listed as having changed communication and helped globalisation?
qa.a: The microchip
qa.e: The telegraph, telephone and microchip are key examples.

qa.q: Globalisation's historical roots include:
qa.a: Long-distance trade and colonialism
qa.e: Trade and colonialism linked distant regions centuries ago.

qa.q: What is new about contemporary globalisation?
qa.a: The scale and speed of flows
qa.e: Trade is old; what is new is speed and scale.

qa.q: How has technology affected the movement of capital?
qa.a: It allows capital to move very quickly across the world
qa.e: Electronic transfers move money instantly.

qa.q: Which older technology is compared with today's communication technologies for its effect on spreading ideas?
qa.a: Printing
qa.e: Printing once spread ideas widely, as the internet does today.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ideas, capital and goods move faster today than ever before. Reason (R): Technologies like the internet have transformed communication.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; technology explains the speed of flows.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Globalisation began only with the internet. Reason (R): Globalisation has historical roots in trade and colonialism.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: According to one view, globalisation has led to a shift from:
qa.a: A welfare state to a minimalist state
qa.e: The state withdraws from welfare to core functions.

qa.q: Which functions does a minimalist state still perform?
qa.a: Law and order and the security of citizens
qa.e: These are its core functions.

qa.q: Who becomes the prime determinant of economic and social priorities in the 'erosion' view?
qa.a: The market
qa.e: Market forces gain influence as the state retreats.

qa.q: Which argument supports the view that state capacity has increased?
qa.a: Technology helps the state collect information about citizens
qa.e: Better information can make governance more effective.

qa.q: Which view holds that globalisation has not seriously challenged state sovereignty?
qa.a: The state remains the basis of political community and controls security
qa.e: States still decide on law, order and security.

qa.q: How do multinational companies affect states in the 'erosion' view?
qa.a: They reduce governments' ability to take decisions on their own
qa.e: Their power can limit government choices.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Some scholars say globalisation has weakened the welfare state. Reason (R): Under globalisation, the market becomes the prime determinant of economic and social priorities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains the weakening of the welfare state.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Globalisation has made the state irrelevant. Reason (R): The state continues to handle law and order and national security.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Economic globalisation involves:
qa.a: Greater trade and investment and reduced restrictions on imports
qa.e: It means more economic flows between countries.

qa.q: Which has increased LEAST under globalisation?
qa.a: Movement of people across borders
qa.e: Developed countries restrict immigration.

qa.q: Which institutions are mentioned as playing a key role in economic globalisation?
qa.a: IMF and WTO
qa.e: These set economic and trade policies.

qa.q: Critics of economic globalisation argue that it:
qa.a: Increases economic inequality
qa.e: They say it benefits a small section.

qa.q: Supporters of economic globalisation argue that it:
qa.a: Raises growth and well-being for many
qa.e: They see more growth and opportunity.

qa.q: What is the purpose of social safety nets?
qa.a: To protect the economically weak from the negative effects of globalisation
qa.e: They cushion vulnerable groups.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The movement of people has not increased as much as goods and capital. Reason (R): Developed countries guard their borders and visa policies carefully.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Everyone agrees that economic globalisation benefits all equally. Reason (R): Economic globalisation reduces restrictions on trade and investment.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: there is sharp debate. R is true.

qa.q: 'McDonaldisation' refers to:
qa.a: Cultural homogenisation, the spread of a uniform Western culture
qa.e: It describes the fear of a single global culture.

qa.q: Cultural heterogenisation means:
qa.a: Cultures mixing to create new, distinctive hybrid forms
qa.e: Mixing makes cultures more varied.

qa.q: Wearing blue jeans with a khadi kurta is an example of:
qa.a: Cultural heterogenisation
qa.e: It combines Western and Indian dress into something new.

qa.q: Critics argue that cultural homogenisation is really:
qa.a: The imposition of Western, especially American, culture
qa.e: They see it as Western dominance.

qa.q: Which statement about outside cultural influences is supported in the book?
qa.a: They can enlarge choices and modify culture without overwhelming it
qa.e: Influences can enrich as well as threaten.

qa.q: The fear of cultural homogenisation is that:
qa.a: Traditional cultures may be weakened by a dominant Western culture
qa.e: A uniform culture may crowd out local ones.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Globalisation can create hybrid cultures. Reason (R): Cultures in contact with each other borrow and combine elements.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; mixing explains hybrid cultures.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Globalisation always makes all cultures identical. Reason (R): Some fear the spread of a uniform Western culture.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: heterogenisation also occurs. R is true.

qa.q: During colonial rule, India became:
qa.a: An exporter of raw materials and a consumer of finished goods
qa.e: Colonial trade made India a supplier of raw materials.

qa.q: After independence, India's economic policy was mainly:
qa.a: Protectionist, aiming at self-reliance
qa.e: India restricted imports and built domestic industry.

qa.q: India's major economic reforms began in:
qa.e: Reforms began in 1991 after a financial crisis.

qa.q: What triggered India's 1991 reforms?
qa.a: A financial crisis and the desire for higher growth
qa.e: The balance of payments crisis prompted reforms.

qa.q: Which is a criticism of India's experience with globalisation?
qa.a: Benefits may not have reached the poor equally
qa.e: Critics question who gained.

qa.q: Which sector is often cited as having gained after 1991?
qa.a: Information technology and services
qa.e: IT and services grew rapidly after reforms.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India opened its economy in 1991. Reason (R): India faced a serious financial crisis at that time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the crisis was a key reason for the reforms.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India followed an open, globalised economic policy right from 1947. Reason (R): After 1991, India sought to remove barriers to trade and investment.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: India was protectionist after 1947. R is true.

qa.q: The first meeting of the World Social Forum was held in:
qa.a: Porto Alegre, Brazil, in 2001
qa.e: The WSF began in Porto Alegre in 2001.

qa.q: The World Social Forum is:
qa.a: A platform for groups opposed to neo-liberal globalisation
qa.e: It brings together activists opposed to neo-liberal globalisation.

qa.q: Left critics of globalisation mainly argue that it:
qa.a: Makes the rich richer and the poor poorer
qa.e: Their concern is economic inequality.

qa.q: Which is a concern of RIGHT critics of globalisation?
qa.a: Loss of traditional culture
qa.e: The right worries about culture, self-reliance and the state.

qa.q: Indian groups resisted attempts by foreign firms to patent:
qa.a: Neem
qa.e: Patent attempts on neem were opposed.

qa.q: Which city hosted the World Social Forum in 2004?
qa.a: Mumbai
qa.e: The fourth WSF was held in Mumbai.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Critics of globalisation are not necessarily opposed to global interconnectedness itself. Reason (R): They mostly oppose a particular programme of globalisation that they see as a form of imperialism.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Case: A farmers' union protests the entry of a multinational seed company, and a cultural group objects to a foreign festival. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Both are forms of resistance to globalisation in India, from different concerns
qa.e: Economic and cultural objections are both part of resistance in India.

qa.q: Who delivered the 'Tryst with Destiny' speech?
qa.a: Jawaharlal Nehru
qa.e: Nehru spoke at midnight to the Constituent Assembly.

qa.q: The 'Tryst with Destiny' speech was addressed to:
qa.a: A special session of the Constituent Assembly
qa.e: Nehru addressed the Constituent Assembly at midnight.

qa.q: Which was the FIRST and immediate challenge for independent India?
qa.a: Shaping a nation that was united yet accommodative of diversity
qa.e: Unity and integrity came first.

qa.q: The challenge of 'development' meant:
qa.a: Ensuring the well-being of the entire society, not only some sections
qa.e: Development with equality and justice was the aim.

qa.q: The challenge of 'democracy' was mainly about:
qa.a: Establishing representative government with rights and the vote for all
qa.e: The Constitution guaranteed fundamental rights and universal franchise.

qa.q: India became independent on:
qa.a: 15 August 1947
qa.e: Independence came on 15 August 1947; the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Independent India had to build a united nation while respecting diversity. Reason (R): India has many languages, cultures and religions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; India's diversity is why unity had to be accommodative.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Independence in 1947 was a moment of pure celebration everywhere. Reason (R): Independence came along with the Partition of the country.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Partition brought violence and suffering. R is true.

qa.q: The 'two-nation theory' was advanced by:
qa.a: The Muslim League
qa.e: The Muslim League argued for a separate nation for Muslims.

qa.q: On what basis was the Partition of British India carried out?
qa.a: Religious majorities: Muslim-majority areas went to Pakistan
qa.e: The principle was religious majority.

qa.q: Why was Pakistan created in two wings?
qa.a: There was no single belt of Muslim-majority areas
qa.e: Muslim-majority areas were in the west and the east.

qa.q: Who was the leader of the North-West Frontier Province who opposed the two-nation theory?
qa.a: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
qa.e: Known as 'Frontier Gandhi', he opposed Partition, but his voice was ignored.

qa.q: Which two provinces were divided because they had large non-Muslim populations?
qa.a: Punjab and Bengal
qa.e: Punjab and Bengal were split at district level or below.

qa.q: Which of these was a difficulty in implementing Partition?
qa.a: Large minorities remained on both sides of the border
qa.e: Minorities on both sides faced great insecurity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Partition faced many difficulties. Reason (R): Muslim-majority areas did not form one continuous belt, and minorities lived on both sides.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R gives the reasons for the difficulties.

qa.q: Assertion (A): All Muslim-majority areas wanted to join Pakistan. Reason (R): Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan opposed the two-nation theory.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows the opposition in the NWFP.

qa.q: Which best describes the transfer of population during Partition?
qa.a: Large, abrupt, unplanned and tragic
qa.e: It was one of the largest and most tragic transfers in history.

qa.q: Which of these was divided between India and Pakistan after Partition?
qa.a: Financial assets, liabilities and government employees
qa.e: Even assets and staff had to be divided.

qa.q: Which group suffered particular violence during Partition?
qa.a: Women, many of whom were abducted and attacked
qa.e: Women faced abduction, assault and forced conversion.

qa.q: How did the Indian government respond to the refugee crisis?
qa.a: It set up camps and rehabilitation programmes
qa.e: Refugees were resettled through rehabilitation efforts.

qa.q: Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated on:
qa.a: 30 January 1948
qa.e: He was killed on 30 January 1948.

qa.q: What kind of state did India commit to after Partition?
qa.a: A secular state treating all religions equally
qa.e: India chose secularism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's leaders committed to secularism after 1947. Reason (R): Partition had been carried out on religious lines amid terrible communal violence.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the experience of communal violence strengthened the resolve for secularism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Partition caused little loss of life. Reason (R): Lakhs of people were killed in the communal violence.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: How many princely states were there at the time of independence?
qa.e: There were 565 princely states.

qa.q: Who led the integration of the princely states?
qa.a: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
qa.e: Patel, as Home Minister, led the process.

qa.q: The document by which a ruler agreed that his state would become part of India was the:
qa.a: Instrument of Accession
qa.e: Most rulers signed it before 15 August 1947.

qa.q: What did the British announce about princely states when they left?
qa.a: Paramountcy lapsed; rulers could join India or Pakistan or remain independent
qa.e: This created the danger of fragmentation.

qa.q: Which ruler announced that his state would remain independent?
qa.a: The ruler of Travancore
qa.e: Travancore and Hyderabad announced independence.

qa.q: Which was one of the considerations guiding the government's approach?
qa.a: Most people of the princely states wanted to join India
qa.e: Popular sentiment favoured joining India.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The integration of princely states was a major challenge in 1947. Reason (R): Rulers were legally free to remain independent after paramountcy lapsed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains the challenge.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The government was completely rigid in dealing with all princely states. Reason (R): The government was flexible in giving autonomy to some regions.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows flexibility.

qa.q: The ruler of Hyderabad was known by the title:
qa.a: Nizam
qa.e: The Nizam ruled Hyderabad.

qa.q: The Razakars were:
qa.a: A paramilitary force of the Nizam
qa.e: They used violence against the people.

qa.q: The Indian army moved into Hyderabad in:
qa.a: September 1948
qa.e: The police action came in September 1948.

qa.q: Manipur held elections under universal adult franchise in:
qa.a: June 1948
qa.e: Manipur held elections in June 1948, before the first general election.

qa.q: Why was the Manipur Merger Agreement of 1949 resented by many?
qa.a: It was signed without consulting the elected Legislative Assembly
qa.e: Bypassing the elected assembly caused anger.

qa.q: How was the Junagadh issue resolved?
qa.a: A plebiscite confirmed the people's wish to join India
qa.e: The plebiscite settled the matter in favour of India.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Nizam of Hyderabad eventually surrendered. Reason (R): The Indian army moved in to control the Nizam's forces in September 1948.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the military action led to the surrender.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Hyderabad was a small princely state with no popular movement. Reason (R): A peasant struggle took place in the Telangana region against the Nizam's rule.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Hyderabad was the largest state and had a strong movement. R is true.

qa.q: Potti Sriramulu fasted for a separate state for speakers of:
qa.a: Telugu
qa.e: He led the demand for a Telugu-speaking Andhra state.

qa.q: The States Reorganisation Act was passed in:
qa.e: The SRC was appointed in 1953; the Act came in 1956.

qa.q: How many states were created by the States Reorganisation Act of 1956?
qa.e: It created 14 states and 6 union territories.

qa.q: The States Reorganisation Commission was appointed in:
qa.e: It was appointed in 1953.

qa.q: Why were national leaders initially hesitant about linguistic states?
qa.a: They feared it might threaten unity so soon after Partition
qa.e: The trauma of Partition made leaders cautious.

qa.q: Where did the Congress recognise the linguistic principle in 1920?
qa.a: Nagpur session
qa.e: The Nagpur session of 1920 reorganised its provincial committees by language.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A separate Andhra state was announced in December 1952. Reason (R): Potti Sriramulu's death after a long fast led to widespread protests.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the protests after his death led to the announcement.

qa.q: How many years passed between the Nagpur session (1920) and the States Reorganisation Act (1956)?
Maharashtra and Gujarat were created from the Bombay state in:
qa.e: The bilingual Bombay state was split in 1960.

qa.q: Haryana was created out of Punjab in:
qa.e: Punjab was reorganised in 1966.

qa.q: Which three states were created in 2000?
qa.a: Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand
qa.e: These three were carved out in 2000.

qa.q: Telangana became a separate state in:
qa.e: It was carved out of Andhra Pradesh in 2014.

qa.q: Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura became states in:
qa.e: All three became states in 1972.

qa.q: Jharkhand was carved out of:
qa.a: Bihar
qa.e: Jharkhand was created from Bihar in 2000.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Linguistic reorganisation strengthened national unity. Reason (R): It accommodated regional diversity democratically instead of suppressing it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; accommodating diversity explains the strengthened unity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Linguistic states led to the break-up of India. Reason (R): Many states in India are organised mainly on the basis of language.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: unity was strengthened. R is true.

qa.q: Who was the first Chief Election Commissioner of India?
qa.a: Sukumar Sen
qa.e: Sukumar Sen conducted the first general elections.

qa.q: The Election Commission of India was set up in:
qa.e: It was set up in January 1950.

qa.q: Universal adult franchise means:
qa.a: Every adult citizen has the right to vote
qa.e: India gave the vote to all adults from the start.

qa.q: The first general election in India was held:
qa.a: From October 1951 to February 1952
qa.e: It stretched over several months.

qa.q: In the first two general elections, how did voters cast their vote?
qa.a: By dropping a ballot paper into the box of the candidate they chose, marked with a symbol
qa.e: Each candidate had a separate box with a symbol.

qa.q: By which year had the whole country shifted to Electronic Voting Machines?
qa.e: EVMs were used across the country by 2004.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's first general election was a remarkable achievement. Reason (R): It involved about 17 crore voters, most of whom were not literate.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the scale and challenges explain why it was remarkable.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indian voters had to pass a literacy test to vote in 1952. Reason (R): India adopted universal adult franchise.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows there was no such test.

qa.q: How many Lok Sabha seats did the Congress win in the 1952 election?
qa.e: The Congress won 364 of the 489 seats.

qa.q: Which party came second in the 1952 Lok Sabha election?
qa.a: Communist Party of India
qa.e: The CPI won 16 seats.

qa.q: Which party formed the government in Kerala in 1957?
qa.a: Communist Party of India
qa.e: The CPI won and E.M.S. Namboodiripad became Chief Minister.

qa.q: Who led the Communist government in Kerala in 1957?
qa.a: E.M.S. Namboodiripad
qa.e: E.M.S. Namboodiripad became Chief Minister.

qa.q: Under which article was the Kerala government dismissed in 1959?
qa.a: Article 356
qa.e: Article 356 deals with President's rule in states.

qa.q: Why did the Congress win a much larger share of seats than votes?
qa.a: The first-past-the-post system and a divided opposition
qa.e: FPTP rewards the leading candidate, and a split opposition helped the Congress.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Under FPTP, a party can win most seats without a majority of votes. Reason (R): The candidate who gets the most votes in a constituency wins, even if it is less than half.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: How many more seats did the Congress win than the CPI in 1952?
Which party is cited as an example of one-party dominance under non-democratic conditions?
qa.a: The PRI of Mexico
qa.e: The PRI ruled Mexico for about sixty years.

qa.q: How was the Congress's dominance different from that of the PRI?
qa.a: It was achieved through free and fair democratic elections
qa.e: Indian dominance was democratic.

qa.q: A major reason for the Congress's dominance was:
qa.a: Its legacy of leading the national movement and its wide organisation
qa.e: It inherited the national movement's prestige and network.

qa.q: The Congress as a 'social coalition' means it:
qa.a: Brought together many classes, castes and communities
qa.e: It included peasants, industrialists, urban and rural people.

qa.q: The Congress as an 'ideological coalition' means it:
qa.a: Accommodated left, right and centre views
qa.e: Diverse ideas coexisted within it.

qa.q: Which group was part of the Congress's social base?
qa.a: Both peasants and industrialists
qa.e: Its base cut across classes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Congress was able to stay dominant for many years. Reason (R): It brought together diverse social groups and ideologies within one party.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its coalition character explains its long dominance.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Congress dominance in India was achieved by banning other parties. Reason (R): Many opposition parties contested the first three elections.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Groups within a political party are called:
qa.a: Factions
qa.e: Factions are internal groupings.

qa.q: How did factions in the Congress act?
qa.a: As an internal opposition
qa.e: They criticised and checked the leadership from within.

qa.q: What encouraged tolerance of factions within the Congress?
qa.a: Its coalition-like character
qa.e: Its broad character made room for differences.

qa.q: What did a faction unhappy with the Congress leadership usually do in this period?
qa.a: Stayed inside and tried to change the party
qa.e: Tolerance meant factions stayed and pushed from within.

qa.q: How did the factional system affect opposition parties?
qa.a: It made it harder for them to grow, since many concerns were voiced within the Congress
qa.e: The Congress absorbed many demands.

qa.q: Factions in the Congress were based on:
qa.a: Ideology or personal ambitions and rivalries
qa.e: Both ideas and personal rivalry created factions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Factions became a strength of the Congress system. Reason (R): They acted as an internal opposition, keeping the leadership in check.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains why factions were a strength.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Congress expelled every group that disagreed with its leaders. Reason (R): The Congress was tolerant of internal differences.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: The Congress Socialist Party was formed within the Congress in:
qa.e: It was formed in 1934; socialists left in 1948.

qa.q: Why did the socialists leave the Congress in 1948?
qa.a: The Congress barred dual party membership
qa.e: The ban on dual membership forced them to form a separate party.

qa.q: Which of these was a leader of the Socialist Party?
qa.a: Ram Manohar Lohia
qa.e: Lohia was a prominent socialist.

qa.q: Communist groups in India emerged in the early 1920s, inspired by:
qa.a: The Bolshevik revolution in Russia
qa.e: The 1917 revolution inspired them.

qa.q: Which of these was a leader of the CPI?
qa.a: A.K. Gopalan
qa.e: A.K. Gopalan was a leading communist.

qa.q: The CPI split and the CPI(M) was formed in:
qa.e: The split came in 1964.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The CPI was the largest opposition party in the first Lok Sabha. Reason (R): It won 16 seats in 1952, more than any other opposition party.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Jayaprakash Narayan was a leader of the Communist Party of India. Reason (R): Jayaprakash Narayan was a socialist leader.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was formed in:
qa.e: It was founded in 1951 with Syama Prasad Mookerjee as founder-president.

qa.q: Who was the founder-president of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh?
qa.a: Syama Prasad Mookerjee
qa.e: Mookerjee founded the Jana Sangh.

qa.q: The Swatantra Party was formed in:
qa.e: It was formed in August 1959.

qa.q: Which of these was a leader of the Swatantra Party?
qa.a: C. Rajagopalachari
qa.e: Rajagopalachari was its leading figure.

qa.q: The Swatantra Party was formed after the Congress's Nagpur resolution, which called for:
qa.a: Land ceilings, state trading in food grains and cooperative farming
qa.e: Its founders opposed these measures.

qa.q: Which economic policy did the Swatantra Party favour?
qa.a: A free-market economy with less government control
qa.e: It opposed state control and the licence system.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Opposition parties played an important role despite winning few seats. Reason (R): They offered principled criticism and kept the ruling party accountable.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains their importance.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Nehru's first cabinet after independence included only Congress members. Reason (R): B.R. Ambedkar and Syama Prasad Mookerjee were members of Nehru's first cabinet.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Why are development decisions called 'political'?
qa.a: They involve choices between groups with competing interests
qa.e: Development creates winners and losers, so it is contested.

qa.q: Which state is the book's example of debate over iron-ore mining and steel plants?
qa.a: Odisha
qa.e: Odisha has large iron-ore reserves.

qa.q: Why did tribal communities oppose some mining projects?
qa.a: They feared displacement and loss of livelihood
qa.e: Mining threatened their land and way of life.

qa.q: Environmentalists opposed mining projects mainly because of:
qa.a: Pollution and damage to forests
qa.e: Ecological damage was their worry.

qa.q: What did supporters of the steel plants argue?
qa.a: They would bring investment, jobs and growth
qa.e: Supporters stressed economic gains.

qa.q: The Odisha example shows that development:
qa.a: Raises questions of values and whose interests count
qa.e: Development choices are value-laden and contested.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Development projects are often contested in a democracy. Reason (R): Different groups gain and lose from the same project.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mining projects in Odisha were supported by everyone. Reason (R): Tribal communities feared displacement.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows the opposition.

qa.q: In the 1950s, 'development' was commonly understood as:
qa.a: Becoming modern like the industrialised countries
qa.e: Modernisation meant industrial growth on the Western pattern.

qa.q: The two models of development available at that time were:
qa.a: Liberal-capitalist and socialist
qa.e: The US and Soviet models were the two main options.

qa.q: The socialist model of development was followed by:
qa.a: The USSR
qa.e: The Soviet Union used central planning and state ownership.

qa.q: Which is a 'right' position on development?
qa.a: Free competition and a market economy with less state interference
qa.e: The right favours markets.

qa.q: Which is a 'left' position on development?
qa.a: Pro-poor policies and a strong state role to reduce inequality
qa.e: The left stresses the state's role in helping the poor.

qa.q: Did India copy either model of development completely?
qa.a: No, it combined elements of both
qa.e: India chose a mixed path.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many Indian leaders were attracted to the Soviet model. Reason (R): The Soviet Union had achieved rapid industrialisation through planning.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's leaders agreed that the state should play no role in development. Reason (R): Indian leaders debated how large the state's role should be.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: they agreed the state had a key role. R is true.

qa.q: The Bombay Plan of 1944 was drafted by:
qa.a: A group of big industrialists
qa.e: Industrialists proposed a planned economy.

qa.q: The Planning Commission was set up in:
qa.e: It was set up in March 1950.

qa.q: How was the Planning Commission set up?
qa.a: By a simple resolution of the Government of India
qa.e: It was neither constitutional nor statutory.

qa.q: Who was the chairperson of the Planning Commission?
qa.a: The Prime Minister
qa.e: The PM chaired it.

qa.q: The Planning Commission was replaced by:
qa.a: NITI Aayog
qa.e: NITI Aayog was set up in 2015.

qa.q: A Five Year Plan is:
qa.a: A government document setting income and spending priorities for five years
qa.e: It is a plan for the economy over five years.

qa.q: Assertion (A): There was broad agreement in India in favour of planning. Reason (R): Even big industrialists proposed a planned economy in the Bombay Plan.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R shows how widely planning was supported.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Planning Commission was created by the Constitution. Reason (R): The Planning Commission was an advisory body chaired by the Prime Minister.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it was set up by a government resolution. R is true.

qa.q: The main focus of the First Five Year Plan was:
qa.a: Agriculture, including dams and irrigation
qa.e: Agriculture had been hit by Partition and needed investment.

qa.q: Who argued that India should 'hasten slowly' in the first two decades?
qa.a: K.N. Raj
qa.e: K.N. Raj, a young economist, made this argument.

qa.q: The Second Five Year Plan was drafted under the leadership of:
qa.a: P.C. Mahalanobis
qa.e: Mahalanobis led the Second Plan's industrial strategy.

qa.q: The Second Five Year Plan stressed:
qa.a: Heavy industrialisation
qa.e: It emphasised rapid growth of heavy industry.

qa.q: The period of the First Five Year Plan was:
qa.e: The First Plan ran from 1951 to 1956.

qa.q: How did the government protect domestic industries under the Second Plan?
qa.a: By imposing substantial tariffs on imports
qa.e: Tariffs shielded domestic industry from foreign competition.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The First Plan gave priority to agriculture. Reason (R): Agriculture had been badly affected by Partition.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains the priority.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Second Plan focused mainly on agriculture and irrigation. Reason (R): P.C. Mahalanobis led the drafting of the Second Plan.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it focused on heavy industry. R is true.

qa.q: A mixed economy is one in which:
qa.a: Both public and private sectors exist
qa.e: India combined public and private sectors.

qa.q: Import substitution means:
qa.a: Producing goods at home that were earlier imported
qa.e: It aimed at self-reliance.

qa.q: In the planning era, which sector led in industries like steel and power?
qa.a: The public sector
qa.e: The state took the lead in key industries.

qa.q: Which was a criticism of planning from the right?
qa.a: The state controlled too much, creating a licence-permit system
qa.e: The right criticised excessive state control.

qa.q: Which was a criticism of planning from the left?
qa.a: The private sector and the rich gained too much while the poor gained little
qa.e: The left said benefits went disproportionately to the rich.

qa.q: Why were tariffs imposed on imports during the planning era?
qa.a: To protect domestic industries
qa.e: Tariffs supported import substitution.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India is described as having a mixed economy. Reason (R): Both the public sector and the private sector operated, with the state playing a key planning role.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India copied the Soviet economic model completely. Reason (R): India gave the public sector a leading role in key industries.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: India kept a private sector too. R is true.

qa.q: Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with the promotion of international peace and security?
qa.a: Article 51
qa.e: Article 51 is a Directive Principle on international peace.

qa.q: Article 51 belongs to which part of the Constitution?
qa.a: Directive Principles of State Policy
qa.e: It is a Directive Principle.

qa.q: Who was both the Prime Minister and the Foreign Minister of India from 1946 to 1964?
qa.a: Jawaharlal Nehru
qa.e: Nehru shaped foreign policy in both roles.

qa.q: Which was one of Nehru's three major foreign policy objectives?
qa.a: Preserving the country's sovereignty
qa.e: His goals were sovereignty, territorial integrity and rapid economic development.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT among the directions in Article 51?
qa.a: Join a military alliance with a superpower
qa.e: Article 51 says nothing about military alliances.

qa.q: India became independent in a world dominated by:
qa.a: The Cold War between the US and Soviet blocs
qa.e: The Cold War shaped the international context.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Nehru had a decisive influence on India's foreign policy. Reason (R): He served as both Prime Minister and Foreign Minister.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; holding both posts explains his influence.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Article 51 is enforceable in courts like a Fundamental Right. Reason (R): Article 51 is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Directive Principles are not enforceable in courts. R is true.

qa.q: The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement was held in:
qa.a: Belgrade, 1961
qa.e: The first NAM summit was in Belgrade in September 1961.

qa.q: Which leaders were co-founders of NAM with Nehru?
qa.a: Tito and Nasser
qa.e: Tito of Yugoslavia and Nasser of Egypt were co-founders.

qa.q: The Asian Relations Conference was held in New Delhi in:
qa.e: Nehru convened it in March 1947.

qa.q: The Bandung Conference (1955) was held in:
qa.a: Indonesia
qa.e: Bandung is in Indonesia.

qa.q: Non-alignment meant:
qa.a: Staying out of the military alliances of both blocs while taking independent positions
qa.e: It was an active, independent policy.

qa.q: Which statement about non-alignment is correct?
qa.a: It was not neutrality; India took active stands on issues like decolonisation
qa.e: Non-alignment was active engagement.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Bandung is seen as a step towards NAM. Reason (R): The Bandung Conference built solidarity among newly independent Afro-Asian nations.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the solidarity at Bandung paved the way for NAM.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Non-alignment meant that India stayed isolated from world politics. Reason (R): India played an active role in decolonisation and disarmament debates.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Panchsheel was signed in:
qa.e: Nehru and Zhou Enlai signed it on 29 April 1954.

qa.q: Who signed Panchsheel on behalf of China?
qa.a: Zhou Enlai
qa.e: Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai signed it with Nehru.

qa.q: Which of these is one of the five principles of Panchsheel?
qa.a: Mutual non-interference in each other's internal affairs
qa.e: Non-interference is one of the five principles.

qa.q: Panchsheel is about:
qa.a: Peaceful coexistence between states
qa.e: It sets out five principles of peaceful coexistence.

qa.q: The Dalai Lama sought political asylum in India in:
qa.e: He crossed into India in 1959 after a rebellion in Tibet.

qa.q: How did China react to India granting asylum to the Dalai Lama?
qa.a: It strongly objected, and relations worsened
qa.e: The asylum was a major strain on ties.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India-China relations worsened after 1959. Reason (R): India granted political asylum to the Dalai Lama, to which China strongly objected.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Panchsheel includes the principle of mutual non-aggression. Reason (R): Panchsheel was signed by India and Pakistan.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: it was signed by India and China.

qa.q: China invaded India's disputed border regions in:
qa.a: October 1962
qa.e: The invasion began in October 1962.

qa.q: Which Defence Minister had to leave the cabinet after the 1962 war?
qa.a: V.K. Krishna Menon
qa.e: Krishna Menon was blamed for unpreparedness.

qa.q: Which was a political consequence of the 1962 war in India?
qa.a: The first no-confidence motion against the Nehru government
qa.e: The defeat led to a no-confidence motion.

qa.q: The two disputed regions in the 1962 war were:
qa.a: Aksai Chin (Ladakh) and NEFA (now Arunachal Pradesh)
qa.e: China attacked in both these areas.

qa.q: Full diplomatic relations between India and China were restored in:
qa.e: Restoration came in 1976.

qa.q: Who visited China as External Affairs Minister in 1979?
qa.a: Atal Bihari Vajpayee
qa.e: Vajpayee visited in 1979.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 1962 war damaged Nehru's standing. Reason (R): India suffered a defeat after being unprepared for China's attack.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 1962 war had no effect on Indian domestic politics. Reason (R): Differences over China contributed to the CPI's split in 1964.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows a domestic effect.

qa.q: The Indus Waters Treaty was signed by Nehru and:
qa.a: General Ayub Khan
qa.e: Nehru and Ayub Khan signed it in 1960.

qa.q: The Tashkent Agreement was signed in:
qa.e: It was signed in January 1966.

qa.q: The Tashkent Agreement was brokered by:
qa.a: The Soviet Union
qa.e: Soviet mediation led to the agreement.

qa.q: Who was India's Prime Minister during the 1965 war?
qa.a: Lal Bahadur Shastri
qa.e: Shastri led India in 1965.

qa.q: In April 1965, Pakistan launched armed attacks in:
qa.a: The Rann of Kutch
qa.e: The first attacks were in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat.

qa.q: How did the 1947-48 Kashmir conflict end?
qa.a: With a ceasefire, after the issue was taken to the UN
qa.e: A UN-brokered ceasefire ended the fighting.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India and Pakistan cooperated on river waters despite their conflicts. Reason (R): The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960 with World Bank mediation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R shows the cooperation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 1965 war ended with the Shimla Agreement. Reason (R): The Tashkent Agreement was signed by Shastri and Ayub Khan.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: 1965 ended with Tashkent; Shimla followed 1971. R is true.

qa.q: The Shimla Agreement was signed by Indira Gandhi and:
qa.a: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto
qa.e: Bhutto was Pakistan's leader after the 1971 war.

qa.q: Why did lakhs of refugees flee to India in 1971?
qa.a: The Pakistani army cracked down on the people of East Pakistan
qa.e: The crackdown after the 1970 election caused a refugee flood.

qa.q: To counter the US-China-Pakistan axis in 1971, India signed a treaty with:
qa.a: The Soviet Union
qa.e: The 20-year Indo-Soviet treaty was signed in August 1971.

qa.q: The Shimla Agreement was signed in:
qa.e: It followed the 1971 war.

qa.q: Which of these is a sector where the 1999 Kargil conflict took place?
qa.a: Dras
qa.e: Mashkoh, Dras, Kaksar and Batalik saw fighting.

qa.q: Approximately how many refugees came to India from East Pakistan in 1971?
qa.a: 80 lakh
qa.e: About 80 lakh refugees fled to India.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India took the Bangladesh refugee crisis very seriously in 1971. Reason (R): About 80 lakh refugees had come to India, putting heavy pressure on its resources.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the scale of the crisis explains India's response.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 1971 war ended with the Tashkent Agreement. Reason (R): The Shimla Agreement was signed after the 1971 war.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Tashkent followed 1965. R is true.

qa.q: Who led India's atomic energy programme in its early years?
qa.a: Homi J. Bhabha
qa.e: Bhabha founded India's nuclear programme.

qa.q: India's first nuclear explosion took place in:
qa.e: It was in May 1974 at Pokhran.

qa.q: Why did India refuse to sign the NPT and the CTBT?
qa.a: It considers them discriminatory
qa.e: They allow existing nuclear powers to keep weapons.

qa.q: 'No first use' means that India will:
qa.a: Not be the first to use nuclear weapons in a conflict
qa.e: India's weapons are for retaliation and deterrence.

qa.q: Which is part of India's nuclear doctrine?
qa.a: Credible minimum nuclear deterrence
qa.e: India seeks a minimum credible deterrent.

qa.q: India conducted a series of nuclear tests in May:
qa.e: The 1998 tests were followed by Pakistan's tests.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India calls the NPT discriminatory. Reason (R): The NPT lets states that tested before 1967 keep their nuclear weapons while denying others the right.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Nehru supported the development of nuclear weapons by India. Reason (R): Nehru had great faith in science and technology.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Nehru opposed nuclear weapons. R is true.

qa.q: Who succeeded Nehru as Prime Minister in 1964?
qa.a: Lal Bahadur Shastri
qa.e: Shastri was chosen unanimously as leader.

qa.q: Who gave the slogan 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'?
qa.a: Lal Bahadur Shastri
qa.e: Shastri coined it during the 1965 war and food crisis.

qa.q: Shastri died suddenly in 1966 at:
qa.a: Tashkent
qa.e: He died soon after signing the Tashkent Agreement.

qa.q: In 1966, Indira Gandhi defeated which leader in the contest for the Congress leadership?
qa.a: Morarji Desai
qa.e: She won the secret ballot against Morarji Desai.

qa.q: The 'Syndicate' was:
qa.a: An informal group of senior Congress leaders who controlled the party organisation
qa.e: It included Kamaraj, Patil, Nijalingappa, Reddy and Atulya Ghosh.

qa.q: Who led the Syndicate as Congress President?
qa.a: K. Kamaraj
qa.e: Kamaraj, a former Chief Minister of Madras, was Congress President.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The transition after Nehru's death was smooth. Reason (R): Shastri was chosen unanimously as leader of the Congress parliamentary party.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the unanimous choice made the transition smooth.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indira Gandhi became Prime Minister without any contest. Reason (R): The Syndicate played a key role in choosing Prime Ministers after Nehru.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: she won a secret ballot against Morarji Desai. R is true.

qa.q: Who gave the strategy of 'non-Congressism'?
qa.a: Ram Manohar Lohia
qa.e: Lohia urged the opposition to unite against the Congress.

qa.q: The rupee was devalued in:
qa.e: Devaluation came in June 1966.

qa.q: Why was the 1967 election called a 'political earthquake'?
qa.a: The Congress lost power in many states and several big leaders were defeated
qa.e: The scale of the Congress setback surprised observers.

qa.q: Which regional party came to power in Madras in 1967?
qa.a: DMK
qa.e: The DMK won a clear majority.

qa.q: Which was part of the economic background to the 1967 election?
qa.a: Drought and serious food shortages
qa.e: The years before 1967 saw economic crisis.

qa.q: In 1967, the Congress lost its majority in how many states, with defections preventing it from forming governments in two more?
qa.e: Seven states plus two more due to defections, making nine non-Congress states.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 1967 elections were a setback for the Congress. Reason (R): The country was facing an economic crisis with drought, food shortages and rising prices.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the crisis explains the setback.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Congress lost its majority in the Lok Sabha in 1967. Reason (R): Half the ministers in Indira Gandhi's cabinet lost their seats.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the Congress kept a reduced majority. R is true.

qa.q: What does SVD stand for?
qa.a: Samyukta Vidhayak Dal
qa.e: SVD means joint legislature party.

qa.q: The phrase 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' is associated with:
qa.a: Frequent defections by legislators
qa.e: It describes legislators switching parties.

qa.q: Gaya Lal, whose name gave rise to the phrase 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram', was an MLA from:
qa.a: Haryana
qa.e: He changed parties three times in a fortnight in 1967.

qa.q: Defection means:
qa.a: An elected representative leaving the party on whose symbol he or she was elected and joining another
qa.e: It is switching party after election.

qa.q: The SVD government in Bihar included:
qa.a: Socialist parties, the CPI and the Jana Sangh
qa.e: It brought together left, socialist and right parties.

qa.q: Which state's coalition was called the 'Popular United Front'?
qa.a: Punjab
qa.e: Punjab's coalition included Akali groups, left parties and the Jana Sangh.

qa.q: Assertion (A): State governments formed after 1967 often fell. Reason (R): Frequent defections and ideological differences weakened coalitions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): All SVD coalitions were made of parties with the same ideology. Reason (R): The Bihar SVD included both the CPI and the Jana Sangh.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows the variety.

qa.q: Who was the official Congress candidate in the 1969 presidential election?
qa.a: N. Sanjeeva Reddy
qa.e: The Syndicate got Reddy nominated.

qa.q: Who won the 1969 presidential election?
qa.a: V.V. Giri
qa.e: Giri, an independent backed by Indira Gandhi, won.

qa.q: Indira Gandhi's call to Congress MPs and MLAs in the 1969 presidential election was for a:
qa.a: Conscience vote
qa.e: She asked them to vote according to their conscience.

qa.q: How many private banks were nationalised in July 1969?
qa.e: Fourteen leading private banks were nationalised.

qa.q: Who was removed as Finance Minister before the bank nationalisation?
qa.a: Morarji Desai
qa.e: Desai was removed and banks were nationalised.

qa.q: Which of these was in the Ten-Point Programme of 1967?
qa.a: Public distribution of food grains
qa.e: It aimed at a pro-poor agenda.

qa.q: Assertion (A): V.V. Giri won the 1969 presidential election. Reason (R): Indira Gandhi supported him and called for a conscience vote.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; her support and the conscience vote helped Giri win.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Syndicate and Indira Gandhi agreed on the presidential candidate in 1969. Reason (R): The Syndicate nominated N. Sanjeeva Reddy as the official candidate.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Indira Gandhi backed V.V. Giri. R is true.

qa.q: In 1969 the Congress split into:
qa.a: Congress (O) and Congress (R)
qa.e: O meant Organisation; R meant Requisitionists.

qa.q: 'Congress (R)' stood for:
qa.a: Requisitionists
qa.e: Indira Gandhi's faction was called the Requisitionists.

qa.q: Who expelled Indira Gandhi from the Congress in November 1969?
qa.a: Congress President S. Nijalingappa
qa.e: Nijalingappa, the party President, expelled her.

qa.q: Privy purses were:
qa.a: Grants given to former rulers of princely states
qa.e: They were promised at the time of integration.

qa.q: Why did the 1970 attempt to abolish privy purses fail?
qa.a: The constitutional amendment did not get the needed majority in the Rajya Sabha
qa.e: It failed in the Rajya Sabha.

qa.q: How did Indira Gandhi present the 1969 split?
qa.a: As an ideological struggle between socialists and conservatives
qa.e: She cast it as pro-poor versus pro-rich.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Congress split in 1969. Reason (R): The official Congress candidate lost the presidential election to a candidate backed by the Prime Minister.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the election defeat formalised the split.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Privy purses were abolished before the 1971 election. Reason (R): The Supreme Court struck down the order de-recognising the princes.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: they were abolished after the 1971 election. R is true.

qa.q: Indira Gandhi's slogan in the 1971 election was:
qa.a: Garibi hatao
qa.e: 'Garibi hatao' meant remove poverty.

qa.q: The 'Grand Alliance' of 1971 used the slogan:
qa.a: Indira hatao
qa.e: The opposition campaigned to remove Indira Gandhi.

qa.q: How many Lok Sabha seats did the Congress (R) alone win in 1971?
qa.e: The Congress (R) won 352 seats.

qa.q: How many seats did the Congress (O) win in 1971?
qa.e: The Congress (O) was badly defeated.

qa.q: Which event of December 1971 further boosted Indira Gandhi's popularity?
qa.a: Victory in the Bangladesh war
qa.e: The war victory raised her stature.

qa.q: How was the restored Congress different from the old Congress system?
qa.a: It depended heavily on the popularity of one leader
qa.e: Dominance now rested on Indira Gandhi's appeal.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Congress (R) won a sweeping victory in 1971. Reason (R): Indira Gandhi offered a positive programme with the slogan 'Garibi hatao'.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; her pro-poor programme helped her win.

qa.q: How many more seats did the Congress (R) win than the Congress (O) in 1971?
Who led the nationwide railway strike of 1974?
qa.a: George Fernandes
qa.e: Fernandes led the National Coordination Committee for Railwaymen's Struggle.

qa.q: Who gave the call for 'Total Revolution'?
qa.a: Jayaprakash Narayan
qa.e: JP called for Sampoorna Kranti.

qa.q: The Gujarat movement of 1974 was started by:
qa.a: Students protesting against price rise and corruption
qa.e: Students began protests in January 1974.

qa.q: On what condition did JP agree to lead the Bihar movement?
qa.a: It would be non-violent and not confined to Bihar
qa.e: JP insisted on non-violence and a national scope.

qa.q: Which international event in 1973 worsened India's economic situation?
qa.a: A sharp rise in oil prices
qa.e: Oil price rises fuelled inflation.

qa.q: Who went on an indefinite fast demanding fresh elections in Gujarat?
qa.a: Morarji Desai
qa.e: Desai's fast pressed for assembly elections.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Popular discontent grew in India in 1973-74. Reason (R): Prices rose sharply, and unemployment was high.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; economic hardship explains the discontent.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The railway strike of 1974 succeeded in all its demands. Reason (R): The government declared the railway strike illegal.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the strike was called off after twenty days. R is true.

qa.q: The Allahabad High Court declared Indira Gandhi's election invalid on:
qa.a: 12 June 1975
qa.e: The verdict came on 12 June 1975.

qa.q: Who filed the election petition against Indira Gandhi?
qa.a: Raj Narain
qa.e: Raj Narain, a socialist who contested against her in 1971, filed it.

qa.q: Which judge delivered the Allahabad High Court verdict of 1975?
qa.a: Justice Jagmohan Lal Sinha
qa.e: Justice Sinha set aside her election.

qa.q: In 1973, the government appointed Justice A.N. Ray as Chief Justice by:
qa.a: Superseding three senior judges
qa.e: The supersession was seen as an attack on judicial independence.

qa.q: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment (1973) held that:
qa.a: Parliament cannot change the basic structure of the Constitution
qa.e: Amendments are allowed, but not to the basic structure.

qa.q: What did the Supreme Court's partial stay of 24 June 1975 allow?
qa.a: Indira Gandhi could remain an MP but not take part in Lok Sabha proceedings
qa.e: It was a partial stay pending appeal.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The supersession of judges in 1973 was criticised. Reason (R): It set aside the convention of appointing the senior-most judge as Chief Justice.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains the criticism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Allahabad High Court upheld Indira Gandhi's election. Reason (R): Raj Narain had filed an election petition against her.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the court declared her election invalid. R is true.

qa.q: The Emergency was declared on:
qa.a: 25 June 1975
qa.e: It was proclaimed on the night of 25 June 1975.

qa.q: The 1975 Emergency was declared under:
qa.a: Article 352
qa.e: Article 352 provides for a national emergency.

qa.q: The ground cited for the 1975 Emergency was:
qa.a: Internal disturbance
qa.e: The 1975 proclamation cited internal disturbance.

qa.q: Which President proclaimed the Emergency in 1975?
qa.a: Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
qa.e: Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed was President in 1975.

qa.q: Which of these was a measure taken during the Emergency?
qa.a: Press censorship requiring prior approval
qa.e: Newspapers needed approval before publishing.

qa.q: In the ADM Jabalpur case (1976), the Supreme Court:
qa.a: Accepted that citizens could not move courts for habeas corpus during the Emergency
qa.e: The ruling was later widely criticised.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The government said the Emergency was needed. Reason (R): It argued that there was a threat of internal disturbance after the opposition's calls for protest.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R gives the government's stated reason.

qa.q: Assertion (A): During the Emergency, citizens could freely approach courts against detention. Reason (R): Preventive detention was widely used under laws like MISA.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the ADM Jabalpur ruling denied habeas corpus. R is true.

qa.q: Which organisations were banned during the Emergency?
qa.a: The RSS and the Jamaat-e-Islami
qa.e: The government banned organisations such as the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and the Jamaat-e-Islami, and did not allow protests or strikes.

qa.q: The 42nd Amendment was passed in:
qa.e: It was passed during the Emergency in 1976.

qa.q: Under the 42nd Amendment, the term of the Lok Sabha was changed from five years to:
qa.a: 6 years
qa.e: It was extended to six years.

qa.q: Who headed the commission that inquired into the Emergency's excesses?
qa.a: Justice J.C. Shah
qa.e: The Shah Commission was set up in May 1977.

qa.q: Which of these was an excess during the Emergency?
qa.a: Compulsory sterilisation drives
qa.e: Forced sterilisation was among the worst excesses.

qa.q: An amendment passed during the Emergency (the 39th, in 1975) declared that the elections of which office-holders could not be challenged in court?
qa.a: President, Vice-President and Prime Minister
qa.e: This amendment, passed after the Allahabad High Court verdict, put these elections beyond the courts. It was separate from the 42nd Amendment of 1976.

qa.q: The Shah Commission was appointed by:
qa.a: The Janata government in 1977
qa.e: The new government appointed it after the 1977 election.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Civil liberties suffered during the Emergency. Reason (R): Fundamental rights were in effect suspended and the press was censored.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 42nd Amendment strengthened the powers of the courts. Reason (R): The 42nd Amendment was passed in 1976.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it curbed the courts. R is true.

qa.q: The 44th Amendment changed the ground for a national emergency on internal grounds to:
qa.a: Armed rebellion
qa.e: 'Armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance'.

qa.q: The 44th Amendment was passed in:
qa.e: It was passed in 1978 by the Janata government.

qa.q: According to the 44th Amendment, the advice of the Council of Ministers to the President for proclaiming an emergency must be:
qa.a: In writing
qa.e: Written advice adds accountability.

qa.q: Which is a key lesson of the Emergency?
qa.a: It is extremely difficult to do away with democracy in India
qa.e: Democracy returned within about two years.

qa.q: What happened to civil liberties organisations after the Emergency?
qa.a: Many new ones emerged
qa.e: Awareness of civil liberties grew.

qa.q: Which ground was used in 1975 that was later considered too vague?
qa.a: Internal disturbance
qa.e: The vague ground was replaced in 1978.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'. Reason (R): The Emergency had shown that the earlier ground was vague and open to misuse.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Emergency strengthened the habit of obeying any order from the ruling party. Reason (R): The Emergency raised awareness of civil liberties.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it highlighted the need for officials to follow the law. R is true.

qa.q: Who became Prime Minister after the 1977 election?
qa.a: Morarji Desai
qa.e: Desai led the Janata government.

qa.q: How many Lok Sabha seats did the Congress win in 1977?
qa.e: The Congress was reduced to 154 seats.

qa.q: Which leader left the Congress in 1977 to form the Congress for Democracy?
qa.a: Jagjivan Ram
qa.e: Jagjivan Ram's party later merged with the Janata Party.

qa.q: The Congress returned to power in:
qa.e: Elections in January 1980 brought it back.

qa.q: Who formed a short-lived government after Morarji Desai's government fell?
qa.a: Charan Singh
qa.e: Charan Singh's government, formed with the promise of Congress support, lasted only a few months.

qa.q: Which was a legacy of the 1977 election?
qa.a: Rise of backward-class politics in north India
qa.e: The period saw growing political assertion of backward classes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Janata government did not last its full term. Reason (R): It lacked a common programme, and its leaders competed for the top post.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: By how many seats did the Janata Party and its allies outnumber the Congress in 1977?
The Indian approach to regional aspirations is to:
qa.a: Accommodate them through democratic means
qa.e: India uses negotiation and constitutional arrangements.

qa.q: Which of these was a major area of regional tension in India?
qa.a: The North-East
qa.e: J&K, Punjab and the North-East were key areas.

qa.q: India's view of unity is best described as:
qa.a: Unity with diversity, not uniformity
qa.e: Unity does not require uniformity.

qa.q: Which constitutional arrangement helps accommodate tribal regions?
qa.a: Autonomous councils
qa.e: Autonomous councils give tribal areas self-government.

qa.q: Regional demands in India have included:
qa.a: Autonomy, new states and, in a few cases, secession
qa.e: Demands varied widely.

qa.q: What is the aim of balancing regional diversity with national unity?
qa.a: To let regional aspirations strengthen rather than weaken democracy
qa.e: Accommodation keeps both unity and diversity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India has created new states in response to regional demands. Reason (R): The Indian approach accommodates regional aspirations through democratic means.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the democratic approach explains the creation of new states.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Every regional demand in India is anti-national. Reason (R): Regional aspirations are a part of democratic politics.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Who was the ruler of Jammu and Kashmir in 1947?
qa.a: Maharaja Hari Singh
qa.e: Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession.

qa.q: What were the three regions of Jammu and Kashmir?
qa.a: Jammu, the Kashmir valley and Ladakh
qa.e: These were the three regions of the state.

qa.q: In October 1947, why did the Maharaja ask India for military help?
qa.a: Tribal infiltrators sent from Pakistan were trying to capture Kashmir
qa.e: The invasion led him to seek help and sign the Instrument of Accession.

qa.q: Which party did Sheikh Abdullah lead?
qa.a: National Conference
qa.e: He led the National Conference.

qa.q: Which article gave Jammu and Kashmir special status?
qa.a: Article 370
qa.e: Article 370 gave greater autonomy.

qa.q: Sheikh Abdullah became Chief Minister after an agreement with Indira Gandhi in:
qa.e: The 1974 agreement brought him back.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India sent its army to Kashmir in 1947. Reason (R): The Maharaja signed the Instrument of Accession and asked for help against the infiltrators.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Maharaja Hari Singh wanted to join Pakistan in 1947. Reason (R): Pakistan claimed Kashmir.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: he wanted to join neither country at first. R is true.

qa.q: The existence of Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (POJK) is part of which dimension of the Kashmir issue?
qa.a: The external dispute between India and Pakistan
qa.e: POJK is the part of the state under Pakistan's occupation, so it belongs to the external dispute. The internal dimension is about the state's status and demands for autonomy within India.

qa.q: When were the provisions of Article 370 giving special status to Jammu and Kashmir abrogated?
qa.a: 5 August 2019
qa.e: Parliament acted on 5 August 2019.

qa.q: Into which Union Territories was Jammu and Kashmir reorganised in 2019?
qa.a: Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh
qa.e: The Reorganisation Act created two UTs.

qa.q: Which coalition formed the government in Jammu and Kashmir after the 2002 election?
qa.a: PDP and Congress
qa.e: Mufti Mohammad Sayeed led a PDP-Congress coalition.

qa.q: Many people questioned the fairness of which assembly election in Jammu and Kashmir?
qa.e: Many believed the 1987 results did not reflect popular choice.

qa.q: Which community was displaced from the Kashmir valley due to militant violence?
qa.a: Kashmiri Pandits
qa.e: Kashmiri Pandits had to leave the valley.

qa.q: Which law reorganised Jammu and Kashmir in 2019?
qa.a: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019
qa.e: The 2019 Act created two Union Territories.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Jammu and Kashmir saw years of President's rule in the 1990s. Reason (R): A militant movement had grown in the state from 1989.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the militancy explains the period of President's rule.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Jammu and Kashmir remained a state with special status after 2019. Reason (R): Under the 2019 Reorganisation Act, Ladakh became a Union Territory.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: special status ended and the state became two UTs. R is true.

qa.q: The Anandpur Sahib Resolution was passed in:
qa.e: The Akali Dal passed it in 1973.

qa.q: The Anandpur Sahib Resolution mainly asserted:
qa.a: Regional autonomy and redefinition of centre-state relations
qa.e: It was a call for greater autonomy.

qa.q: Operation Blue Star took place in:
qa.a: June 1984
qa.e: The army operation was in June 1984.

qa.q: Who signed the Punjab Accord with Rajiv Gandhi in 1985?
qa.a: Harchand Singh Longowal
qa.e: Longowal was the Akali Dal president.

qa.q: Indira Gandhi was assassinated on:
qa.a: 31 October 1984
qa.e: She was killed by her bodyguards on 31 October 1984.

qa.q: Punjab was reorganised, with Haryana carved out and the hill areas merged with Himachal Pradesh, in:
qa.e: The Punjabi Suba demand was met in 1966.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Punjab was reorganised in 1966, and Haryana was carved out of it. Reason (R): The Akali Dal had led a movement for a Punjabi Suba.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the Punjabi Suba movement led to the 1966 reorganisation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Normalcy returned to Punjab by the mid-1990s. Reason (R): Elections and democratic politics were restored after years of violence.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; restoring democratic politics helped bring normalcy.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of the 'seven sisters'?
qa.a: Sikkim
qa.e: The seven sisters are Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura.

qa.q: Who led the Mizo National Front?
qa.a: Laldenga
qa.e: Laldenga led the MNF and later became Chief Minister.

qa.q: The Mizoram Accord was signed in:
qa.e: Rajiv Gandhi and Laldenga signed it in 1986.

qa.q: Who led the Naga movement and declared independence on 14 August 1947?
qa.a: Angami Zapu Phizo
qa.e: Phizo led the Naga National Council.

qa.q: Nagaland became a state in:
qa.e: Nagaland was created in 1963.

qa.q: The North-East is linked to the rest of India by a narrow corridor about:
qa.a: 22 km wide
qa.e: The corridor is about 22 km wide.
